3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.title: SMS_F2014_11
3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.frame: Rolling at half speed but four strands at once doubles productivity. Brief callback from prior lecture.

3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.title: SMS_F2014_10
3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.frame: Gordon Forward (MIT graduate, Canadian) at Chaparral. Mandatory week-per-year with the salesman discovers 20-30% premium on 3/8 inch rebar. First attempt: roll faster — instabilities, maimed workers. Second attempt: slow down and split the bar — one in, two out, then one in, four out. Took over the 3/8 inch market with quality gains as a bonus.
3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.case_name: Chaparral Steel 3/8 inch rebar productivity case

3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.title: SMS_F2013_07
3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.frame: Chaparral cannot run rolling mill faster than 60 mph (instabilities at 70). Solution: run slower, split into two strands, then four. Doubles productivity; takes over the 3/8" rebar premium market.
3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.case_name: 3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity case

3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.title: MSE_F2016_11
3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.frame: Tom's worked example within the Chaparral story — the #3 rebar premium and the four-strand discovery (run slower, split more times, double productivity).

3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.title: SMS_S2016_11
3/8 inch rebar rolling mill productivity.frame: The specific Chaparral product/market discovery: smallest-diameter rebar carried a price premium because rolling speed bottleneck; Chaparral solved by splitting strands rather than accelerating.

Boeing door product center.frame: ~$50,000 per fuselage door derived from $150K sales-per-employee × 750 employees ÷ 250 doors. Cost accountants didn't know the per-door cost. Hand-drilled rivet holes drive labor share.

Nucor/Chaparral mini-mill competitive ch.frame: Iverson's strip-mall start in Charlotte, NC; built mill in South Carolina; mini mill capital cost ($25–50M) vs integrated BOF shop ($1B); progression from 50-ton to 165-ton electric furnace heats.

Bethlehem Steel and Burns Harbor.frame: Burns Harbor (1965) as the last new integrated mill before the mini mill era. Bethlehem culture: stratified executive dining room, "Taj Mahal" research labs, manual of permitted internal correspondence, rules about who could have carpet or drapes.

Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.title: SMS_F2014_11
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.frame: Cultural counterpoint to Bethlehem: blame attaches to *not* trying new things; weekly profit posted on bulletin board; profit-sharing; folding-table "executive dining room." Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.case_name: Gordon Forward and the Chaparral culture

Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.title: SMS_F2013_05
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.frame: The mini-mill founder figure. Tom names Forward as the most successful mini-mill builder, though he attributes him to Nucor rather than Chaparral.
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.case_name: Gordon Forward mini mill competition strategy

Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.title: SMS_F2013_07
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.frame: Gordon Forward (1975 MIT 3-department graduate) founds Chaparral Steel in Texas. Tom recurringly slips and calls him "Gordon Forward."
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.case_name: Gordon Forward mini mill competition strategy

Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.title: DP_S2012_06
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.frame: Gordon Forward's economic insight: scrap steel at $100/ton vs. $200/ton blast-furnace cast iron gave mini mills a $100/ton advantage on a $300–400/ton product. Forward was on the MIT DMSE visiting committee during Tom's department headship.
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.case_name: Gordon Forward mini mill competition strategy

Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.title: MSE_F2016_11
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.frame: Forward's $30/ton-labor-vs-Japanese-shipping-cost rule; profit sharing; "what have you done for me lately" culture; corporate-dining-room asceticism.
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.case_name: Gordon Forward mini mill competition strategy

Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.title: SMS_S2016_11
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.frame: Gordon E. Forward (MIT, student of John Elliott who was student of John Chipman) as president of Chaparral Steel. Sent mill workers with salesmen to customers. Discovered the 3/8" rebar price premium and the split-rolling innovation: split bar in two then four through the rolling mill, halving speed but doubling productivity.
Gordon Forward mini mill competition str.case_name: Gordon Forward mini mill competition strategy

Ford Motor Company executive dining room.title: SMS_F2014_11
Ford Motor Company executive dining room.frame: Sirloin-into-grinder anecdote illustrating opacity of corporate cost vs perceived quality. Paired with Bethlehem dining room as foil to Chaparral.
Ford Motor Company executive dining room.case_name: Ford executive dining room hamburger (Iacocca anecdote)

Ford Motor Company executive dining room.title: DP_S2012_06

Ford Motor Company executive dining room.case_name: Ford Motor Company executive dining room hamburger story

Sleepy Hollow Glass bullseye demonstrati.title: SMS_F2014_11
Sleepy Hollow Glass bullseye demonstrati.frame: Historical: untaxed scrap glass over door lintels for light without windows; today: art glass at $55 for a 6-inch square. Pricing inversion (scrap → art).
Sleepy Hollow Glass bullseye demonstrati.case_name: Sleepy Hollow Glass and bullseye glass economics

Sango Bath (Saint-Gobain) founding and l.title: SMS_F2014_11
Sango Bath (Saint-Gobain) founding and l.frame: Abraham Thévart, 1688, pours glass on metal table, rollers, anneal, grind, polish. Saint-Gobain provides windows and mirrors to Versailles. French trade secret in stirring molten glass (Guinand 1798, perfected 1805) holds for ~100 years before British acquire it. MIT departmental tie: alum Kapoor ran Saint-Gobain Northborough research center; funds MadMec.

Sango Bath (Saint-Gobain) founding and l.title: SMS_S2016_12
Sango Bath (Saint-Gobain) founding and l.frame: Origin (1688) as a mirror-glass maker pouring molten glass onto plates and polishing with corundum. Used to make the long-time-horizon company-strategy point; contrasted with U.S. firms of which only five of the 1900 top 100 survived to 2000. Tom's former student is among Saint-Gobain's top 100 managers.

Sango Bath (Saint-Gobain) founding and l.title: SMS_F2013_03
Sango Bath (Saint-Gobain) founding and l.frame: Opener for the long-term-economics framing. Saint-Gobain's 400-year history and "will we be in business 100 years from now" decision criterion is contrasted with the 95% mortality rate of 1900-era top-100 US companies.
Sango Bath (Saint-Gobain) founding and l.case_name: Sango Bath (Saint-Gobain) founding and long-term strategy

Pittsburgh Plate Glass (PPG) mile-long b.title: SMS_F2014_11
Pittsburgh Plate Glass (PPG) mile-long b.frame: Turn-of-20th-century Pittsburgh facility: cast at one end, grind and polish moving straight (glass is brittle, can't be turned), exit as plate glass typically ½" or thicker. Now superseded by float glass, but PPG remains active.

Ford Motor Company and Libby Owens Ford.title: SMS_F2014_11
Ford Motor Company and Libby Owens Ford.frame: Continuous ribbon production invented at Ford 1920; in production by 1926 (glass over weir from tank furnace). Pilkington Brothers commercialized; developed continuous grinding-polishing by 1925. Motivated by Model T / Model A windshield demand.
Ford Motor Company and Libby Owens Ford.case_name: Libbey-Owens-Ford / Ford Motor Company continuous ribbon glass

Ford Motor Company and Libby Owens Ford.title: SMS_S2016_12
Ford Motor Company and Libby Owens Ford.frame: 1920s continuous-pour plate-glass process developed by Henry Ford with Libby-Owens-Ford for mass automobile production. Intermediate step between Pittsburgh Plate Glass and the Pilkington float process.
Ford Motor Company and Libby Owens Ford.case_name: Ford Motor Company and Libby-Owens-Ford continuous plate glass

Pilkington float glass process.title: SMS_F2014_11
Pilkington float glass process.frame: Post-WWII development; molten tin bath, 15 ft wide, few inches deep; pull thin glass (⅛" to ¼") off; anneal and cut. Footprint reduced from mile-long PPG building to ~couple hundred yards. Tom toured an Ohio float glass plant; furnace at 1550°C, half a football field.

Pilkington float glass process.title: SMS_F2013_05
Pilkington float glass process.frame: Pilkington's 1920s development of floating molten glass on tin to eliminate the half-mile polishing line used by Pittsburgh Plate Glass. Tom's example of how a process innovation can collapse manufacturing cost.
Pilkington float glass process.case_name: Corning float glass dual-surface manufacturing / Pilkington float glass process

Pilkington float glass process.title: SMS_S2016_12
Pilkington float glass process.frame: Sir Alastair Pilkington, 1953–1957: continuous pour onto molten tin bath, natural-gas atmosphere, replaces the mile-long polishing line. The defining modern process. Also: Pilkington's earlier (~1900) wire-mesh laminated glass.

Pilkington float glass process.title: DP_S2012_12
Pilkington float glass process.frame: Referenced as background covered in casting lectures.

Jenna Germany historical window.title: SMS_F2014_11
Jenna Germany historical window.frame: 200-year-old plate glass window with visible chemical-inhomogeneity distortion; modern replacement pane (float glass) in same frame shows undistorted reflection. Used to illustrate pre-stirring vs post-stirring glass quality.

Jenna Germany historical window.title: SMS_S2016_12
Jenna Germany historical window.frame: Visual aid: an old European window of bullseye-derived glass with one corner pane replaced by modern undistorted glass, illustrating the historical transition.
Jenna Germany historical window.case_name: Jena/Germany old window with replaced corner pane

Corning trade-secret manufacturing cultu.title: SMS_F2014_11
Corning trade-secret manufacturing cultu.frame: Highest-security site Tom has ever entered (NDAs, no cameras, Corning takes/reviews/sends pictures). Inbred ceramics workforce that moves to Alfred University in retirement. Two 1970s product lines: incandescent light bulb envelopes and TV cathode ray tubes. Losing CRT business spawned new businesses including LCD substrate glass.

Corning ultra-thin slim glass for LCDs.title: SMS_F2014_11
Corning ultra-thin slim glass for LCDs.frame: 0.3 mm thick (12 thousandths of an inch), available in 1.5 × 1.8 m sheets. Fusion-drawn alkaline-earth boroaluminosilicate. Melting furnace nozzle and tube made of platinum (~$10M of platinum per furnace).
Corning ultra-thin slim glass for LCDs.case_name: Corning ultra-thin slim glass for LCDs

Liquid crystal display glass-stack archi.title: SMS_F2014_11
Liquid crystal display glass-stack archi.frame: Six-layer build: polarizing film / glass substrate with indium tin oxide / twisted nematic liquid crystal / second glass substrate with ITO / polarizing film / reflective or backlit rear surface. Aside on indium tin oxide as a rare conductive-transparent material; "transparent aluminum is only on Star Trek."

Glass fiber humidity degradation in fibe.title: SMS_F2014_11
Glass fiber humidity degradation in fibe.frame: Freshly pulled E-glass (aluminum borosilicate): 600–700 ksi tensile. One hour later: 500 ksi. Next day: 400 ksi. Month later: brittle. Hence epoxy-coat within 24 hours for fiberglass. Critical flaw size from Ashby fracture-toughness plot: ~10⁻⁴ mm, i.e. tens of angstroms — only modest surface etching is needed.
Glass fiber humidity degradation in fibe.case_name: Glass water-vapor corrosion (E-glass fiber strength decay)

Glass fiber humidity degradation in fibe.title: MSE_F2016_11
Glass fiber humidity degradation in fibe.frame:
fresh glass fibers as strong as steel; must be plastic-coated within one to two hours or humidity attack creates surface flaws and ruins strength.

Optical fiber manufacturing (Corning).title: SMS_F2014_11
Optical fiber manufacturing (Corning).frame: Silicon tetrachloride flame-sprayed on a starting rod; graded composition for graded index of refraction; drawn into miles of fiber. Drying step removes moisture (hydroxide formation degrades optical properties).

Optical fiber manufacturing (Corning).title: AM_F2019_04
Optical fiber manufacturing (Corning).frame: Lead case for the "real innovations" tour. Flame-vapor-deposited preform, drawn into ten-thousand-mile fibers. Solved New York City's late-1970s copper-wire crisis.

Optical fiber manufacturing (Corning).title: DP_S2012_12
Optical fiber manufacturing (Corning).frame: Functionally graded glass rod made by plasma-spraying glass frit on a lathe, then dieless-drawn using a temperature gradient as the "die". Exploits glass's Newtonian behavior (m = 1).

Optical fiber manufacturing (Corning).title: SMS_F2013_08
Optical fiber manufacturing (Corning).frame: Corning's optical fiber breakthrough — kept Corning in business; transformed transatlantic data transmission from repeater-every-10-km to no-repeater.

Attleboro gold alloy and casting operati.title: CAS_Su2011_01
Attleboro gold alloy and casting operati.frame: Tom's late-1970s consulting at the Attleboro gold-stock manufacturer; used to make the "time dominates cost" point — gold processing throughput was constrained by interest cost on the bullion, not by manufacturing cost.

Attleboro gold alloy and casting operati.title: DP_S2012_06

Tom installed a gold welding machine sourced from a one-man Steamboat Springs machine shop. Used here to set up the die-design redesign story (next entry).
Attleboro gold alloy and casting operati.case_name: Attleboro gold alloy and casting operations

Attleboro gold alloy and casting operati.title: CAS_Su2011_05
Attleboro gold alloy and casting operati.frame: The two continuous casters at the Attleboro firm that uses more gold than any company in the country. Drives home why continuous casting pays even for short runs when the metal is precious. Connects to the US Mint Sacagawea-dollar contract.
Attleboro gold alloy and casting operati.case_name: Attleboro gold alloy and casting operations

The 1558 law forbade felling trees for iron-making but exempted the Weald of Kent — Tom's example of how "even the lobbyists worked back in 1558." Saugus Ironworks.title: SMS_F2013_05
Saugus Ironworks.frame: New England blast furnace built in the 1630s to solve Britain's energy crisis by exporting iron from a region that still had forests. The structural answer to the 1558 law.

Saugus Ironworks.title: SMS_F2014_10
Saugus Ironworks.frame: Established 1620s in response to English wood shortage. Failed within 10-20 years. Iron industry migrated to Chesapeake Bay (Northeast Forge 1735, principal forge 1724) for water power.

Saugus Ironworks.title: SMS_S2016_12
Saugus Ironworks.frame: Time-marker — "the days of Saugus Ironworks" — to date the bullseye-glass era to the early 17th century.

Saugus Ironworks.title: SMS_F2014_04
Saugus Ironworks.frame: Productivity baseline — hand-forged, 3,000+ hours per ton.

Saugus Ironworks.title: WM_S2014_02
Saugus Ironworks.frame: Used twice — first to anchor the historical practice of mixing charcoal with iron ore, then as the physical site Tom walks the class through (the shaft furnace, the sand-floor pig-iron casting, the bellows and water wheel). The Saugus furnace is the central physical referent of §8.

Saugus Ironworks.title: MSE_F2016_09
Saugus Ironworks.frame: Early-American blast furnace; used as the baseline productivity datum (~3000 person-hours/ton circa 1600) in the productivity curve at §10.

Saugus Ironworks.title: WM_Su2014_11
Saugus Ironworks.frame: The historical baseline for steel productivity (4,000 person-hours/ton) and for early American cast iron production (frying pans, kettles, hand-forged nails).

Saugus Ironworks.title: SMS_F2014_03
Saugus Ironworks.frame: New England answer to the British wood shortage — they came to the colonies and built it in the 1620s because we had lots of trees.

Saugus Ironworks.title: WM_Su2015_03
Saugus Ironworks.frame: 1630s wrought iron production, illustrating the inefficient pre-Bessemer process of heating, reheating, and oxidizing carbon out.
Saugus Ironworks.case_name: Saugus Iron Works wrought iron production

Saugus Ironworks.title: WM_Su2014_09
Saugus Ironworks.frame: Recommended Saugus, Massachusetts national park visit. Saugus Ironworks brought over from England as part of the cast-iron industry relocation driven by the English wood shortage.

Saugus Ironworks.title: WM_S2014_03
Saugus Ironworks.frame: Origin of "pig iron" terminology (sow bar casting bed); 1630s establishment driven by England's wood-charcoal energy crisis; America's natural resource was trees. Used as a historical lead-in to why we have cast iron vs. steel.

Saugus Ironworks.title: MSE_F2017_06
Saugus Ironworks.frame: ~1600s. One person-year per ton of steel produced — the baseline anchor for Tom's productivity chart. Manual charcoaling, manual ore mining, manual limestone, 60-hour weeks.

Saugus Ironworks.title: SMS_S2016_04
Saugus Ironworks.frame: Seventeenth-century energy externality. England's wood crisis (cannon iron, masts, window glass all charcoal-fueled) drove the founding of Jamestown glassworks and Saugus Ironworks. "The energy crisis of 1973 was not the first energy crisis."

Saugus Ironworks.title: SMS_S2016_11
Saugus Ironworks.frame: First American iron mill (Saugus, MA, 1642–1688). Used bog iron and oyster-shell flux. Eight tons per week. Failed by 1688 from litigation and timber depletion. National Historical Site.

Saugus Ironworks.title: MSE_F2017_05
Saugus Ironworks.frame: First cast-iron foundry in the United States, with waterwheel-driven bellows reaching the 1150°C needed to melt cast iron. Anchors the productivity-revolution arc that closes the lecture (3,000 person-hours per ton at Saugus vs. 20 minutes today).

USS Constitution (Old Ironsides).title: SMS_F2013_05
USS Constitution (Old Ironsides).frame: Materials selection example — white oak (probably live white oak) from North Carolina. Tom uses it to make the point that you "selected different woods for different applications," and that the same oak is still in demand today for *Mayflower II* restoration and Navy minesweeper construction.

HMS Victory (Nelson's flagship).title: SMS_F2013_05
HMS Victory (Nelson's flagship).frame: 2100 tons of wood per ship — datum supporting the argument that warship construction was consuming forests at the same rate as the iron industry.

HMS Victory (Nelson's flagship).title: SMS_F2014_03
HMS Victory (Nelson's flagship).frame: 2,100 tons of oak in the final ship; "probably took two or three times that for all the shavings."

Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.case_name: Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Austria

Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.title: SMS_F2014_04
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.frame: Linz, Austria, 1958 commercial trial; mid-60s commercialization. Part of the productivity-revolution catalog.
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.case_name: Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Austria

Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.title: SMS_F2013_07
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.frame: 1956 Austrian innovation after Allied bombing destroyed open-hearth capacity. Origin story of the BOF.
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.case_name: Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Austria

Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.title: MSE_F2016_09
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.frame: Post-WWII Austrians, lacking capital to compete with US Big Steel, innovate the BOF using liquefied oxygen (a German WWI-era process); make 300 tons in 20 minutes vs. open-hearth 450 tons in 24 hours.
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.case_name: Linz, Austria basic oxygen furnace development

Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.title: CAS_Su2011_03
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.frame: 1958 Austrian innovation: supersonic oxygen jet replaces 24-hour Open Hearth cycle with 45-minute cycle for the same 300-ton heat. Productivity revolution between 1965 and 1980.
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.case_name: Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Austria

Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.title: WIE_F2015_06
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.frame: LD firm in Austria, 1950s. Switched from air to pure oxygen blowing. Cycle time fell from 24 hours / 400 tons (open hearth) to 1 hour, now 20 minutes / 300 tons. Tom's productivity-revolution headline example.
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.case_name: Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Austria

Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.title: SMS_S2016_11
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.frame: Post-WWII Austrian innovation: water-cooled copper lance, supersonic oxygen jet, 20–30 minute refining vs. 24 hours for open hearth. The productivity revolution that displaced Andrew Carnegie's basic open-hearth furnaces.
Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Aus.case_name: Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Austria

Continuous casting and steel industry ca.title: CAS_Su2011_01
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.case_name: Continuous casting and steel industry capacity collapse

Continuous casting and steel industry ca.title: SMS_F2013_05
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.frame: The core teaching case of the lecture. Tom contrasts ingot casting (sixty-seven percent yield at Bethlehem Steel in the mid-1980s) with continuous casting (ninety-five percent yield), explains the 1968 Armco Steel decision to install ingot casters anyway, and frames the late-1970s retrofits as the moment US steel managers finally accepted what they should have known a decade earlier.
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.case_name: Continuous casting and steel industry capacity collapse

Continuous casting and steel industry ca.title: SMS_F2013_06
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.frame: 1970s continuous casting raised yield from 65% to 97%, creating 30% global overcapacity, collapsing prices, leading mills to scrap rather than resell.
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.case_name: Continuous casting and steel industry capacity collapse

Continuous casting and steel industry ca.title: SMS_F2014_04
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.frame: Today ~97% yield via continuous casting; eight-story-tall plants pouring I-beams via a curved water-cooled copper mold, cut to length with oxygen torches (no fuel gas needed). Tom uses a photograph as a teaching aid. Lineage note: gold and copper were continuously cast decades before steel.
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.case_name: Continuous casting and steel industry capacity collapse

Continuous casting and steel industry ca.title: SMS_F2013_07
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.frame: Technical exposition of the continuous caster — tundish, water-cooled copper mold, breakout risk, copper-check defect on startup.
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.case_name: Continuous casting and steel industry capacity collapse

Continuous casting and steel industry ca.title: DP_S2012_06
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.frame: Yield jumped from 65% (ingot casting) to 97% (continuous casting) over 1965–1985. Effective capacity grew 50% with no capital expansion. Overcapacity drove price competition that nearly bankrupted the integrated mills. Tom's "be careful what you wish for" — disruptive productivity gains were painful for incumbents.
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.case_name: Continuous casting and steel industry capacity collapse

Continuous casting and steel industry ca.title: MSE_F2016_09
Continuous casting and steel industry ca.frame: Continuous casting raises buy-to-fly ratio from 65% (ingot) to 97%; another billion-dollar process innovation the integrated US producers were slow to adopt. Bethlehem and Armco both put in ingot casting at greenfield mills then had to rip it out within a decade.

Boeing 747-400 catalytic converter titan.title: WM_Su2014_34
Boeing 747-400 catalytic converter titan.frame: Engelhard contracted to weld thin-walled titanium ducting for ozone catalytic converters on the 747-400. Boeing's spec required no flaws larger than ten thousandths of an inch on x-ray. They were failing one out of two welds. Tom diagnosed contamination from commercial-grade acetone and fingerprint oils; reagent-grade acetone and white gloves got them to ninety percent. Problem recurred when they slipped back to old process. **Central case of §5.**

Boeing 747-400 catalytic converter titan.title: CS_Su2012_05
Boeing 747-400 catalytic converter titan.frame: Engelhard was building a titanium catalytic converter (for cabin-air ozone removal) for the 747-400 long-haul jet, replacing a stainless steel design to save weight. Boeing's spec disallowed any flaw larger than 10 thousandths of an inch — about four human hairs — which Tom shows was a CYA spec written by someone who set acceptance criteria at the limit of x-ray detectability rather than at any engineering-based size. With a 50% reject rate on four required welds and one repair allowed, statistics doomed throughput. Tom's diagnosis: 55-gallon-drum acetone left an oil film causing hydrogen porosity; switching to reagent-grade acetone dropped rejects from 50% to 10%. Engelhard reverted to old practice twice and had to be re-told three times.

Soviet titanium submarine (Alpha-class).frame: Tom traces the full arc: the 1980 *International Herald Tribune* announcement that caught the U.S. Navy flat-footed; the thirty-year prior U.S. Navy titanium program at David Taylor (welding 1–4 inch titanium since the 1950s); the Naval Research Lab's identification of creep-fatigue interaction as the Achilles heel; Tom's 1980 visit to the Paton Institute under the Carter-era U.S.–Soviet electrometallurgy exchange, where he spent two hours with Gurevich (Mr. Titanium, who had stopped publishing in 1972 when Alpha design began); the discovery that the Soviets never solved creep-fatigue and the subs cracked and became acoustically detectable within three years; and the Reagan administration's slamming of the exchange door. The case carries the lecture's deepest teaching: that the U.S. Navy's caution was vindicated, one titanium sub costs ten steel subs, and Congress later zeroed Millard Firebaugh's SSN-21 budget in pursuit of composite submarines.

1980 technical exchange with Soviet weld.title: WM_Su2015_17
1980 technical exchange with Soviet weld.frame: Carter-era exchange program; first delegation of 30 American scientists, then 8, then 2. Tom is one of the final 2, accompanying Julius Szekely. Two-hour interview with Gurevich at Paton Institute in Kiev. KGB surveillance.

This was simultaneously the public disclosure of the Alpha sub and the moment Tom's heavy-section titanium welding work (begun 1977 under ONR funding) became urgently relevant.

1980 technical exchange with Soviet weld.title: WM_Su2014_14
1980 technical exchange with Soviet weld.frame: Extended travelogue/case sequence. Tom's 1980 visit to the Paton Welding Institute in Kiev. Two specific demonstrations: (a) underwater wet welding electrodes producing weld quality unattainable in the West, later licensed (Tom suspects) to Broco; (b) titanium welding under Gurevich, the welding expert who taught the Soviets to weld the Alpha submarine.

Tom's two-hour interview with Gurevich at the Soviet welding institute, conducted in front of Mariinsky the KGB minder, established that the Soviets had abandoned gas metal arc welding for titanium and were using electroslag and semi-submerged GTA — technology the US Navy was still chasing.

Deep TIG (Deep Gas Tungsten Arc) develop.frame: Gurevich's semi-submerged arc / deep-TIG technique: half-millimeter painted flux layer on top surface enables deep penetration via surface-tension-driven convection (Marangoni). Ken Mills at National Physical Lab hypothesized mechanism for stainless. Tom and Szekely modeled it in 1983, award-winning paper.

Deep TIG (Deep Gas Tungsten Arc) develop.title: WM_Su2014_33
Deep TIG (Deep Gas Tungsten Arc) develop.frame: The Soviets' "semi-submerged arc" was what the US now calls deep TIG. With a thin fluoride flux (calcium / strontium / sodium fluoride), gas tungsten arc at 1,000–2,000 amps with a quarter-inch tungsten electrode can weld 1.5–2 inch titanium in horizontal position in four passes. Navy funded EWI / Ohio State; sort-of works in aluminum and steel; really works in titanium.
Deep TIG (Deep Gas Tungsten Arc) develop.case_name: Deep TIG (Deep Gas Tungsten Arc) development for thick-section horizontal welding

Naval shipyard X-ray inspection ineffici.frame: The closing teaching beat. Around 1996–97, NAVSEA permitted UT (ultrasonic testing) as an alternative to radiography; commercial shipyards (Electric Boat, David Taylor, Bath, Ingalls) all converted within a year. Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill th.title: WM_Su2014_35
Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill th.frame: Tom's graduate student Julie investigates thickness variation on hot-rolled aluminum plate at Alcoa's Davenport, Iowa works. Diagnosis: the deliberately mismatched roll speeds (to give the plate slight upward curvature and keep it from cobbling into the mill bed) create a water-pooling cup at the slower end. Film-boiling heat transfer at the cooled end explains 80% of measured thickness variation. Proposed fix: a compressed-air "air knife" to blow standing water off the plate after each pass. Cost: ~$10,000 in piping; the compressed air infrastructure is already in place. Payback: one scrapped plate. Owen Richmond (head of metal forming, Alcoa Research) personally promises to see it implemented. A year later: not done. Tom uses this as his closing parable for "the way it's done in American industry."
Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill th.case_name: Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill thickness variation

Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill th.title: WM_Su2014_34
Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill th.frame: Tom's LFM (Leaders for Manufacturing) student Julie diagnosed the world's largest rolling mill's biggest reject category — plate thickness variation — by ultrasonic survey instead of single-point micrometer measurement. Pattern showed thickening at plate ends; cause traced to water pooling at one end because the top roll ran slightly slower than the bottom roll. **Central case of §8.**
Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill th.case_name: Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill thickness variation

Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill th.title: DP_S2012_02
Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill th.frame: Closing anecdote on the limits of deformation-process tolerance for thick aluminum plate (2–4 inch). Tom's LFM student "Julie" diagnosed a 5–10% thickness variation that was causing wing-plate scrap rejection; Alcoa never implemented the fix despite a one-day payback. Used to set up the larger theme: deformation processing can hold thousandth-of-an-inch tolerances, but only within geometric limits, and industrial uptake of academic findings is patchy.
Alcoa Davenport aluminum rolling mill th.case_name: Aluminum plate thickness variation, Alcoa Davenport rolling mill

King Street Bridge failure.title: WM_Su2014_25
King Street Bridge failure.frame: Fatigue crack at weld toe leading to brittle fracture through web; top flange intact due to deflection-limited geometry. Tom uses it as the opening case for the day; references it as discussed the prior session.

King Street Bridge failure.title: WM_S2014_21
King Street Bridge failure.frame: Melbourne, Australia, 1960s. Plate-on-plate fillet weld run all the way around the closure produced a fatigue crack that brought the bridge down. Now a forbidden detail in the codes — illustrates the principle that codes encode failure history. Tom does not recall whether anyone was killed.

King Street Bridge failure.title: WM_Su2014_23
King Street Bridge failure.frame: Classic case of a doubler plate welded all around its tip, creating a fatigue crack initiation site at the change in stress concentration. Used to motivate the AISC fatigue-class restrictions on wrap-around welds.

King Street Bridge failure.title: WM_S2014_24
King Street Bridge failure.frame: Cruciform fillet weld detail with full wrap-around at a doubler plate; hydrogen crack at the high-restraint location grew in fatigue on the tension side until the bridge collapsed. Used as the case for why modern codes prohibit wrapping welds around the ends.

King Street Bridge failure.title: WM_Su2015_11
King Street Bridge failure.frame: Brittle fracture of welded bridge in Melbourne, late 1970s. Doubler-plate detail with weld going across the loaded direction; hydrogen crack from welding grew by fatigue to critical size. Major thoroughfare lost for ~1 year. Used to justify the welding-detail prohibition (don't weld around the corners).

New York City building crack near George.title: WM_Su2014_25

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: WIE_F2015_05
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: Cited as an example of WWII engineering achievement (two-week keel-to-launch) that competed with the physicists' Manhattan Project for postwar prestige.

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: SMS_S2016_02
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: The case that motivated fracture mechanics. ~5,000 ships built; ~40 with major cracks; several total fractures. Used to teach the distinction between strength (force of fracture) and toughness (energy of fracture).

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: SMS_S2016_09
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: The Schenectady at dry dock as the photograph in every fracture-mechanics textbook. Subsidiary to the broader WWII vessel case.

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: CS_Su2012_05
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: Tom reads from the 1946 Maritime Commission report: 4,694 welded merchant vessels investigated, 970 with fracture casualties, 24 complete strength-deck fractures, 8 vessels lost (4 broke in two, 4 abandoned), 26 lives lost. Schenectady famous photo (split at dock); SS Manhattan more dramatic (mid–North Atlantic). Three postwar investigation centers: NRL (Pellini), British Welding Institute, MIT metallurgy (Cohen, Averbach). Outcome includes the Pellini explosion bulge test.

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: FW_Su2013_04
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: Submerged arc welding (originally Union Melt, Union Carbide) is invoked as the engineering solution to plasma-jet instability at high currents: the flux blanket constrains the molten metal so currents of 600–700 A become workable. Roosevelt's letter to Churchill describing the new process for Liberty Ship welding is cited.
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.case_name: Liberty Ships and submerged arc (Union Melt) welding

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: SMS_S2016_10
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: The Liberty ship hull fractures of WWII as the historical pivot that elevated energy of fracture (Charpy toughness) from a Griffith abstraction to a Navy specification. The 1946 Navy inquiry found problem plates averaging five foot-pounds; the Navy mandated ten, then fifteen (safety factor), then twenty (Coast Guard, 1960), then sixty-to-seventy for line pipe (Alaskan pipeline era).

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: WM_Su2015_07
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: Brief reference: "we didn't know we needed good toughness until after all the Liberty ship failures" — frames why plate-application alloy steels developed post-WWII.

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: WM_Su2014_23
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: Single-sentence reference to low-temperature brittle fracture in Liberty ships. Foreshadows later discussion not in this segment.

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: MSE_F2016_08
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: Origin story for fracture mechanics. 4,694 welded merchant vessels built in WWII; 970 (~20%) suffered fracture casualties; 24 had complete strength-deck fractures, 8 lost, 26 lives lost. USS Schenectady fractured at the dock; SS Esso Manhattan fractured mid-Atlantic.

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: MSE_F2017_04
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: The historical motivation for fracture mechanics as a discipline. George Irwin at NRL extends Griffith's brittle-material formula to ductile materials in response to WWII Liberty-ship failures.
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.case_name: Liberty ships and Irwin's extension of Griffith

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.title: WM_Su2014_09
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady.frame: Anchoring case for the entire brittle-fracture arc. Bethlehem Steel Burns Harbor.title: DP_S2012_06

Space Shuttle main tank friction stir we.title: SMS_F2013_03
Space Shuttle main tank friction stir we.frame: Brief reference. NASA's Michoud friction-welding program for aluminum structures, post-shuttle-retirement.
Space Shuttle main tank friction stir we.case_name: Space Shuttle main tank friction stir welded aluminum

Welding handbook electrode consumption s.title: WM_Su2014_34
Welding handbook electrode consumption s.frame: Tom's keynote-lecture survey of 199 welding processes in the welding handbook, used to show the explosion of process development 1900–1950 and the near-cessation of new process development after 1975 (with friction stir as the lone exception).

Welding handbook electrode consumption s.title: WM_S2014_08
Welding handbook electrode consumption s.frame: Tom's 1980s back-of-envelope estimate of US welder population (700,000 full-time equivalent → ~2 million total counting part-time). Calculated from stick-electrode pounds sold ÷ pounds-per-hour deposition rate ÷ assumed hours. Estimate later appeared in the eighth edition of the AWS welding handbook (~early 1990s) attributed to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which had in fact called AWS for the number — Tom's number.

Welding handbook electrode consumption s.title: TQI_S2018_02
Welding handbook electrode consumption s.frame: Tom's circa-1980 back-of-envelope estimate (half-million full-time + half-million part-time welders in US) was later cited as a Bureau of Labor Statistics figure in the *Welding Handbook*. Used to make the point about questionable provenance of authoritative-looking facts.
Welding handbook electrode consumption s.case_name: Tom's welder-population estimate and the Welding Handbook

Soviet Alpha-class submarine.title: WM_Su2014_34
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.frame: Used to make the point that titanium welding requires aerospace-grade cleanliness, not shipyard conditions. Tom's David Taylor conversations about whether a full-scale titanium submarine could be built in a US shipyard.
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.case_name: Soviet Alpha-class submarine / heavy-section titanium welding shipyard cleanliness

Soviet Alpha-class submarine.title: WM_S2014_27
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.frame: Centerpiece case of the lecture. Soviets deployed all-titanium attack submarines around 1980 — deeper diving than US depth charges, faster underwater than US destroyers on the surface. Mothballed within two years due to (1) fatigue cracks producing acoustic signature audible to sonar dropped from helicopters, and (2) unsolved creep-fatigue interaction at near-room-temperature seawater. Tom learned of the deployment from an *International Herald Tribune* article on a flight from Europe; learned in 1982 that the Soviets had not solved the creep-fatigue problem — they had built the submarines anyway.

Soviet Alpha-class submarine.title: CS_Su2012_01
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.frame: Background to Seawolf budget zeroing — congressional perception that Soviets had leapfrogged US submarine technology.

Soviet Alpha-class submarine.title: FW_Su2013_04
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.frame: By the mid-1980s the Alphas were being mothballed — they had cracking, were extremely noisy, and were expensive to maintain — which deflated U.S. interest in pursuing titanium submarines and set up the pivot to composites described in the workshop case.

Soviet Alpha-class submarine.title: DP_S2012_10
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.frame: Mentioned only obliquely via the US Navy's interest in non-ferromagnetic submarine hulls (titanium, then stainless steel) to evade SQUID detection.

Soviet Alpha-class submarine.title: WM_Su2014_14
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.frame: Referenced as the titanium-hull submarine Gurevich's group taught the Soviets to weld. Tom notes a deferred discussion ("we may talk about some of this when we get to titanium welding").

Soviet Alpha-class submarine.title: CAS_Su2011_02
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.frame: 1980 wake-up moment Tom recalls reading about in the International Herald Tribune flying back from Europe. Faster than US destroyers, deeper than US depth-charge collapse depth — but very noisy and full of cracks within years (Soviet Naval Research Lab had identified fracture problems they hadn't actually solved before building). Triggered US Navy titanium research funding competition (Jim Williams at Carnegie Mellon vs. Tom at MIT) and later the post-Alpha composite-submarine workshop in Reston.

Soviet Alpha-class submarine.title: WM_Su2014_32
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.frame: The Alfa sub becoming public knowledge ~1980; leapfrog of US submarine technology by ~2 years; creep-fatigue cracking failures; Congressional alarm and the David Taylor conferences. Tom's eventual inference that Gurevich used electroslag welding to build the heavy-section titanium hull.

Soviet Alpha-class submarine.title: WM_S2014_28
Soviet Alpha-class submarine.frame: The Alpha sub revelation on the *International Herald Tribune* front page in 1980 is the moment Tom realized why Gurevich had been publishing on electroslag — the Soviets had built a titanium-hulled submarine. Two years later the Alpha subs were mothballed: noisy, fatigue-cracked.

IBM stainless steel high-purity semicond.title: WM_Su2014_34
IBM stainless steel high-purity semicond.frame: IBM would reject $15,000 stainless steel gas piping trains if any heat-tint colors appeared on weld surfaces — concerned about contamination reaching gallium arsenide semiconductor processes.
IBM stainless steel high-purity semicond.case_name: IBM stainless steel high-purity semiconductor piping rejection

General Electric spot weld adaptive cont.title: WM_Su2014_34
General Electric spot weld adaptive cont.frame: GE Lynn contracted GE Schenectady Research at $1M/year for seven years to develop spot welding adaptive control for nickel superalloy combustor cans. Tom hired at $150K as "whipping boys" after Lynn cut Schenectady's funding. Tom and his students discovered the controller wasn't adapting until six cycles after the four-cycle weld was over.
General Electric spot weld adaptive cont.case_name: General Electric spot weld adaptive control system

General Electric adaptive weld control f.title: WM_Su2014_34
General Electric adaptive weld control f.frame: Same engagement as above, but specifically the technical finding — the adaptive controller's response lag (six cycles) exceeded the weld duration (four cycles). Tom presents this finding in front of GE Lynn's boss and the GE Research engineer who admits "we fixed that last week."
General Electric adaptive weld control f.case_name: General Electric adaptive weld control feedback timing failure

Automobile spot welding quality.title: WM_Su2014_34
Automobile spot welding quality.frame: Used to introduce resistance spot welding — Elihu Thomson, GE/MIT co-founder, ~1900. Tom's recurring "3,000 spot welds, 2,000 good ones" figure for automotive practice.
Automobile spot welding quality.case_name: Resistance spot welding (Elihu Thomson invention) — automotive

Automobile spot welding quality.title: DP_S2012_10
Automobile spot welding quality.frame: 3,000 spot welds per car / 2,000 good ones; ~$0.05 per weld; aggregate worldwide volume ~90 billion welds per year (Tom's live arithmetic). Used to demonstrate that joining cost equals material cost in automotive bodies.

Automobile spot welding quality.title: WIE_F2015_04
Automobile spot welding quality.frame:
Used as a self-illustrative example of communication-driven pedagogy. Tom recounts giving the 1989 Gatlinburg keynote on resistance welding and discovering that the memorable framing ("three thousand spot welds because you need two thousand good ones") got quoted back to him a year later. The case stands in for a recurring corpus topic (automotive spot weld reliability) but is deployed here as a story about how to teach, not about the welding itself.

## Figures and recurring numeric anchors
Automobile spot welding quality.case_name: Automobile spot welding quality (3000 welds / 2000 good)

Automobile spot welding quality.title: DP_S2012_09
Automobile spot welding quality.frame: Tom's example of a sound bite with content — used to illustrate the Thurow lesson. Quoted back to him by a stranger at a welding conference a year later. Likely connects to cluster "Automotive spot welding quality" but is delivered specifically as a *rhetorical-form* anecdote, not as a forensic teaching case.
Automobile spot welding quality.case_name: Spot welding sound-bite anecdote (3,000 welds for 2,000 good ones)

Japanese Maritime Self-Defense Force hel.title: CS_F2012_03
Japanese Maritime Self-Defense Force hel.frame: The first known failure of the Reali-Slim swashplate bearing — a heavy-lift Navy helicopter crashes in the Sea of Japan, late 1980s. Spends years on the ocean floor, recovery too corroded to diagnose definitively. Sets up the U.S. failure to come.
Japanese Maritime Self-Defense Force hel.case_name: Japanese Maritime Self-Defense Force helicopter swashplate seizure

Kaydon bearing conformity failure and he.title: CS_F2012_03
Kaydon bearing conformity failure and he.frame: The most fully developed version of this case in the corpus. Two U.S. test pilots killed during a two-hour acceptance hover; subsequent Cherry Point near-crash; fleet grounding; FBI takeover under the Emergency Powers Act; perfect new bearings still failing within two months; Tom's forensic discovery that 188 of 192 brinelling marks are ellipses (open conformity), not hourglasses (closed conformity); the potato-chipped aluminum swashplate as actual cause; the helicopter manufacturer's destruction of the milling machine and sibling swashplates; the new CEO's decision to settle anyway for $15M to clear his watch.
Kaydon bearing conformity failure and he.case_name: Kaydon bearing conformity failure and helicopter crashes

Kaydon bearing conformity failure and he.title: CS_F2012_06
Kaydon bearing conformity failure and he.case_name: Bearing manufacturer Chemical Safety Board participation

Kaydon bearing conformity failure and he.title: CS_Su2012_02
Kaydon bearing conformity failure and he.frame: The Stratford crash, the closed-vs-open conformity hypothesis, Tom's forensic insight (barrel-shaped wear marks prove the conformity was correct), the discovery that the aluminum swash plate housing was potato-chipped because the helicopter company had scrapped its three-year-old milling machine, the FBI takeover of bearing QC, and the new bearing-company president settling for $15M to avoid taking the blame.
Kaydon bearing conformity failure and he.case_name: MH-53 helicopter swashplate bearing case (Stratford / Sikorsky)

USS aircraft carrier steam system weld f.title: CS_F2012_03
USS aircraft carrier steam system weld f.frame: Digression illustrating military urgency. The Atlantic carrier defending against Soviet preemptive attack develops steam leaks mid-invasion (October 1983); emergency repair at Jacksonville Naval Shipyard; technicians flown in by helicopter from their homes at 3 a.m.
USS aircraft carrier steam system weld f.case_name: USS aircraft carrier steam system weld failure during Grenada invasion

V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged c.title: CS_F2012_03
V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged c.frame: Parallel case to Kaydon, invoked at the lecture's close to generalize the "rigged board of inquiry" pattern. The court was instructed to find a fixable cause to protect the $40 billion program from Congressional cancellation. Tom served as expert witness in the subsequent civil suit by widows; his hydraulic-leak-in-the-upper-nacelle theory (one miracle) displaced the Navy's nacelle-fire theory (six miracles); the JAG investigation eventually adopted Tom's theory.
V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged c.case_name: V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged court of inquiry

V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged c.title: WM_Su2014_05
V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged c.frame: Tom worked on the case. Used to illustrate the military/civilian liability split: Boeing and Bell settled with military families immediately; civilian families had to file suit and go to trial.
V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged c.case_name: V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged court of inquiry

V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged c.title: MSE_F2016_06
V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged c.frame: Tom's expert witness work. Crash at Patuxent River killed crew. Navy's 4,400 findings of fact blamed engine fire from below; Tom testified the fire started in the upper hydraulics; JAG Corps reversed the Navy's finding to match Tom's analysis.
V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged c.case_name: V-22 Osprey Ship Four crash and rigged court of inquiry

Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip.title: CS_F2012_03
Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip.frame: Cited to explain why conventional helicopters are speed-limited around 200 mph — once the advancing blade tip approaches Mach 1, vibrations and instabilities will rip the blades off. NASA built and flew an experimental helicopter with a jet engine on the back to break the barrier deliberately; it's now an outdoor exhibit at the NASA Hampton facility.
Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip.case_name: NASA Langley supersonic helicopter blade-tip experiment

Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip.title: SMS_F2013_06
Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip.frame: NASA Langley fitted rocket motors to a helicopter to push forward speed to 240 mph, driving advancing blade tips supersonic to study the instability.
Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip.case_name: Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip experiment

Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip.title: MSE_F2016_06
Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip.frame: NASA Langley pushed a test helicopter past sonic tip speed for a few seconds. The general lesson: helicopters are noise-and-vibration-limited at ~200 mph because the advancing rotor tip approaches Mach 1.
Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip.case_name: Langley helicopter supersonic blade tip experiment

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: CS_F2012_03
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: Cited in passing as the tilt-rotor solution to the Mach-1 blade-tip limit — tilts to airplane mode for 300 mph forward flight. Distinct from the Ship Four crash case treated in §11.

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: SMS_F2013_06
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: Tilt-rotor design rationale — 300–350 mph forward speed, lower acoustic signature than helicopter blades, used in bin Laden raid alongside Blackhawks.

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: FW_Su2013_04
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: Cited as the first aircraft built from composites, and only because no other material would let it fly with usable payload — used to underscore that the aerospace composites community at the time of the DARPA submarine workshop had no all-composite aircraft experience to draw on.
V-22 Osprey aircraft.case_name: V-22 Osprey as first all-composite aircraft

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: MSE_F2017_03
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: First all-composite major aircraft. Tilt-rotor, 300 mph, used in bin Laden raid. Started at $15M per unit, ended at $65M — "one of the more notable overruns in the Defense Department."

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: SMS_F2013_09
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: Brief reference back to a prior lecture's discussion: the Osprey could not have flown without high-performance composites. Used as the marquee aerospace-composite example.

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: SMS_F2014_08
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: Cited as the first all-composite aircraft; the design "would never fly" without the lightweight of composites. Mentioned as a candidate topic for student presentations, not developed.
V-22 Osprey aircraft.case_name: V-22 Osprey: composites necessitated by design [mention]

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: SMS_F2013_08
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: First large all-composite aircraft. Graphite-epoxy structure that would have been impossible in aluminum. Used as the high-end ("boutique," thousands of dollars per pound) composite case.

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: SMS_S2016_01
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: Cited as the first large all-composite aircraft, ~$60M per unit, all graphite carbon fiber composite. Used to make the structural-materials-in-use point. No discussion of the Ship 2 or Ship 4 crashes here.

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: SMS_S2016_06
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: Tilt-rotor that could not have been built without carbon fiber composite — all-composite by necessity. Cost: $15M → $60M per unit. Cited again in §7 to illustrate that military aircraft economics permit full composites where commercial does not.

V-22 Osprey aircraft.title: SMS_F2014_05
V-22 Osprey aircraft.frame: First aircraft (1990s) designed with 100% composite structure. Tilt-rotor helicopter where composites were the only path to flyable weight. Also referenced in §3.p6 for its 3,000 psi hydraulics as a comparison point with America's Cup yacht's 7,500 psi.

Large ship forging fraud and delayed jus.title: CS_F2012_03
Large ship forging fraud and delayed jus.frame: Mentioned in one sentence as an analogue to Kaydon — Tom got the chance "about 20 years later, to screw that company that screwed the other company, just by chance." No further detail given here; presumably developed in another lecture.

MIT machine shop mushroomed tool discove.title: DP_S2012_05
MIT machine shop mushroomed tool discove.frame: Tom confiscated a fifty-year-old mushroomed steel bar from the MIT machine shop and cut a section to pass around class as a deformation specimen. Linked to a recurring eye-injury hazard from chips flying off mushroomed hammer heads.
MIT machine shop mushroomed tool discove.case_name: MIT machine shop mushroomed tool discovery

Mushroomed hammer head eye injuries.title: DP_S2012_05
Mushroomed hammer head eye injuries.frame: Tom cites "three or four cases" of chips breaking off mushroomed hammer heads and blinding the user. Used to motivate the discarded tool as a teaching artifact.

Mushroomed hammer head eye injuries.title: WM_Su2014_13
Mushroomed hammer head eye injuries.case_name: Hammer head shards in the eye

SS Great Britain propeller shaft forging.title: DP_S2012_05
SS Great Britain propeller shaft forging.frame: Carl corrected Tom's earlier reference to "Kingdom Brunell" — Isambard Kingdom Brunel was the engineer behind a huge 1830s ship. Tom is correcting his own attribution from a prior lecture's case.
SS Great Britain propeller shaft forging.case_name: SS Great Britain propeller shaft forging

SS Great Britain propeller shaft forging.title: DP_S2012_04
SS Great Britain propeller shaft forging.frame: James Nasmyth's painting of his patented steam hammer forging a 30-inch wrought-iron propeller shaft for Brunel's SS Great Britain. Tom uses the V-shaped anvil visible in the painting to make a delta/triaxial-stress point.
SS Great Britain propeller shaft forging.case_name: Nasmyth steam hammer and SS Great Britain propeller shaft

Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.title: DP_S2012_05
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.frame: Alcoa's Davenport, Iowa rolling mill — "the world's largest" — rolls aluminum plate up to four inches thick for 747 wings, then mechanically stress-relieves it by 1–3% stretch in a large hydraulic machine. Used to introduce the T651 / T63 temper designations as mechanical-stress-relief codes.
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.case_name: Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hydraulic jacking

Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.title: SMS_F2013_12
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.frame: Referenced as the production-scale analog to the washer's -51 treatment. World's largest rolling mill — for aluminum, not steel — produces aircraft wing plates for Boeing and the former McDonnell Douglas. Hydraulic expanders pull 30-foot, 4-inch plates 1–3% in plastic strain to relieve quench stresses.
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.case_name: Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hydraulic jacking

Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.title: WM_Su2014_28
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.frame: Cross-reference for the mechanical (T-51) stress relief mechanism. Tom invokes the Davenport six-inch-thick plate stretching as the canonical example of the operation Sikorsky's washer process destroyed.
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.case_name: Alcoa Davenport plate stretch stress relief

Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.title: WM_Su2015_11
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.frame: Mechanical stress relief example. Six-inch plate, ten feet wide, pulled 3% in hydraulic jacks the size of half a football field. Used as the canonical case of mechanical (not thermal) stress relief in heavy aluminum plate.
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.case_name: Davenport Iowa Alcoa plate stress relief

Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.title: WM_S2014_23
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.frame: Alcoa's Davenport Works rolls aluminum aircraft-wing plate up to six inches thick on the world's largest rolling mill, then relieves residual stresses by hydraulically stretching the plate one to three percent (the "T51" temper designation). Tom has visited the facility. Used to teach that aluminum residual stresses cannot be relieved by heat treatment for metallurgical reasons, so a mechanical solution is required.
Davenport Iowa plate stress relief by hy.case_name: Davenport Iowa heavy aluminum plate stress relief by stretching

Aluminum washer stress-corrosion crackin.title: DP_S2012_05
Aluminum washer stress-corrosion crackin.frame: Customer bought aluminum in T651 (stress-relieved) condition, machined washers, reheat-treated them, and did not re-relieve the residual stresses. Resulting 8 ksi residual stress exceeded the 5 ksi SCC threshold for the alloy; washers cracked. Resolved by going to overage temper with higher SCC tolerance.

Welded steel crane component failure.title: DP_S2012_05
Welded steel crane component failure.frame: A two-inch-thick steel crane component with un-stress-relieved welds failed in brittle fracture under bending, dropping a seventy-ton water bag onto a worker (back injury). Boiler-and-pressure-vessel code requires post-weld heat treatment above 1.5 inches; this code was not followed.

Submarine first deep dive stress relief.title: DP_S2012_05
Submarine first deep dive stress relief.frame: Submarines cannot be furnace-stress-relieved after outfitting (rubber, plastics, O-rings inside). The Navy uses hydrostatic compression on the first deep dive to mechanically relieve weld residual stresses — and requires shipyard top management to ride that first dive. Tom's "favorite quality-control story."
Submarine first deep dive stress relief.case_name: US Navy submarine first-dive stress relief

Submarine first deep dive stress relief.title: WM_S2014_14
Submarine first deep dive stress relief.frame: Used as the teaching counterpoint to thermal post weld heat treatment. A nuclear submarine pressure hull is too large for furnace stress relief and contains heat-sensitive internals; instead, mechanical stress relief on the first deep dive accomplishes the same end. Tom adds the cultural point that shipyard top management goes on the first deep dive — quality control via skin-in-the-game.

Trolley wire manufacturing by Conform pr.title: DP_S2012_05
Trolley wire manufacturing by Conform pr.frame: Phelps Dodge produced trolley wire by the Conform process (invented at a UK national lab), which knead-deforms powder/rod through a circular cavity to ~1,000% equivalent plastic strain. Output had near-superplastic elongation. British purchasers attempted to reject the wire on a too-much-elongation specification reading — Tom alludes to legal consequences (lost passports).

Trolley wire manufacturing by Conform pr.title: DP_S2012_11
Trolley wire manufacturing by Conform pr.frame: Tom passes a section of trolley wire around the class while explaining the Conform extrusion process. The wire is the artifact; the case is the process. Includes Tom's own failed attempt to use Conform for copper-niobium superconductor wire 30 years earlier (broken dies).

50,000-ton Wyman-Gordon forging press st.title: DP_S2012_05
50,000-ton Wyman-Gordon forging press st.frame: Tom visited Wyman-Gordon (North Grafton, MA; later acquired by Krupp) in the early 1980s to investigate a crack in a forged I-beam at the base of the Air-Force-built 50,000-ton press. Six 300-ton I-beams at top and bottom; one had cracked at a weld over thirty years of service. Replacement estimated at two billion dollars in 1983.

50,000-ton Wyman-Gordon forging press st.title: WM_Su2014_21
50,000-ton Wyman-Gordon forging press st.frame: One of two free-world 50,000-ton presses (the other at Alcoa Cleveland). Six I-beams ten feet tall, ten-inch web, fifteen-inch flanges, holding the press structure six stories below grade. 10-foot crack in one beam, $2 billion replacement cost in 1980 dollars. Tom consulted; recommended rigging the beam up and out for stress relief in a built furnace rather than in-place. Critical flaw size 10 inches — fatigue crack initiating at the toe of a fillet weld on a 50-pound rigging block someone had left attached. Punchline: "We didn't know how to weld 10-inch-thick material without stress relieving it. We lost that technology when a lot of people died of old age."
50,000-ton Wyman-Gordon forging press st.case_name: West Grafton Wyman Gordon 50,000-ton forging press I-beam crack

50,000-ton Wyman-Gordon forging press st.title: WM_S2014_18
50,000-ton Wyman-Gordon forging press st.case_name: Wyman Gordon 50,000-ton forging press I-beam fatigue crack

50,000-ton forging press development (Ai.title: DP_S2012_05
50,000-ton forging press development (Ai.frame: The Air Force built two 50,000-ton presses in the early 1950s for large bomber forgings because welding was not yet trusted for structural components. Wyman Gordon (Grafton MA) and Alcoa (Cleveland) operate them; titanium/nickel-superalloy forgings vs. aluminum forgings respectively.

Forging press anvil base fracture.title: DP_S2012_05
Forging press anvil base fracture.frame: Tom and Professor Pelloux compared fractures; Pelloux's case was a 10-foot by 20-foot fracture in a cast anvil base of a large forging press.

LNG carrier tail shaft fracture.title: DP_S2012_05
LNG carrier tail shaft fracture.frame: Used as a scale comparator in Tom's exchange with Pelloux. Possibly an instance of the canonical "LNG carrier tail shaft fracture" or "SS Libra LNG vessel tail shaft failure" — flagged in editorial register for confirmation.

LNG carrier tail shaft fracture.title: SMS_S2016_10
LNG carrier tail shaft fracture.frame: Mid-1980s, Philippine Sea. One of the Quincy-built LNG ships had its tail shaft fail mid-voyage between Indonesia and Japan with a full LNG cargo. Offloaded onto a returning empty ship; Learjets flew fittings halfway around the world; out-of-the-way Philippine harbor; nobody hurt. Fatigue crack grew from a casting flaw the Seattle steel shop's inspector had found and the manager had suppressed by throwing him out of the office. Crack grew over five years until shaft broke in two. Pelloux brought in for forensic analysis.

Air Force 100,000-ton forging press proj.title: DP_S2012_05
Air Force 100,000-ton forging press proj.frame: The Air Force had 1950s plans to site a 100,000-ton press in a Colorado granite mountain (mountain itself as foundation). Never built — electron beam welding emerged as a more economical solution for the swept-wing fighter center-box parts that motivated the press. Plans would have cost ~$2B in 1980s dollars.

Swept-wing fighter aircraft center box f.title: DP_S2012_05
Swept-wing fighter aircraft center box f.frame: Late-1950s swept-wing fighters (wings move from sonic to supersonic configuration) required a large structural center box. Initially the motivating part for the 100,000-ton press; instead solved by electron beam welding.

7,000-ton forging press weld repair.title: DP_S2012_05
7,000-ton forging press weld repair.frame: Tom's welding-course teaching specimen — a 20-inch-thick weld repair on the head of a 7,000-ton press that stamps eighteen-wheeler aluminum truck wheels. Head dome ~10 feet high, ~350 tons, would fill a third of the classroom volume.
7,000-ton forging press weld repair.case_name: 7,000-ton forging press weld repair (aluminum truck wheels)

7,000-ton forging press weld repair.title: FW_Su2013_03
7,000-ton forging press weld repair.frame: Tom passes around a ~13-inch-thick SMAW repair weld (500–800 passes) from a 1950s-era 7,000-ton forging press in Erie, Pennsylvania. The press had cracked; a replacement would cost ~$100M, so "good old boys" repaired it. Tom uses the sample to discuss WWII-era armor-plate practice of peening every half inch as a mechanical stress relief — knowledge lost by the 1980s when the Navy tried to repair the USS Iowa turret.

7,000-ton forging press weld repair.title: WM_Su2014_20
7,000-ton forging press weld repair.frame: 17-inch-thick weld on a top casting of a 1948-vintage 7,000-ton forging press, repaired by skilled Georgia-based welders without adequate preheat-through-section or post-weld heat treatment. Cracked twice (first from residual stress alone, second on the first forging stroke). Used to illustrate that excellent welder craft is not a substitute for engineering oversight on heavy sections. Cost: ~$5M.

Longfellow Bridge renovation welding con.title: WM_S2014_07
Longfellow Bridge renovation welding con.frame: Used as the prototypical "client calls with old steel of unknown composition" example. Tom describes the recurring pattern: a thirty-year consulting relationship with an MIT mechanical-engineering spinoff firm that would call him when they needed to weld old steel in renovation projects (Longfellow Bridge cited as example), and he could not develop a procedure without composition and thickness data.

Technology Review interview on metal 3D.title: SMS_S2016_02
Technology Review interview on metal 3D.frame:
Tom uses a media-interview question as the spine for a full lecture on why metals resist 3D printing — mechanical (volume change, residual stress), surface (oxidation, surface tension), and heat-transfer reasons — and his own Navy electron-beam proposal as the would-be solution.

## Cases referenced
Technology Review interview on metal 3D.case_name: Why no 3D printing of metals? (the Technology Review question)

Stereolithography invention (Chuck Hull,.title: SMS_S2016_02
Stereolithography invention (Chuck Hull,.frame: First 3D printing technology — liquid polymer + two intersecting UV lasers. Used as origin point.

Cima-Sachs MIT 3D printing invention (la.title: SMS_S2016_02
Cima-Sachs MIT 3D printing invention (la.frame: Coined the term "3D printing." Adapted dot-matrix printheads to deposit ceramic slurry. First parts were ceramic molds for artificial hips.

Enzyme strips for blood sugar testing.title: SMS_S2016_02
Enzyme strips for blood sugar testing.frame: Tom recommended adopting 2D printheads for enzyme deposition; the company refused. Used to make the point that 2D printing applications outside the obvious ones were emerging in parallel with 3D.

3D-printed solder droplet circuit boards.title: SMS_S2016_02
3D-printed solder droplet circuit boards.frame: Tom's research contract gave to a mech eng colleague to attempt 3D-printed PCBs. Motorola and Intel also tried; everyone gave up because of surface tension (developed quantitatively in §7).

3D-printed solder droplet circuit boards.title: SSW_S2013_09
3D-printed solder droplet circuit boards.frame: Tom's collaboration with Prof. Sonin (MIT mechanical engineering) on jetting lead-tin solder droplets to print circuit boards. Used to illustrate how Young's equation breaks down outside equilibrium and simple geometry. "Tens and hundreds of millions of dollars" of industry effort have failed at this for twenty years.

NASA X-33 space plane.title: CAS_Su2011_02
NASA X-33 space plane.frame: Tom uses the X-33 as the central morality tale of post-Gulf-War rapid prototyping. NASA awarded Lockheed Martin Skunk Works a $1.3B contract on a ~33-month schedule for a single-stage-to-orbit replacement for the Space Shuttle. The team spent six months designing a 3D-woven carbon composite ring-stiffened liquid hydrogen tank, discovered the design would blow the budget 4–5×, then improvised a Nextel-honeycomb / carbon-tape sandwich design in one month at $50M per tank, ~2,000 lb each. Cryogenic fill test at Huntsville appeared successful until video showed frost popping off — the carbon composite was permeable to hydrogen. Project cancelled; the tanks still sit at Palmdale. The X-33 piece passed around the class ($12,000/lb) anchors the cost-per-pound argument.

NASA X-33 space plane.title: MSE_F2016_12
NASA X-33 space plane.frame: Tom's extended case study of the failed $1.3B Lockheed Martin Skunk Works program. Used to teach: (1) rapid prototyping as a buzzword that can override engineering judgment; (2) how a 2.0 safety factor degraded to 1.05 through autoclave delamination; (3) how NASA misread the 3M epoxy data sheet (10% remaining strength after 10 days, not 80–90%); (4) the unverified hydrogen permeability number off by three orders of magnitude that became the final Achilles heel.

NASA X-33 space plane.title: SMS_F2013_03
NASA X-33 space plane.frame: The lecture's flagship case study. Three failure modes braided: (1) the 3D woven graphite-fiber composite cost overrun that ate the budget before tanks were built; (2) the 10-day-shelf-life adhesive bullet point that hid a 100%→20% strength curve; (3) the post-test leak from CTE mismatch between graphite-epoxy, Nomex, and adhesive joints under cryogenic-to-room-temperature cycling. Outcome: $50M tanks scrapped, $1.3B program cancelled.

Delrin (polyformaldehyde) toilet valve f.frame: The sustained case of the lecture. DuPont's Delrin (introduced 1958) was tested against 200 solvents but not against water. Toilet float valves cracked under 60 psi water pressure and blew the ceramic lid off. Tom: "I made a lot of money off that."

Delrin (polyformaldehyde) toilet valve f.title: WM_Su2014_05
Delrin (polyformaldehyde) toilet valve f.frame: The lecture's center case. DuPont's 1958 paper tested Delrin against 200 solvents — but never against water. 1962 German study found chlorine-induced stress corrosion cracking. Hoechst paid $900M settlement; DuPont paid more than $1B (confidential). Toilet float valves made of Delrin became brittle after 2–3 years and failed under 60 psi water pressure, blowing off ceramic tank tops. Teaching point: plastics corrode, and "corrosion resistant" specifications depend critically on what was tested.

Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (Al.frame: Wendell Wilkening's MIT doctoral thesis under Backofen on the brittle fracture of granite. Used to introduce microcracking at crack tips as the mechanism explaining why Egyptian obelisks survived lifting.

Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (Al.title: MSE_F2016_08
Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (Al.frame: Wendell W. Wilkening's 1976 MIT PhD thesis. With 1976 knowledge of stone toughness, an obelisk being raised from horizontal should fracture under its own weight from natural flaws. Wilkening found micro-cracking ahead of the crack tip explains how it didn't.

Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (Al.title: SMS_F2014_08
Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (Al.frame: Mid-1970s MIT thesis (Wendell Wilkening under Al Bakaven). Fracture mechanics predicts the obelisk should snap under its own weight during raising; reality is the three-phase granite microstructure forms toughening microcracks at flaw tips, giving 2–3× the toughness predicted from single-phase rocks.
Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (Al.case_name: Egyptian obelisk fracture mechanics (Al Bakaven thesis)

Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (Al.title: WIE_F2015_06
Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (Al.frame: A 1970-era fracture mechanics calculation said obelisks couldn't be raised intact. Tom's office-mate (Wilkening, working under Backofen) discovered microcrack toughening at the crack tip in three-phase granite (silica, feldspar, third phase), giving 5-10× higher toughness than expected. Resolved the engineering paradox and seeded 1980s tough-ceramics research.
Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (Al.case_name: Egyptian obelisk engineering mystery (granite fracture toughness)

Ethanol production centrifuge disc failu.title: SMS_S2016_09
Ethanol production centrifuge disc failu.frame: Forensic case — 3-ton duplex stainless steel disc cast in Pennsylvania, improperly heat-treated, fractured in service in France (near-miss) and China (fatality). 700 worldwide in service; critical flaw size < 2 mm at quarter-inch drilled holes 10 inches deep, raising the inspection problem. Used to demonstrate that flaw size, not material identity, governs catastrophic risk in a brittle-heat-treated condition.

Navtech marine hydraulic piston failure.title: SMS_S2016_09
Navtech marine hydraulic piston failure.frame: Forensic case — 7075-T6 aluminum hydraulic cylinder, 7500 PSI service, 2.5 mm wall, fatigue-initiated fracture running 2/3 through before catastrophic burst. Tom's recommendation: switch to T73 temper (yield 73 → 63 KSI, K_IC 26 → 30 KSI√in, critical flaw 4 mm) for leak-before-break behavior. The signature case for the toughness-versus-strength trade-off in design philosophy.
Navtech marine hydraulic piston failure.case_name: Navtech marine hydraulic piston failure (America's Cup yacht)

America's Cup design philosophy and ligh.title: SMS_S2016_09

America's Cup design philosophy and ligh.title: SMS_F2014_05

America's Cup design philosophy and ligh.case_name: America's Cup design philosophy and lightweight failure margins

Aluminum baseball bat.title: SMS_S2016_09
Aluminum baseball bat.frame:
Highest-strength aluminum (~100 KSI yield) off the chart of Pellini's RAD. Bats engineered to last 100–150 hits and crack, not shatter — manufacturer-favorable degradation behavior at $300 per replacement. Used as closing example of how the strength/toughness trade-off plays out in consumer products.

Carbon nanotubes structural applications.title: DP_S2012_01
Carbon nanotubes structural applications.frame: Tom's argument that carbon nanotubes' theoretical 2–3 million PSI strength is irrelevant because any real nanotube contains atomic vacancies (guaranteed by the second law of thermodynamics above 0 K), which act as defects and drop strength by ~10×. Physicists "getting billions of dollars to study carbon nanotubes" called "money down a rat hole" for structural use; allows for functional/display applications.

Carbon nanotubes structural applications.title: SSW_S2013_02
Carbon nanotubes structural applications.frame: Twenty-five years and a billion dollars of research on carbon nanotubes (and later graphene) for structural applications, promising 3 million PSI carbon-carbon bond strength. Nobody has measured the strength of an actual carbon nanotube. Vacancies forbidden by statistical mechanics at any T > 0 K mean real nanotubes will be 1/5 to 1/10 the predicted strength. Tom: "Don't invest in carbon nanotubes for structural applications."
