Tom's Bethlehem Steel trip reports.frame: Brief autobiographical aside. Tom mentions hating trip reports as a Bethlehem employee and his relief at leaving them behind when he joined MIT as an assistant professor.

Aloha Airlines Flight 243.title: SMS_F2013_12
Aloha Airlines Flight 243.frame: Used to introduce aluminum pressure-vessel fatigue. Tom emphasizes the high cycle count (~60,000) accumulated in only ~40,000 hours due to short inter-island flight legs, and uses the survival of the keel beam to introduce structural redundancy. Treated here as corrosion-fatigue.

Aloha Airlines Flight 243.title: WM_Su2015_07
Aloha Airlines Flight 243.frame: Parallel case to Seawolf. The early-1990s 737 fuselage roof failure attributed to Aloha being the fatigue-leader in the worldwide 737 fleet — 40,000 cycles in 30,000 hours due to 40-minute interisland flights. Boeing's fleet-average inspection schedule missed the outlier. One fatality (unbelted flight attendant). Used to teach: do more inspection on the fatigue leader, the same lesson as Seawolf.

Aloha Airlines Flight 243.title: SSW_S2013_04
Aloha Airlines Flight 243.frame: Compared to the Comet as low-cycle-fatigue precedent. 37,000 cycles, 40,000 flight hours equivalent to 250,000 hours of normal Boeing service due to short inter-island flights.

Aloha Airlines Flight 243.title: SMS_F2014_06
Aloha Airlines Flight 243.frame: The keel-beam-and-rib-cage architecture of pressurized aluminum airliners. Forty-five-minute average flight = forty-five-minute fatigue cycle, plus saltwater corrosion = corrosion-fatigue failure of the upper skin. Used to teach pressurization cycles as fatigue cycles.

Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.title: SMS_F2013_12
Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.frame: Stress-corrosion cracking of 6061-T6 aluminum washer holding the tail rotor of an Army Sikorsky Blackhawk; helicopter lost rotor and crashed in Arkansas. Tom traces the design history: the Coast Guard / Jayhawk team had already switched to T73 and not told the Blackhawk team. Same washers found pre-cracked in Navy supply depots from residual stresses alone (measured 8 ksi vs. 5 ksi SCC threshold).
Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.case_name: Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer failure

Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.title: WM_Su2015_16
Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.frame: Stress corrosion cracking case study. Arkansas night-vision-goggle training crash; 7075-T6 washer should have been T7351 (compression-stress-relieved as T7352). Government contractor defense; Sikorsky settled for $10M two weeks after the chief of rotors testified.
Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.case_name: Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer failure (Arkansas)

Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.title: WM_Su2014_28
Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.frame: Tom's central forensic case for the lecture. 6061-T6 aluminum washer cracking on the shelf due to residual stresses (8 ksi) exceeding the alloy's stress corrosion cracking threshold (5 ksi) in marine atmosphere. Sikorsky had previously seen this on CH-53/MH-53 and switched to T7 over-aged heat treatment but failed to apply the fix to the Blackhawk part. Bars purchased as T-651 (stretched, stress relieved) were sliced, machined, and reheat-treated, wiping out the stretch stress relief. Government contractor defense raised by Sikorsky in subsequent litigation.
Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.case_name: Blackhawk tail rotor washer stress corrosion cracking

Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.title: WM_Su2014_28
Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.frame: The fatal-failure realization of the same washer defect Tom was investigating for the Navy. Night vision goggle training exercise, cracked washer with T6 heat treatment, eight soldiers killed and one in a coma. Triggered the litigation in which Sikorsky raised the government contractor defense.

Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.title: DP_S2012_04
Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.frame: Recap from prior session. Tom brings the physical washers (Seahawk and Army variants, both steel and aluminum), explains the saw-cut residual stress measurement method (8 ksi measured), and the resolution: switch from a heat treatment with 5 ksi SCC threshold to an overaged T73 with 25 ksi threshold.
Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer.case_name: Black Hawk helicopter tail rotor washer failure

Alclad aluminum aerospace sheet \u2014 r.title: SMS_F2013_12
Alclad aluminum aerospace sheet \u2014 r.frame: Seventy-year history of roll-bonding 1100 aluminum onto 2014/2024 cores to prevent galvanic micro-cells from copper precipitates. Recent (~mid-2000s) commercial development by a Spokane WA inventor of continuous direct-chill casting that fuses two alloys at a single fusion line, dropping clad-sheet costs and opening kitchen-appliance and brazed-radiator markets.
Alclad aluminum aerospace sheet \u2014 r.case_name: Aluminum aerospace clad-sheet manufacturing (Alclad and continuously cast variants)

America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress.title: SMS_F2013_12
America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress.frame: 7075-T6 aluminum hydraulic cylinder at 7,500 psi exploding from SCC initiated outside. Solution: 3 mm → 4 mm wall thickness, sacrificing strength to double SCC threshold and convert failure mode to leak-before-break. Used to introduce the America's Cup design philosophy: if your hardware doesn't fail, you've made it too heavy.
America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress.case_name: America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress corrosion cracking

America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress.title: SMS_F2014_05
America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress.frame: MIT Mech E alum runs Connecticut company supplying America's Cup hardware; brought Tom a failed 7,500 psi hydraulic cylinder. Pairs with the "design philosophy" cluster — if it doesn't fail occasionally, you over-built it.
America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress.case_name: America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress corrosion cracking

Naval Research Lab ratio analysis diagra.title: SMS_F2013_12
Naval Research Lab ratio analysis diagra.frame: Framing reference. Tom invokes the NRL diagram (developed out of Liberty ship failures, 1950s–60s) as the parent framework before pivoting to Ashby plots.
Naval Research Lab ratio analysis diagra.case_name: Naval Research Laboratory ratio analysis diagram (Liberty ships heritage)

MIT Berylliosis cases.title: SMS_F2013_12
MIT Berylliosis cases.frame: MIT Manhattan Project beryllium machining work (corner of Mass Ave) discovered berylliosis through machinist deaths in mid-to-late 1940s. Tom adds the contemporary anecdote of Professor Shu finding a 1946-era bottle of beryllium powder in Professor Grant's lab during a department cleanup. Used to explain beryllium's manufacturing cost (toxicity controls) and the 10% genetic predisposition figure.

MIT Berylliosis cases.title: SMS_F2014_13
MIT Berylliosis cases.frame: Manhattan-Project-era machine shop at the corner of Mass Ave and Vassar; workers in 1944–45 contaminated by beryllium machining; building eventually entombed in concrete and dumped in Boston Harbor.

MIT Berylliosis cases.title: SMS_F2014_05
MIT Berylliosis cases.frame: First berylliosis cases ever discovered — at MIT, post-WWII, in the Manhattan Project beryllium machining building at Mass Ave / Vassar. Ten percent of population genetically predisposed; fatal lung disease.

Non-sparking copper-beryllium tools for.title: SMS_F2013_12
Non-sparking copper-beryllium tools for.frame:
Beryllium's principal non-aerospace structural application. Cu-2-3%Be precipitation-hardened to 180–200 ksi; high thermal conductivity prevents frictional sparking. Used as the closing reason to study beryllium beyond spacecraft.

## §8 — Calcium / radium

Portland cement (calcium / dolomite-magn.title: SMS_F2013_12
Portland cement (calcium / dolomite-magn.frame: Calcium counts as a structural material — used in larger quantity than iron, as Portland cement. Limestone → kiln → CaO → Ca(OH)₂ with water. Some Portland is calcium-magnesium from dolomite ore.
Portland cement (calcium / dolomite-magn.case_name: Portland cement as a structural material

Radium cocktail consumer poisoning (1920.title: SMS_F2013_12
Radium cocktail consumer poisoning (1920.frame:
Brief teaching aside in the periodic-table survey. Wealthy consumer drank a daily glass of radium and rapidly decalcified. Used as comic relief and as the "anti-structural material" punchline before Tom turns to magnesium proper.

## §9 — Magnesium

Radium cocktail consumer poisoning (1920.title: FW_Su2013_03
Radium cocktail consumer poisoning (1920.frame: Brief illustrative aside on shifting public attitudes toward radioactivity — used to justify the welding industry's abandonment of thoriated tungsten electrodes in favor of cerium/lanthanum/yttrium oxide variants. Tom mentions the wealthy 1920s consumer who drank hundreds-of-dollars-per-drink radium tonics daily until his bones disintegrated.

Magnesium supply, applications, and Dow.title: SMS_F2013_12
Magnesium supply, applications, and Dow.frame: Quantity overview (250,000 tons globally vs. 40 million for aluminum, 1 billion for steel). Half goes to Al alloying; rest to steel desulfurization, nodular iron, tantalum/Nb reduction, and sacrificial anodes in hot-water tanks. Tom closes with Joel Clark's first PhD student's thesis tracking magnesium and aluminum prices in lockstep 1946–1975, attributing it to a Dow Chemical illegal cartel.
Magnesium supply, applications, and Dow.case_name: Magnesium supply, applications, and Dow Chemical cartel

Navy super-corroding magnesium composite.title: SMS_F2013_12
Navy super-corroding magnesium composite.frame: Navy Port Hueneme diving school developed magnesium-graphite/SiC composites that corroded faster than they could be metallographically polished (Latanision's work). Navy weaponized the corrosion: (1) divers crack-open packets to generate H₂ for salvage lift balloons; (2) divers pierce packets in cold water for exothermic warmth.

Magnesium weld stress-corrosion cracking.title: SMS_F2013_12
Magnesium weld stress-corrosion cracking.frame: Fusion-welded magnesium without stress relief will SCC from atmospheric humidity within two days. Reason most magnesium parts are castings (no residual stress) — auto wheels, dashboard structures.

Magnesium car fire from insurance fraud.title: SMS_F2013_12
Magnesium car fire from insurance fraud.frame: Tom's vivid example of magnesium ignition temperature — NYC arson of junker cars with mag wheels. Magnesium burns at ~4000 °F once gasoline-ignited; used as a flare and fireworks material in powder form.

Blackhawk helicopter high-performance ma.title: SMS_F2013_12
Blackhawk helicopter high-performance ma.frame:
Brief reference to a magazine article Tom has about Blackhawk magnesium use. Tied to US government's recurring multi-million-dollar low-cost-magnesium initiatives, foreshadowing the next lecture's Adam Powell guest talk.

## Figures referenced (not cases)

Mexican airline hot corrosion engine fai.title: WM_Su2014_03
Mexican airline hot corrosion engine fai.frame: Tom uses the NiCrAlY coating corrosion-rate-vs-temperature diagram to explain why Mexican carriers experienced sulfidation failures on turbine blades. The operational cause: skipping the runway preheat warmup and instead climbing to altitude with engines passing slowly through the 800–1000°C hot-corrosion window at full power.
Mexican airline hot corrosion engine fai.case_name: Mexican airline hot corrosion engine failure

Mexican airline hot corrosion engine fai.title: WM_Su2014_01
Mexican airline hot corrosion engine fai.case_name: Mexican airline hot corrosion engine failure

Fenway Frank hot dog cooker stainless st.title: WM_Su2014_03
Fenway Frank hot dog cooker stainless st.frame: The exemplar case for "wrong material" — one of the three legs of the Venn diagram of corrosion (material / stress / environment). A Fenway Franks steam-cooker tunnel in Everett, MA, specified as 316 stainless, had replacement parts fabricated in 304 instead. Within weeks, the 2% molybdenum difference produced visible chloride stress-corrosion cracking in the hot, salt-laden steam environment. Tom did the SEM analysis.
Fenway Frank hot dog cooker stainless st.case_name: Fenway Franks hot dog cooker (316/304 stainless substitution)

Destroyer steam line stress corrosion cr.title: WM_Su2014_03
Destroyer steam line stress corrosion cr.frame: Glancing reference. Tom invokes the case as a parallel example of "wrong material" — a Gulf War-era destroyer lost its 3000 psi steam line to stress-corrosion cracking because the wrong alloy was used. The case is developed elsewhere in the corpus.
Destroyer steam line stress corrosion cr.case_name: Destroyer steam line stress corrosion cracking (Gulf War)

Commercial jet engine in-flight failure.title: WM_Su2014_03
Commercial jet engine in-flight failure.case_name: Commercial jet engine in-flight failure rate

NiCrAlY coating corrosion rate vs. tempe.title: WM_Su2014_03
NiCrAlY coating corrosion rate vs. tempe.case_name: NiCrAlY coating corrosion rate vs. temperature

Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.title: WM_S2014_09
Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.frame: Tom's gold-standard example of disciplined hydrogen control: a 200 ksi steel mast electroplated and oven-baked within five minutes to drive off moisture. Used to set the bar before introducing the peashooter counter-example.
Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.case_name: Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking prevention

Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.title: WM_S2014_20
Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.frame: Critical non-welded high-strength steel part. Electroplated for corrosion resistance; within five minutes of leaving the plating bath it goes into the hydrogen bakeout oven, because the steel is high-strength and there's no redundancy — mast failure means loss of blades and no possibility of auto-rotation.
Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.case_name: Bell Helicopter mast electroplating and hydrogen bakeout

Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.title: WM_Su2014_20
Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.frame: Brief but specific. 4340 steel mast at 240 KSI, electroplating-induced hydrogen baked out at 375°F for 23 hours, transferred from plating bath to furnace in under 5 minutes. Used to illustrate (a) that hydrogen sources are not only welding and (b) that procedural rigor matters in proportion to consequence of failure ("you've only got one mast on a helicopter").
Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.case_name: Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen baking procedure

Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.title: WM_Su2015_06
Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.frame: Used to illustrate the <1 mL/100g hydrogen tolerance at 250 ksi for the highest-strength aerospace steels.
Bell Helicopter mast hydrogen cracking p.case_name: Helicopter rotor mast / blade high-strength steel hydrogen tolerance

Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.title: WM_S2014_09
Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.frame: Engine manufacturer's nitrided spline-shaft drive coupling cracking in service, causing helicopter crashes. The spec required hydrogen bake-out within one to four hours of nitriding; the process sheet started the clock when the metallurgical lab returned the coating-thickness reading two to three days later. Tom's case study in professional engineering duty: he reported the defective process through the attorney chain when he discovered it during litigation.
Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.case_name: Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding failure and lawsuit

Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.title: WM_S2014_26
Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.case_name: Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding failure and lawsuit

Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.title: WM_Su2014_21
Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.frame: Tom's ethical bind as a litigation expert. Manufacturer's QC procedure put parts in the dehydrogenation furnace within four hours of *the lab test results coming back*, not within four hours of the process — defeating the spec's purpose. Splines cracked, helicopters went down, people died. Tom notified through counsel; case tried in Lafayette, Louisiana; manufacturer ultimately fixed the process.
Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.case_name: Helicopter peashooter nitriding failure and lawsuit

Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.title: WM_Su2015_18
Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.frame: Three-quarter-inch high-speed transmission spline, nitrided for surface hardness. The 24-hour hydrogen bake-out was being performed *after* a three-day destructive case-thickness inspection, by which time delayed hydrogen cracking had already taken hold. Engine power loss in flight; people killed. ITAR-classified, so Tom (as US citizen) read the documents while the Canadian investigator could not. Tom invoked his professional duty to public safety to demand the manufacturer be notified outside the litigation timeline.
Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.case_name: Canadian aerospace helicopter spline nitriding hydrogen embrittlement

Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.title: WM_Su2014_20
Helicopter engine peashooter nitriding f.frame: Tom begins the case — nitrided high-hardness steel tube, ~3/4-inch diameter, ~$5,000 part, splined coupling between helicopter engine and transmission. A Vancouver-based metallurgist is mentioned as co-investigator. Recording cuts off before Tom describes the failure mode.

7500-ton forging press failure.title: WM_S2014_09
7500-ton forging press failure.frame: 1949-vintage 7,500-ton forging press used for forging aluminum truck wheels; cracked through a 14-inch section of cast steel cap (~60-ton, ~10 inches thick). Repair welded with 300–400 stick-electrode passes. First repair cracked before reinstallation; second repair cracked on first forging stroke; both failures attributed to hydrogen buried under successive passes without adequate post-heat. Tom uses it to teach why diffusivity (10⁻⁶ cm²/s) makes thick-section hydrogen extraction nearly impossible without staged post-heating.

7500-ton forging press failure.title: WM_S2014_22
7500-ton forging press failure.frame: Cited as the kind of heavy machinery that falls under AWS D14 (welded joints in machinery equipment) rather than D1 (structural) or the ASME boiler and pressure vessel code.

USS Battleship turret hydrogen cracking.title: WM_S2014_09
USS Battleship turret hydrogen cracking.frame: Battleship 16-inch turret explosion (Tom dates ~1980, Puerto Rico). Navy wanted to repair the 14-inch armor plate but had lost the WWII-era welding procedure — last used circa 1947, all the procedure-holders dead. Tom's case study in *technology loss*: a national-defense capability that decayed because nobody had welded that thick in 35 years.
USS Battleship turret hydrogen cracking.case_name: USS Battleship turret hydrogen cracking repair (Puerto Rico, ~1980)

USS Battleship turret hydrogen cracking.title: WM_S2014_18
USS Battleship turret hydrogen cracking.case_name: USS Battleship Iowa turret repair (Puerto Rico)

Shape charge development.title: WM_S2014_09
Shape charge development.frame: Single-sentence reference — shaped charges cutting through 14 inches, 36 inches of solid steel. Used to contextualize why heavy armor plate is no longer a defensive priority.

Pennsylvania roof collapses from 1980s s.title: CS_F2012_13
Pennsylvania roof collapses from 1980s s.frame: Computer-aided design that shaved safety factors via doubler-plate beams; battery plant burned to the ground, fire trucks unable to reach through six-foot snow drifts. No one hurt.

NASA X-33 space plane composite tank fai.title: CS_F2012_13
NASA X-33 space plane composite tank fai.frame: Knowing manufacturing defect; engineers shaved the factor-of-two safety factor down to 1.05 via fracture mechanics calculations and lost the tank to thermal stresses on liquid nitrogen fill. $1.3 billion project cancelled.
NASA X-33 space plane composite tank fai.case_name: NASA X-33 space plane composite tank failure

Liberty ships and the *SS Schenectady* /.title: CS_F2012_13
Liberty ships and the *SS Schenectady* /.frame: The anchoring case for the entire bulking-up arc. 4,700 ships built in WWII; 970 (22%) had major fracture casualties; 24 sustained complete strength-deck fracture. All low-toughness plates: Charpy < 10 ft-lb.
Liberty ships and the *SS Schenectady* /.case_name: Liberty ships and the *SS Schenectady* / *Esso* fracture

Quincy Shipyard LNG tanker aluminum sphe.title: CS_F2012_13
Quincy Shipyard LNG tanker aluminum sphe.frame: Double- and triple-tempered A537 steel barely meeting 20 ft-lb spec; shipyard cut Charpy samples from the rare high-toughness plates, used the rest in production, and the actual ship welds were tested only via runoff tabs that bore no relation to the shipboard joints.
Quincy Shipyard LNG tanker aluminum sphe.case_name: Quincy Shipyard LNG tanker aluminum sphere skirts

Japanese low-sulfur A36 steel market dis.title: CS_F2012_13
Japanese low-sulfur A36 steel market dis.frame: Aside in response to student question. Japanese mills built greenfield with low-sulfur processing baked in; sold garden-variety A36 cheaper than US "premium" steel.
Japanese low-sulfur A36 steel market dis.case_name: Japanese low-sulfur A36 plate market disruption

Japanese low-sulfur A36 steel market dis.title: WM_Su2014_14
Japanese low-sulfur A36 steel market dis.frame: Tom's experience as Bethlehem Steel engineer. Japanese suppliers selling A360 I-beams with 0.005 sulfur as standard; Bethlehem trying to extract a $20/ton (8%) premium for low-sulfur and failing. Part of the broader U.S. Steel industry decline narrative.

Alaska Pipeline brittle fracture risk as.title: CS_F2012_13
Alaska Pipeline brittle fracture risk as.frame: The economic case: $60M/day (1970s) to $200M/day (today) of oil flow means the operator has more skin in the game than any environmentalist. Cited to motivate the 80-ft-lb base-plate proposal that follows.
Alaska Pipeline brittle fracture risk as.case_name: Alaska Pipeline brittle fracture risk assessment

Alaska Pipeline brittle fracture risk as.title: MSE_F2016_08
Alaska Pipeline brittle fracture risk as.frame: Tom worked at Bethlehem Steel on high-toughness steel for the Alaskan pipeline. 70 foot-pound Charpy requirement to stop a running brittle crack, motivated by prior pipeline fractures that ran 30 miles.
Alaska Pipeline brittle fracture risk as.case_name: Alaska Pipeline brittle fracture risk assessment

Gas pipeline brittle fracture propagatio.title: CS_F2012_13
Gas pipeline brittle fracture propagatio.frame: Decompression velocity in gas < fracture velocity → crack tip always sees full pressure → 30-mile cracks. Two responses: A710 crack-arrestor rings; raise base-plate toughness to 80 ft-lb.
Gas pipeline brittle fracture propagatio.case_name: Gas pipeline brittle fracture propagation / Alaska gas pipeline feasibility

V-22 Osprey crash (Ship 4).title: CS_F2012_13
V-22 Osprey crash (Ship 4).frame: Carbon-fiber drive shaft between rotors burned through in hydraulic-fluid engine fire; the redundancy that was supposed to let the aircraft survive engine loss was defeated by the fire-vulnerability of the cross-shaft. Redesigned with titanium drive shafts.

Iran hostage rescue helicopter limitatio.title: CS_F2012_13
Iran hostage rescue helicopter limitatio.frame: Brief — the motivation for tilt-rotor research. Helicopters too noisy; tip-speed approaches Mach 1.

Boeing 747-400 catalytic converter titan.title: CS_F2012_13
Boeing 747-400 catalytic converter titan.frame: Engelhard making titanium catalytic-converter housings for cabin air ozone treatment. Boeing's x-ray spec called for no flaw > 10 thousandths — a limit chosen by NDT detectability, not by any analysis of the service application (low-pressure air). Half of all welds failed; with four welds per part and one allowed repair, virtually nothing could ship. Tom diagnosed the spec as bureaucratic CYA.
Boeing 747-400 catalytic converter titan.case_name: Boeing 747-400 catalytic converter titanium welding "stupid spec"

MAP gas cylinder drop and bending incide.title: CS_F2012_13
MAP gas cylinder drop and bending incide.frame: 30-thousandths steel can't fail by overpressure (safety factor enormous, ~7×) — fails by abuse: torquing off with 80 ft-lb bar bends it; plumber-with-cigar incident; throw-it-on-the-ground crack initiation at 25–30° bend.
MAP gas cylinder drop and bending incide.case_name: MAP gas cylinder drop and bending incidents

Fire sprinkler head misuse as coat hook.title: CS_F2012_13
Fire sprinkler head misuse as coat hook.frame: Precision device with Wood's metal melting sensor at 160°F; creep above 100°F storage temperature degrades the rating. NFPA forbids storage above 100°F; refrigerated trucks used for Texas-origin shipments.
Fire sprinkler head misuse as coat hook.case_name: Fire sprinkler head misuse as coat hook / Wood's metal creep

Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing li.title: CS_F2012_13
Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing li.frame: Three-generation product evolution. Original yellow jacket: 0.1 coulomb capacity (typical strike is 3–5 coulombs). Black carbon-filled: ~5 coulombs. Perforated aluminum sheet: ~80 coulombs. 200–300 fires/year through the transition. Original product taken off North American market only September 2011.
Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing li.case_name: Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing lightning fires

Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing li.title: SMS_S2016_07
Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing li.frame: Japanese-developed corrugated stainless steel tubing with polyethylene coating allows one-day gas plumbing of a new home (vs. three days for black iron pipe) at five dollars/foot. But pinhole "holiday" defects in the coating, while not a problem at 110V, are catastrophic against millions-of-volts lightning bolts. About a hundred home fires per year. The industry denies and admits it; half-a-billion-dollar annual profit keeps the product on market.
Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing li.case_name: Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing lightning fires

Pittsburgh Plate Glass mile-long factory.title: SMS_S2016_12
Pittsburgh Plate Glass mile-long factory.frame: Pre-Ford plate-glass production: cast onto a metal table, rolled and polished along a mile-long building. Used to set up the productivity contrast with the later float process (50-yard building).

Black light bulb eye injury case.title: SMS_S2016_12
Black light bulb eye injury case.frame: Forensic consulting case. Hand-blown black-light incandescent bulb made in Korea for GE, not properly annealed; water drop after a shower caused the bulb to explode and blind the user. Compared to properly-annealed Corning-line bulbs that withstand water drops indefinitely. The teaching example for residual stress from poor thermal annealing of blown glass.
Black light bulb eye injury case.case_name: Black light bulb eye injury case

Black light bulb eye injury case.title: DP_S2012_12
Black light bulb eye injury case.frame: Korean hand-blown black light bulb shattered when soapy water dripped on hot bulb; teenager lost an eye. Tom proposed a drop test he wasn't allowed to run himself; students ran it and confirmed residual stresses caused the failure. Case settled.
Black light bulb eye injury case.case_name: Black light bulb eye injury case (forensic)

Freshly made light bulb strength demonst.title: SMS_S2016_12
Freshly made light bulb strength demonst.frame: Tom's thesis advisor Bob (Uhlmann/Rose — see editorial register) would obtain freshly-made light bulbs from the Sylvania North Shore plant and demonstrate in 3.091 that a bulb thrown against the wall would bounce when fresh and shatter two days later, illustrating humidity-driven Griffith-criterion surface flaw formation.
Freshly made light bulb strength demonst.case_name: Sylvania North Shore light bulb plant (Bob's freshly-made bulb)

Freshly made light bulb strength demonst.title: DP_S2012_12
Freshly made light bulb strength demonst.frame: Combined with the Bob Rose anecdote; explains why fiberglass is coated with epoxy immediately after drawing — to preserve the 200 ksi surface strength before moisture corrosion creates micron-scale flaws that destroy fracture toughness.
Freshly made light bulb strength demonst.case_name: Freshly made light bulb strength demonstration

MRAP armor development for Iraq.title: SMS_S2016_12
MRAP armor development for Iraq.frame: Shaped-charge history (Brooklyn Navy Yard, 1880s) → conical copper liners produce a three-foot molten-copper jet that penetrates three feet of steel → IEDs in Iraq/Afghanistan defeating Humvees → Army study of titanium, steel, aluminum, and six materials → glass selected as MRAP belly armor (six layers of two-inch glass). Textron Systems (Wilmington, MA) makes the copper liners. Aberdeen Proving Ground Army lab demonstration.

Brooklyn Navy Yard shaped-charge discove.title: SMS_S2016_12
Brooklyn Navy Yard shaped-charge discove.frame: 1880s discovery of the shaped-charge effect with conical copper. Origin story for the RPG/IED case.

Brooklyn Navy Yard shaped-charge discove.title: SMS_F2014_12
Brooklyn Navy Yard shaped-charge discove.frame: "The U.S. Navy discovered this in the 1880s at the Brooklyn Navy Yard by mistake, while they were doing some explosives work." Tom's origin story for the shaped charge.

Protective Armor Systems (PAS) bullet-re.title: SMS_S2016_12
Protective Armor Systems (PAS) bullet-re.frame: Western Massachusetts company. Four-layer glass-polycarbonate-glass laminate stops .38 and .45 rounds; thicker versions (4.5") in presidential limousine stop RPGs.

John Hancock Building glass cracking fai.title: SMS_S2016_12
John Hancock Building glass cracking fai.frame: Originally specified plate glass that cracked and fell to the street under wind loading. Required three years of total U.S. chemically-tempered-glass production (lithium-for-sodium/potassium ion exchange) to re-glaze. The classic structural-glass failure case.
John Hancock Building glass cracking fai.case_name: John Hancock Building chemically tempered glass

John Hancock Building glass cracking fai.title: SMS_F2014_12
John Hancock Building glass cracking fai.frame: Tom uses the building both as a structural-glass failure case (wind-induced suction popping windows out) and as a tuned-mass-damper case (whole floor with rotating weight to damp sway). Chemically tempered glass was the fix.

Corningware three-layer glass-ceramic.title: SMS_S2016_12
Corningware three-layer glass-ceramic.frame: Modern Corningware: three glass layers rolled together with the center having higher coefficient of thermal expansion than the skins, producing compressive surface stress on cooling. Stamp-forged into ramekins and casseroles. Replaces the earlier low-CTE glass-ceramic body.

Professor Uhlmann's chemically tempered.title: SMS_S2016_12
Professor Uhlmann's chemically tempered.frame: Tom's teacher (D. R. Uhlmann; cluster name in aggregate uses captioner mishearing "Omen") demonstrated chemically tempered glass by hand-flattening a curved 18″ × 3″ piece without breaking it. The pedagogical demonstration of ion-exchange surface compression.
Professor Uhlmann's chemically tempered.case_name: Professor Uhlmann's chemically tempered glass demonstration

Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home - transpar.title: SMS_S2016_12
Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home - transpar.frame: Rhetorical contrast — Scotty's fictional "transparent aluminum" used to illustrate that real metals cannot be transparent because of free electrons.

60 Wall Street (JP Morgan building) air.title: CS_Su2012_05
60 Wall Street (JP Morgan building) air.frame: Rush erection of a 40-story building with 16-inch air conditioning riser pipes welded in place by welders hanging off I-beams with no inspector access. Welds passed visual inspection from outside but had no penetration past about a quarter inch. Ten years later, JP Morgan spent $7M to relocate an air conditioning compressor to the 10th-floor ledge to protect the 7th-floor trading computers (which could lose ~$1B/minute), and $20M+ more to repair the riser pipe — a $100K inspection problem turned into a $60M+ lawsuit. Used to anchor the "you only get what you pay for" principle.

Hyatt Regency walkway collapse.title: CS_Su2012_05
Hyatt Regency walkway collapse.frame: Suspended walkway in Kansas City Hyatt lobby. As-designed: single threaded rods through the C-channels of multiple walkway levels, requiring a nut threaded up many stories during erection. Erection changed it to extended/doubled rods, converting straight tension on the threaded rod into shear loading on the box-beam C-channel — a connection never sized for shear. Procedure existed for sign-off on changes; it was not followed. 114 dead, 200 injured; the building lobby was subsequently reduced to two stories.

Hyatt Regency walkway collapse.title: WM_Su2014_24
Hyatt Regency walkway collapse.frame: Structural analog. Kansas City, circa 1980. Tension threaded rods (not stainless) in shear connection failed in indoor atrium during a party; several hundred casualties. Tom invokes it as ethical-stakes anchor for his Miami decision: tension connections in occupied space.

Hyatt Regency walkway collapse.title: CS_F2012_11
Hyatt Regency walkway collapse.frame: The lecture's centerpiece forensic case. July 17, 1981, Kansas City. The original detail design called for solid hanger rods, threaded only at the ends; field fabricators, unable to thread a nut 15 feet down a solid rod, substituted a two-rod stagger that doubled the load on the upper rod's C-channel connection. The change was approved (or missed) under the high-volume change-order process. 114 dead, 200+ injured. Used to illustrate the as-designed vs. as-built distinction and to introduce the engineer-of-record concept. Cites Petroski's *To Engineer is Human*.

Ford Taurus air conditioner compressor.title: CS_Su2012_05
Ford Taurus air conditioner compressor.frame: Single-shuttle-piston compressor design — two cylinders, one piston, sub-thousandth clearance. Engineers specified prototype fixturing; the machinist silently used a different fixture because he knew the engineer's design wouldn't hold tolerance. Prototype worked; Ford built a $100M production line to the original (bad) fixture spec; production parts didn't fit. Tom personally affected — bought a Taurus in February, no working A/C until June, dealer had no compressors because all new ones went to assembly. Moral: communicate with hourly workers.

Ford Taurus air conditioner compressor.title: SSW_S2013_08
Ford Taurus air conditioner compressor.frame: Tom bought a Ford Taurus in February 1990; air conditioner didn't work when he tried it in May. Source of the story is Kim Clark (later Harvard Business School dean). Ford had spent $100M tooling a production line based on engineer-designed fixturing for a tight-tolerance compressor piston, but the prototype machinist had ignored the prescribed fixturing and used his own method; production line couldn't replicate the prototype's results. Tom got his car fixed in three weeks after threatening lemon-law action.

Ford Taurus air conditioner compressor.title: CS_F2012_11
Ford Taurus air conditioner compressor.frame: Personal forensic case. Tom bought a 1990 or 1991 Taurus in February; the AC failed when first switched on in May. Ford's $100M production line had been built with clamping fixtures matching the engineering drawings, but the prototype machinist had built his own (correct) clamping fixture and never told the engineers. The as-built of the prototype was lost. Tom invokes the Massachusetts lemon law and his Ford VP connections to get a replacement AC. Used to illustrate prototype-to-production handoff failure. The Harvard Business School story attribution is preserved.

1988 nor'easter structural collapses (Ne.title: CS_Su2012_05
1988 nor'easter structural collapses (Ne.frame: "300-year storm" Pennsylvania snowstorm collapsed mall/shopping-center roofs supported by mini-mill bar joists. Mini-mills had competed by varying truss member thickness using mid-1980s PCs (128K RAM, 20MB disk) — but the computer models assumed symmetric concurrence at joints, while as-built joints had small offsets producing shear loading. Steel sheared just like Hyatt Regency. Tom got two years of forensic work from this storm.

Faberware Millennium cookware hydrogen c.title: DP_S2012_11
Faberware Millennium cookware hydrogen c.frame: Tom's full forensic walkthrough of the case. Farberware came to him through the MIT Industrial Liaison Program after Millennium Cookware pots shipped to Japan developed cracks running parallel to the drawing axis during the voyage. Tom used a magnet to demonstrate that 301 stainless deep-drawing had transformed the FCC austenite to BCC martensite (TRIP behavior), creating the cathode for hydrogen embrittlement. Source of hydrogen identified as the argon-5% hydrogen atmosphere used to spray-deposit the stainless steel powder substrate for the Teflon coating. Tom uses the case to teach: (1) that 70% of metallurgists conflate stress corrosion cracking with hydrogen embrittlement, (2) that the distinction is anode (SCC) vs. cathode (HE), and (3) that delayed cracking with stainless on a bench is the diagnostic giveaway for hydrogen.

Soviet Titanium Aircraft Program (Docket.title: WM_Su2014_26
Soviet Titanium Aircraft Program (Docket.frame: The technical story: Soviets built titanium subs that outran U.S. destroyers and dove below depth-charge collapse depth. But they hadn't solved (or known about) creep-fatigue interaction — the phenomenon NRL had studied, where titanium under sustained compression develops rapidly-growing fatigue cracks. A submarine hull in deep water is exactly that compression case. The Soviet subs cracked and were noisy.

Three Mile Island.title: WM_Su2015_12
Three Mile Island.frame: Used to introduce the stress-corrosion-cracking vs. stress-assisted-cracking distinction as an insurance-policy issue. GPU's attorney reads the policy, finds corrosion is excluded, and the terminology gets rewritten — a "day and a half" later — to remove "corrosion" from the press releases.

Three Mile Island.title: WM_Su2014_05
Three Mile Island.frame: The *sister* reactor (reactor 2) to the famous accident. Restart attempt produced polythionic acid attack on a nickel-based superalloy heat exchanger; stress corrosion cracking in thirty minutes; $30 million repair. Used as the worked example of the legal distinction between "stress corrosion cracking" (insurance-excluded) and "stress-assisted cracking" (insurance-covered) — and as a case study in how attorneys rename phenomena to fit contract language.

Lead-tin solder ban (1978) and Boston fi.title: SMS_S2016_07
Lead-tin solder ban (1978) and Boston fi.frame: Externalities of material selection. The 1978 ban shifted plumbers to 95-5 (tin-antimony) solder, which produced more leaky joints. Combined with Boston's hot-work fire-watch requirement (paid off-duty firefighter at sixty dollars/hour), this drove adoption of mechanical crimp-on copper fittings ("PEX-A" cross-linked polyethylene became dominant in new construction).

Boston cast iron water main failures.frame: Cast iron pipe graphitizes (decarbonizes) over ~100 years, losing strength. Five percent of Boston's water lost through leaks; periodic main breaks cause ten-million-dollar downtown damage events.
Boston cast iron water main failures.case_name: Boston cast iron water main failures

US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe cor.title: SMS_S2016_07
US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe cor.frame: Carbon steel piping corroded out in ~25 years against the 30-year ship life. Tom's anecdote of the ensign whose entire shipboard duty was leak repair. Transition to titanium for 50-year hulls.
US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe cor.case_name: US Navy nuclear submarine titanium piping

US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe cor.title: WM_Su2015_08
US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe cor.frame: Ships originally designed for 30-year service life have been extended to 40, then 50 years. The 1990s–2000s transition period saw extensive carbon-steel piping replacement before the move to copper-nickel seawater piping on new ships.
US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe cor.case_name: US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe corrosion (30-year ship life)

US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe cor.title: WM_Su2014_05
US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe cor.frame: The 25–30 year carbon steel piping life was historically the ship-life limit. NAVSEA's move to 50-year ships forced the substitution to cupro-nickel → Monel → titanium for seawater systems on nuclear subs.
US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe cor.case_name: US Navy nuclear submarine steel pipe corrosion (30-year ship life)

Boeing 747-400 titanium catalytic conver.title: SMS_S2016_07
Boeing 747-400 titanium catalytic conver.frame: Extended teaching case. Boeing's general spec required x-ray inspection of titanium welds with no flaw larger than ten thousandths of an inch. Englehard, accustomed to stainless steel cleanliness practices, was failing 25–50% of welds from hydrogen porosity caused by hydrocarbon contamination. Tom's diagnosis: reagent-grade acetone degreasing and white gloves. The case recurs: Englehard succeeded, then reverted to non-reagent-grade acetone and failed again. Tom flags an identical case at GE Lynn with electron beam welds in titanium.

Boston historical wooden gas pipes (gun-.title: SMS_S2016_07

NASA cold welding research initiative.title: SSW_S2013_05
NASA cold welding research initiative.frame: The Mercury graphite-lubricant failure (knobs sticking in vacuum) motivated NASA to fund cold welding research, including the 1967 ASM conference and the *Adhesion or Cold Welding of Materials in Space Environments* volume Tom holds up.

Mercury/Apollo program graphite lubrican.title: SSW_S2013_05
Mercury/Apollo program graphite lubrican.frame: Used to teach why graphite is a lubricant at atmosphere (CO₂/O₂ absorbed on basal planes) but an abrasive in vacuum. Astronauts' knobs sticking.

Mercury/Apollo program graphite lubrican.title: SSW_S2013_03
Mercury/Apollo program graphite lubrican.frame: Forward reference to Friday's lecture. Graphite is a lubricant on Earth (water vapor intercalates between planes) but an abrasive in vacuum; early Mercury shots seized when this was not understood.

Incandescent light bulb development (Edi.title: SSW_S2013_05
Incandescent light bulb development (Edi.frame: Used to introduce the Langmuir as a unit of contamination time. Edison's carbonized horsehair filaments → tungsten in argon → factor-of-100 longer life from suppressing evaporation.
Incandescent light bulb development (Edi.case_name: Incandescent light bulb development (Edison and Langmuir)

Incandescent light bulb development (Edi.title: WIE_F2015_02
Incandescent light bulb development (Edi.frame: Brief reference. Edison's horsehair filament was superseded by tungsten; GE spent a hundred years perfecting tungsten light bulbs only to have LEDs come along. Used to make the point that engineering investments can be obsoleted by technology transitions.

HMS Sheffield.title: SSW_S2013_05
HMS Sheffield.frame: Galvanic-corrosion theory of why the aluminum superstructure of the Sheffield burned after the Exocet hit. Connects to the steel-aluminum transition joint case (§4.p1). Tom flags this as a disputed theory.

HMS Sheffield.title: WM_Su2014_10
HMS Sheffield.frame: Falkland Islands War — Exocet missile strike; debate over whether aluminum superstructure fire was the cause. Navy operationally believed it was, evidenced by mid-80s waffle-steel superstructure replacement program for surface ships.

HMS Sheffield.title: SSW_S2013_02
HMS Sheffield.frame: A single Argentinian-fired French Exocet missile started an aluminum fire that wiped out a British capital ship. Used to motivate US Navy particle-beam weapon development.

HMS Sheffield.title: REC_F2018_02
HMS Sheffield.frame: Cited as another perennial student-paper topic. Tom summarizes the standard account (Exocet missile, aluminum superstructure fire) and notes the cause "is still debated" — pointing students toward forming their own theory rather than repeating the narrative.

Paper slitter knife company evaluation.frame: Consulting case ca. 1984, Danvers MA. Canadian timber baron client considering acquisition of a small slitter-knife maker who had developed a new heat-treating and brazing process delivering six times blade life. Tom's recommendation: don't buy unless you can grow the market — six-fold life on a $25M business shrinks the business absent new applications.

Norton asphalt reclamation carbide-tip b.frame: Asphalt-reclamation tooling: traditional tungsten carbide tip replaced with brazed sintered-diamond tip for longer life. Roughly 1 cm of sintered diamond brazed to a steel body; survives high-impact road grinding.

Norton asphalt reclamation carbide-tip b.title: SSW_S2013_12
Norton asphalt reclamation carbide-tip b.frame: Tom's student developed an in-situ composite braze alloy (Cu-Sn-TiH2-C) for brazing carbide bits to highway asphalt-reclamation tooling. Titanium hydride decomposes in vacuum brazing, releasing Ti metal which reacts with C to form TiC particles in the joint. Result: braze alloy CTE halved vs. Cu-base; tool life tripled in field test on actual road surfaces. Failure mode addressed: tip loss during overnight road work stopping the whole reclamation machine.

Composite submarine repairability failur.title: FW_Su2013_04
Composite submarine repairability failur.frame: Congress, frustrated with the SSN-21 (later Seawolf) program and still chasing the leapfrog idea even after the titanium-sub case had collapsed, zeroed the Navy's $100M design budget and redirected it to DARPA to design an all-composite submarine. After the Secretary of the Navy lobbied back the $100M, DARPA retained its parallel funding and convened a three-day Reston, Virginia workshop with metals and composites communities. The composites group's conceptual design featured large hatch doors for equipment removal — exposing the fact that the aerospace composites community (which had not yet flown an all-composite aircraft; the V-22 Osprey was the first) had no understanding of submarine interior geometry or the constraint that composite hulls cannot be cut and repaired. The Patrick Henry's hull patchwork was shown as the cautionary case.

Composite submarine repairability failur.title: CAS_Su2011_02
Composite submarine repairability failur.frame: After Congress zeroed Captain ("Admiral"-self-corrected-to-"Captain") Fireball's $100M Seawolf design budget and gave it to DARPA for "something beyond titanium," a three-day Reston VA workshop convened composites proponents. Congress later restored the Seawolf money while keeping DARPA's. Tom files it alongside Star Wars and the National Aerospace Plane as defense fantasy untethered from physics.

Composite submarine repairability failur.title: CAS_Su2011_03
Composite submarine repairability failur.frame: Brief reference — Navy built some all-composite ships and found "they didn't work so well"; steel's modulus advantage at large scale.
Composite submarine repairability failur.case_name: Composite submarine repairability failure / Navy composite ships

Plasma torch discovery by Bob Gage.title: FW_Su2013_04
Plasma torch discovery by Bob Gage.frame: Bob Gage at Union Carbide Speedway Labs (Indianapolis) in the 1950s was studying water-cooled GTA arcs on copper and serendipitously drilled a hole in the copper plate; the plasma flame shooting through the hole was the first plasma torch and led to constricted-arc processes.
Plasma torch discovery by Bob Gage.case_name: Plasma torch discovery by Bob Gage

Space Shuttle External Tank (2219 alumin.title: FW_Su2013_04
Space Shuttle External Tank (2219 alumin.frame: NASA prefers variable-polarity plasma arc (VPPA) over GTA for welding the Shuttle main tanks because the higher heat intensity is better matched to aluminum's high thermal conductivity, and the AC component helps disrupt the stable aluminum oxide.
Space Shuttle External Tank (2219 alumin.case_name: NASA X-33 / Space Shuttle main tank welding (variable polarity plasma arc)

Space Shuttle External Tank (2219 alumin.title: WM_S2014_22
Space Shuttle External Tank (2219 alumin.frame: 2219 chosen as the rare aluminum-copper alloy with good weldability. Tank had to be welded; leaks were unacceptable.

Space Shuttle External Tank (2219 alumin.title: WM_Su2015_14
Space Shuttle External Tank (2219 alumin.frame: Example of why 2219 was chosen for the Space Shuttle main tank — more weldable than other 2000-series Al-Cu alloys. ~4.5% copper.

Space Shuttle External Tank (2219 alumin.title: WM_Su2014_29
Space Shuttle External Tank (2219 alumin.frame: Tom uses 2219 — the external expendable tank alloy — to illustrate aluminum-copper liquation cracking at grain boundaries.

Cadmium oxide electrical switch ban and.title: FW_Su2013_04
Cadmium oxide electrical switch ban and.frame: Silver–cadmium-oxide contacts (~1% CdO) double the current-carrying capacity of light-switch contacts and prevent sustained arcing on switch-off. Sweden banned cadmium on toxicity grounds ~30 years prior to the lecture and within three years had to reverse the ban after house fires from un-extinguished switch arcs. Paracelsus's "the dose makes the poison" framing invoked.
Cadmium oxide electrical switch ban and.case_name: Sweden cadmium electrical switch fire hazard

National Lightning Detection Network.title: FW_Su2013_04
National Lightning Detection Network.frame: Cited as a real-world example of RF detection from electric arcs — 17 U.S. stations triangulate every lightning strike to within 3–5 km and estimate strike current from EMI.

Rosenthal traveling-heat-source equation.title: FW_Su2013_04
Rosenthal traveling-heat-source equation.frame: Daniel Rosenthal — Jewish, fleeing Germany in 1939 through the Netherlands and Morocco, arriving at MIT mechanical engineering by 1940 — solved the traveling distributed point heat source problem during the journey and published three ASME Journal papers. Later UCLA materials science professor.

Nils Christensen and the dimensionless R.title: FW_Su2013_04
Nils Christensen and the dimensionless R.frame: Norwegian freedom fighter during WWII (skiing across the Sweden–Norway border), Christensen came to MIT post-war on scholarship to work with John Chipman on welding fluxes. His first doctoral thesis manuscript was lost — Tom relates Christensen's surmise that Soviet spies at MIT stole it; he redid the work in nine extra months. Later, laid up in a Trondheim hospital bed in the mid-1960s, he extended Rosenthal's solution to dimensionless form, published in the *British Welding Journal* (1966). Returned to MIT for a sabbatical in the early 1980s; now deceased.
Nils Christensen and the dimensionless R.case_name: Nils Christensen and the dimensionless Rosenthal solution

Nunsen Chai distributed heat source PDP-.title: FW_Su2013_04
Nunsen Chai distributed heat source PDP-.frame: Tom's student in the early 1980s, using a PDP-11/23 (16-bit, 10 MB hard drives at ~$1000) with weekend-long runs, extended Rosenthal's point-source solution to a distributed heat source on the GTA arc, computing variable depth-to-width ratios via Green's function superposition. Chai is now number two at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.

Vivek Dave subsurface heat distribution.title: FW_Su2013_04
Vivek Dave subsurface heat distribution.frame: Under DARPA sponsorship in the early 1990s, Dave extended the Chai distributed-surface heat source to include heat distribution beneath the surface (surface depression effects). Cited as the last step in the lineage before finite-element methods made the analytical extensions obsolete.
Vivek Dave subsurface heat distribution.case_name: Vivek Dave subsurface heat distribution work (early 1990s)

USS Patrick Henry hull degradation.title: FW_Su2013_04
USS Patrick Henry hull degradation.frame: At the DARPA composite-submarine workshop, photographs of the Patrick Henry (just then approaching disposal off the Virginia coast) showed dozens of hull cutouts accumulated over 30 years of service — used to argue to the composites team that submarine hulls must be cuttable and repairable.
USS Patrick Henry hull degradation.case_name: USS Patrick Henry hull cutout patchwork

USS Patrick Henry hull degradation.title: WM_Su2015_12
USS Patrick Henry hull degradation.frame: Tom's 1988 picture of the Patrick Henry showed a "patchwork quilt" of hull penetrations. Used to make the point that hull lifetime is limited not by the steel's corrosion or metallurgy but by geometric deviation from a perfect cylinder after thirty years of cut-and-reweld work.

Spot welding excessive current test.title: FW_Su2013_04
Spot welding excessive current test.frame: Brief callback to the prior session's story about pushing spot welding to ~2000 A — at which point the J² scaling of the plasma jet force makes the molten metal spray uncontrollably, the same physics that limits GTA above ~200 A to "humped bead" defects.

Arc blow magnetization in shipyard weldi.title: FW_Su2013_04
Arc blow magnetization in shipyard weldi.frame: Tom references his Friday discussion of stud welding as the original setup for the arc-blow discussion — current turning 90° through a long thin workpiece concentrates the magnetic field on the inside of the bend and pushes the arc outward.
Arc blow magnetization in shipyard weldi.case_name: Stud welding (Friday lecture callback) and arc blow

Arthur Amos Noyes MIT to Caltech transit.title: FW_Su2013_04
Arthur Amos Noyes MIT to Caltech transit.frame: Cited (Tom couldn't recall the name on tape; bracketed in L3) as illustration of the German dominance of physical chemistry through ~1900 — the founder of Caltech, formerly MIT acting president, had studied in Germany around the turn of the century. Used to motivate why MIT undergraduates were required to read German in the 1880s.
Arthur Amos Noyes MIT to Caltech transit.case_name: Arthur Amos Noyes / Caltech founding (German scientific dominance)

MIT Leeb fluorescent light loudspeaker p.title: FW_Su2013_04
MIT Leeb fluorescent light loudspeaker p.frame: MIT EECS professor Steven Leeb patented use of fluorescent lighting fixtures as building-wide loudspeakers for emergency announcements, exploiting the same arc-modulation physics by which a 20-kW transistorized arc supply in Tom's lab could be talked through. A European company sells $10,000 GTA-based audiophile speakers exploiting the same effect (with Tom's "you can sell anything to a music aficionado" aside on monster cables).

Central Artery tunnel project (Boston).title: FW_Su2013_04
Central Artery tunnel project (Boston).frame: Tom's pun-bridge between "depressing" the weld pool and depressing the Central Artery — $17B final cost vs. $2B original estimate; the depression concept was proposed by one of Tom's MIT civil-engineering classmates. The Keverian/Dukakis "how do you depress the Central Artery" jokes are characteristic Tom local-color material.

Ragnar and Else Holm electric contacts a.title: FW_Su2013_04
Ragnar and Else Holm electric contacts a.frame: German émigré scientist Ragnar Holm (with his wife Else, both PhDs, of Saint Marys, Pennsylvania) at Westinghouse wrote *Electric Contacts* (now in its 4th edition) and derived the contact-asperity heating equivalence between the voltage and temperature fields (both Laplace's equation). His table of softening/melting/boiling voltages (Ag at 90 mV softening, 0.41 V melting Cu, 1.1 V melting W, etc.) explains that arc ignition in welding occurs by boiling metal asperities during contact separation at sub-volt voltages — *not* by Paschen breakdown or field emission as welding handbooks still claim. The IEEE Holm Conference is named for him.
Ragnar and Else Holm electric contacts a.case_name: Ragnar and Else Holm electric-contacts research

1985 RPG armor penetration demonstration.title: SMS_F2014_12
1985 RPG armor penetration demonstration.frame: Same demonstration as above, viewed from the RPG side: "they shot an RPG and it went through six layers of armor, through both sides of all three tanks." Likely the same event as the Aberdeen test.

1984-1986 composite armor development cy.title: SMS_F2014_12
1984-1986 composite armor development cy.frame: "In 1984 there was no armor that could not be penetrated; by 1986 there was no propellant that could penetrate the modern armor." The composite metal-ceramic armor solution.

Four-inch and eight-inch IED escalation.title: SMS_F2014_12
Four-inch and eight-inch IED escalation.frame: Tom traces the technical escalation: four-inch pipe (~200 kJ) → eight-inch pipe (1.6 MJ), with foreign-machined copper liner discs. The pipe was Iraqi oilfield stock; the precision-machined copper liner came from a country Tom cannot name on tape (classified).
Four-inch and eight-inch IED escalation.case_name: Four-inch and eight-inch IED escalation in Iraq

Watertown Arsenal Civil War shot tower.title: SMS_F2014_12
Watertown Arsenal Civil War shot tower.frame: Background context for the Army materials lab — "since the 1860s that was the U.S. Army's materials lab. They used to make cannonballs there."
Watertown Arsenal Civil War shot tower.case_name: Watertown Arsenal Civil War shot tower

Williams Tower elevator marble finishes.title: SMS_F2014_12
Williams Tower elevator marble finishes.frame: Twelve elevators with twelve different European marbles — Tom's example of marble as a beautiful but limited material when sealed.

Corian countertop thermal cracking.title: SMS_F2014_12
Corian countertop thermal cracking.frame: Tom's own kitchen — DuPont Corian countertops, mid-1980s. Hot griddle without reflective trivet caused thermal-expansion compression; on cooling, the surface cracked. DuPont reformulated three years later.

Andrew Mellon all-aluminum Pierce Arrow.title: SMS_F2014_12
Andrew Mellon all-aluminum Pierce Arrow.frame: Slide image. Aluminum horse carriages and Pierce-Arrow at New Kensington, Pennsylvania in 1909, as part of Tom's aluminum-history pivot.

Mellon Bank funded Charles Martin Hall's Alcoa; the all-aluminum Pierce Arrow appears in a book Tom owns.

Alcoa monopoly and price fixing with Dow.title: SMS_F2014_12
Alcoa monopoly and price fixing with Dow.frame: George Kenney's doctoral thesis (under Joel Clark, 1975) showed Alcoa and Dow had matched aluminum/magnesium prices from 1945 to 1975, evidence of a market-division agreement: Alcoa stays out of magnesium, Dow stays out of aluminum.

Washington Monument design safety factor.title: SMS_F2014_12
Washington Monument design safety factor.frame: Tom uses the Washington Monument's aluminum-tip lightning rod as evidence of aluminum's once-precious status in the 1880s. Not a structural-design story in this telling.

Washington Monument design safety factor.course: How to be a Successful Engineer
Washington Monument design safety factor.frame: Brief mention via Petroski — crushing safety factor of 9, designed in the 1870s. Used to give a worked example of period-typical safety factors for masonry.

Washington Monument design safety factor.frame: Aluminum tip of the Washington Monument used to illustrate that aluminum was almost half the value of gold at the time of dedication.

Washington Monument design safety factor.frame: Contrast case to the Egyptian obelisks — the Washington Monument is brick assembly, not monolithic stone. Used to highlight that Egyptian obelisks really are single pieces.

1880s Hall-H\u00e9roult process commerci.title: SMS_F2014_12
1880s Hall-H\u00e9roult process commerci.frame: Hall (1886) cuts aluminum price in half. Tom uses this to land his materials-economics rule: cut the price in half and quantity used goes up four times.

Ceramic coating on turbine blades therma.title: SSW_S2013_09
Ceramic coating on turbine blades therma.frame: Used as the canonical dissimilar-material thermal-mismatch problem. Zirconia chosen because its thermal expansion matches that of metals; bond coat deliberately porous to absorb strain.
Ceramic coating on turbine blades therma.case_name: Ceramic coating on turbine blades thermal stress

Ceramic coating on turbine blades therma.title: MSE_F2016_03
Ceramic coating on turbine blades therma.frame: Bond-coat / graded-layer architecture for thermal barrier coatings on turbine blades. Used to set up the discussion of porous-surface adhesion and the cost of repair vs. losing an engine.
Ceramic coating on turbine blades therma.case_name: Ceramic coating on turbine blades thermal stress

Doctoral research on ceramic-metal joint.title: SSW_S2013_09
Doctoral research on ceramic-metal joint.frame: Tom's student's thesis showing strength peaks near 10% interfacial porosity for ceramic-metal joints; strain-energy framework as the diagnostic.
Doctoral research on ceramic-metal joint.case_name: Doctoral research on ceramic-metal joint porosity optimization

Doctoral research on ceramic-metal joint.title: SSW_S2013_07
Doctoral research on ceramic-metal joint.frame: Brief reference. Thesis showed ~10 volume percent porosity in the proper pattern at the interface produces the strongest ceramic-metal joint. Used as theoretical follow-up to the cookware insight about porous interfaces accommodating CTE mismatch.

Farberware cooking pot thermal warping.title: SSW_S2013_09
Farberware cooking pot thermal warping.frame: Brief callback. Used as the everyday analogue for deliberately incomplete bonding in turbine coatings — aluminum-to-stainless cold bond with 10% bonded area to allow for thermal mismatch.

Rocky Flats activated diffusion bonding.title: SSW_S2013_09
Rocky Flats activated diffusion bonding.frame: Worked example of plating a soft, oxide-resistant interlayer (silver) to permit low-temperature diffusion bonding of high-strength steel that would lose its martensitic structure at the temperatures needed for direct bonding. O'Brien, Rice and Olson research paper cited.
Rocky Flats activated diffusion bonding.case_name: Rocky Flats activated diffusion bonding of maraging steel

Etruscan gold bead diffusion bonding.title: SSW_S2013_09
Etruscan gold bead diffusion bonding.frame: Cited as evidence that soldering predates the modern process by thousands of years; the joint was effectively a transient liquid phase diffusion bond.

Etruscan gold bead diffusion bonding.title: SSW_S2013_08
Etruscan gold bead diffusion bonding.frame: Etruscan gold earrings used tin between copper-base and gold beads to make TLP diffusion bonds, ~600 BC. Sectioned jewelry shows tin gradient by microprobe. Tom's rhetorical move: "the Etruscans didn't file an infringement" against the Pratt & Whitney patent.

Etruscan gold bead diffusion bonding.title: SSW_S2013_02
Etruscan gold bead diffusion bonding.frame: Etruscans used tin to bond gold beads to copper objects ca. 600 BC by furnace heating, producing diffusion bonds. Tom's recurring joke: Pratt & Whitney patented the process in 1972 only because the Etruscans didn't file an infringement.
Etruscan gold bead diffusion bonding.case_name: Etruscan gold-bead diffusion bonding / Pratt & Whitney 1972 patent

Lead-tin solder obsolescence and lead-fr.title: SSW_S2013_09
Lead-tin solder obsolescence and lead-fr.frame: Brief context. Fifteen years of industry/government effort to find a lead-free replacement has not produced anything that wets as well or as fast as lead-tin.
Lead-tin solder obsolescence and lead-fr.case_name: Lead-tin solder obsolescence and lead-free transition

VAX 9000 bonding failure.title: SSW_S2013_09
VAX 9000 bonding failure.frame: Extended case study. TAB-bonded chips made in Cupertino, then outer-lead bonded three to four weeks later in Arizona, well past the one-hour cleanliness window. With 400 I/O bonds per chip, yield was near zero. Tom uses this as the consequential example of the "bond within an hour" rule from §6–§7. The technical failure compounded Digital Equipment's bankruptcy.

Digital Equipment Corporation bankruptcy.title: SSW_S2013_09
Digital Equipment Corporation bankruptcy.frame: Strategic-management coda to the VAX 9000 case. Ken Olsen's dismissal of RISC ("RISC is a fad") combined with the failed VAX 9000 mainframe play against IBM's $40B business. Hewlett Packard, which adopted RISC, captured the printer market and grew accordingly. MIT divested its 7% Digital stake "well before they could have made a few hundred million."

Northridge earthquake.title: SMS_S2016_10
Northridge earthquake.frame: Brief reference. Used to illustrate that codes designed only to force-of-fracture (not energy-of-fracture) failed when static structures were vibrated. Five billion dollars of damage led to code revision in California.

Northridge earthquake.title: MSE_F2017_03
Northridge earthquake.frame: Used to illustrate how buildings absorbed Irwin's energy-of-fracture lesson 40 years late. "Building snapped in the earthquake and caused billions of dollars worth of damage." Triggered impact / energy-of-fracture requirements being added to the steel-in-buildings codes in the 1990s.

Northridge earthquake.title: WM_S2014_21
Northridge earthquake.frame: Referenced as the empirical source for the modern LRFD (load-and-resistance factor design) approach in the AISC code. Tom credits Northridge building failures as a major input to the new methodology.

Northridge earthquake.title: MSE_F2016_08
Northridge earthquake.frame: $5–10 billion in building damage from steels lacking a fracture-toughness specification. Building toughness specs only entered civil engineering codes by 2000, decades after the Coast Guard and Navy required them.

Northridge earthquake.title: SMS_F2014_08
Northridge earthquake.frame: $20B damage event that finally brought fracture mechanics into civil engineering codes. Welded steel connections snapped during seismic vibration.

Northridge earthquake.title: MSE_F2017_04
Northridge earthquake.frame: Used to make the "codes lag the science" point. Buildings built in the 1960s, when fracture energy was understood but not coded, snapped at connections.

Northridge earthquake.title: CS_F2012_12
Northridge earthquake.frame: Tom (mis)dates as "early '80s" — actually 1994. Code response was not to increase strength safety factor but toughness safety factor. Buildings designed as statically loaded became dynamically loaded under earthquake; impact loading produced brittle fractures at connections. Triggered transition from beam-formula design to Load Factor Resistance Design (LRFD). Buildings condemned not from collapse but from broken connections too expensive to repair.

Northridge earthquake.title: WM_S2014_01
Northridge earthquake.frame: Cited as the canonical example of how engineering codes get rewritten after major failures — $15 billion in damage, building codes modified to accommodate earthquake vibrations.

LNG tanker steel development for cryogen.title: SMS_S2016_10
LNG tanker steel development for cryogen.frame: Tom's own work at the steel company developing minus-60°F-toughness steel for the cylindrical skirts that hold the aluminum spheres on LNG tankers built at Quincy shipyard (Bethlehem Steel → General Dynamics). Sets up the Sparrows Point runoff-plate fraud (§2.p6).
LNG tanker steel development for cryogen.case_name: LNG tanker steel development for cryogenic service

LNG tanker steel development for cryogen.title: CAS_Su2011_03
LNG tanker steel development for cryogen.frame: 1975. Tom developed a special steel for an LNG carrier and traveled to Bethlehem's Sparrows Point BOP shop to observe the heat. Highest-paid hourly employee (~$100,000/year, responsible for $100,000/hour of product) threw Tom out of the pulpit on discovering he had an MIT doctorate — incident triggered by Tom sitting in the operator's chair and asking whether he'd shoot for high or low end of the chemistry range. The heat came in off-chemistry.
LNG tanker steel development for cryogen.case_name: LNG tanker steel development at Sparrows Point

LNG tanker shipyard plate selection and.title: SMS_S2016_10
LNG tanker shipyard plate selection and.frame: The runoff-plate fraud. Sparrows Point steel typically barely passed 20 foot-pound spec at ~20.5; once a month a plate would come in at 30; the yard cut that plate up into runoff tabs for *all* the other welds. They tested the best plate, not the plate going into the ship.
LNG tanker shipyard plate selection and.case_name: LNG tanker shipyard plate selection and testing circumvention

Quincy Shipyard liquid natural gas tanke.title: SMS_S2016_10
Quincy Shipyard liquid natural gas tanke.frame: Quincy as the construction site for the LNG tankers whose steel Tom developed. Shipyard "now closed, turning into a parking lot for imported cars." Referenced again in §8 as the origin of the tail-shaft case.
Quincy Shipyard liquid natural gas tanke.case_name: Quincy Shipyard liquid natural gas tanker construction (mid-1970s)

Quincy Shipyard liquid natural gas tanke.title: MSE_F2016_08
Quincy Shipyard liquid natural gas tanke.frame: Five or six LNG tankers built at Quincy with aluminum spheres on steel skirts. Coast Guard required 20 foot-pound Charpy; Sparrows Point plates averaged 20.5 — "just barely making it." Shipyard then cherry-picked 30 foot-pound plates for the weld-test runoff tabs. Foam insulation failure led to Coast Guard non-certification; ships sat unused for years off Newport.
Quincy Shipyard liquid natural gas tanke.case_name: Quincy Shipyard liquid natural gas tanker construction

Prudhoe Bay offshore ice islands.title: SMS_S2016_10
Prudhoe Bay offshore ice islands.frame: Ice as a structural material. Civil engineers from MIT designed man-made islands with sloping rock walls so accreting sea ice would build up above the waterline. Cites Professor Kingery's mid-1950s ice strength research as the academic foundation.

Ice fishers dynamite accident.title: SMS_S2016_10
Ice fishers dynamite accident.frame: Lateral teaching aside. Minnesota or Wisconsin ice fishers used dynamite to break holes in lake ice; dog retrieved the lit stick and ran under the pickup truck. Tom's "supposedly true story" used as a caution-against-overengineering / drinking-and-engineering parable.

Arizona pipeline stacker bracket failure.title: SMS_S2016_10
Arizona pipeline stacker bracket failure.frame: Worked example of ductile-vs-brittle visual diagnosis. Arizona, ~2015. Big forklift lifting fifty tons of pipeline pipe; the holding container failed; millions of dollars damage. From photos alone Tom saw the steel had bent before breaking — ductile, therefore overload failure. "I didn't even have to go see it."

Arizona pipeline stacker bracket failure.title: WM_Su2015_16
Arizona pipeline stacker bracket failure.frame: Tom's insurance-adjuster consulting case. Carbon steel weld on a special bracket on a pipe-stacker forklift failed without I-beam deformation — Tom diagnosed defective welds from a single photograph using the Lincoln Electric reference: properly made fillet weld in mild steel will outpull the metal.

Duplex stainless steel centrifuge brittl.title: SMS_F2013_10
Duplex stainless steel centrifuge brittl.frame: Physical demonstration. Cast duplex stainless centrifuge (~1 ton, 3000 RPM, 4 ft diameter) for separating starch in corn-methanol production. Embrittled by iron-chrome intermetallic phases. Shows orange-peel surface where large casting grains stretched before fracture.
Duplex stainless steel centrifuge brittl.case_name: Duplex stainless steel centrifuge brittle failure

1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobile.title: WM_S2014_02
1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobile.frame: Used to make the point that aluminum cars existed long before mass-market aluminum vehicles. JP Morgan's all-aluminum Pierce Arrow is mentioned in the same breath.

1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobile.title: DP_S2012_10
1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobile.frame: Cited as proof that all-aluminum vehicles are technically feasible at luxury cost — used to set up the contrast with mass-market Taurus economics.

1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobile.title: SMS_F2013_02
1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobile.frame: Brief mention as evidence that all-aluminum automobiles are not a new idea — used to undermine the 1990s prediction that steel would disappear from cars.
1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobile.case_name: Andrew Mellon all-aluminum Pierce Arrow automobile / 1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobiles

1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobile.title: SSW_S2013_02
1930s all-aluminum Duesenberg automobile.frame: Used to make the point that all-aluminum automotive bodies have been attempted for 80 years.

Audi all-aluminum automobiles.title: WM_S2014_02
Audi all-aluminum automobiles.frame: "$90,000 Audi, all made out of aluminum" — twenty years of production by 2014.

Audi all-aluminum automobiles.title: DP_S2012_10
Audi all-aluminum automobiles.frame: The luxury-segment proof-of-concept that drove the early-1990s hype cycle.

Audi all-aluminum automobiles.title: SMS_F2013_02
Audi all-aluminum automobiles.frame: Cited as a real but niche product proving the cost barrier — you can buy an all-aluminum Audi, but you can't buy an all-aluminum Ford Taurus at Taurus prices.

Audi all-aluminum automobiles.title: SMS_F2014_03
Audi all-aluminum automobiles.frame: Cited as the 1990s entry point for all-aluminum production vehicles.

Chaparral Steel.title: DP_S2012_06
Chaparral Steel.frame: **The lecture's central case.** Founded by Gordon Forward, MIT DMSE grad. Mini mill at 1/10 the capital cost of an integrated mill. Product met both A36 and grade 50 specs simultaneously, allowing inventory consolidation. Wiped out I-beam imports to US, exported 20% of product overseas including Asia. Folding-table corporate dining room contrasted with Bethlehem's executive dining room.

Seawolf submarine hydrogen cracking.title: WM_S2014_20
Seawolf submarine hydrogen cracking.frame: The principal forensic case of the lecture. The Seawolf was supposed to be welded with HY-100 (100 ksi) steel, but high-side chemistry on every alloying element (carbon, manganese, chromium) drove the weld metal strength to 130 ksi with martensitic rather than acicular-ferrite structure. Hydrogen cracking ensued. Repair cost an additional $2 billion, doubling the submarine's price; Congress was unhappy. Only one Seawolf-class was built, partly for this reason and partly because the Cold War ended.

Sea Wolf submarine weld cracking (SSN-21.title: WM_Su2015_01
Sea Wolf submarine weld cracking (SSN-21.frame: The weld metal ran 30–40% higher strength than intended because of carbon and alloy content; toughness dropped; 1 mm microscopic flaws formed that the original inspection wasn't looking for; a grinder noticed magnetized swarf aligning with the cracks, an inspector was called, and every weld in the sub had to be cut out. 18% of the ship had been built. Cost the Navy $2 billion.

Persian Gulf destroyer brass valve stres.title: WM_Su2015_01
Persian Gulf destroyer brass valve stres.frame: A destroyer in the Persian Gulf lost its 3,000 psi air system mid-attack; root cause was stress corrosion cracking in a brass valve made of the wrong alloy. Discovered at the Naval Supply Center in Philadelphia that twenty-some percent of brass valves in inventory were the wrong alloy. Two students in the same cohort had worked on different parts of the failure.
Persian Gulf destroyer brass valve stres.case_name: Persian Gulf destroyer brass valve stress corrosion cracking (Second Gulf War)

Dan Rather CBS building collapse.title: WM_Su2015_01
Dan Rather CBS building collapse.frame: Six-story Manhattan building under construction for CBS, early 1980s. Concrete beams with steel rebar; rebars were tack-welded where they crossed; high-carbon rebar at the tack-weld became brittle, fracture toughness dropped by a factor of eight, fifth-floor beam failed in bending tension, dominoed all the beams. $50 million loss, one workman's leg broken. The Steinway Piano factory tour (CBS-owned at the time) is a coda.

Boeing 747-400 titanium catalytic conver.title: WM_Su2015_01
Boeing 747-400 titanium catalytic conver.frame: Air tubing switched from stainless steel to titanium to save weight for the extended-range 747-400; Engelhard built the catalytic converters for ozone scrubbing in the cabin air system. Introduced here mainly as a vehicle for the aircraft-range discussion (10,000 → 13,000 mile aircraft) rather than as a developed failure case. Tom flags it as a long story not fully told.
Boeing 747-400 titanium catalytic conver.case_name: Boeing 747-400 titanium catalytic converter / air tubing

Cruise missile graphite engine.frame: Cited as the existence proof that brittle-material jet engines can be built — when the engine only has to last an hour, the inspection problem becomes tractable. Graphite is tougher than most ceramics; coatings prevent burn-up.

Cruise missile graphite engine.title: WM_Su2014_29
Cruise missile graphite engine.frame: Cited in passing as another "limited-life engine, hour-and-a-half service" parallel to NASCAR magnesium use.

Harvard Stadium reinforced concrete (191.frame: Cited as the oldest reinforced concrete structure in the country, used to illustrate that concrete continues to harden over years and decades — "you have to have a hammer drill with a carbide tip" to drill it now.

Harvard Stadium reinforced concrete (191.frame: named 1983 National Historical Landmark, one of the first major reinforced concrete structures in the US, c. 1900.

CH-53/MH-53 helicopter washer corrosion.title: WM_Su2014_28
CH-53/MH-53 helicopter washer corrosion.frame: Sikorsky's earlier encounter with the same washer corrosion problem on a different helicopter line, which they fixed by switching from T6 to T7 over-aged heat treatment. Tom uses this to set up the indictment: Sikorsky knew the fix and failed to apply it to the Blackhawk part.

New England Aquarium exterior panel corr.title: WM_Su2015_16
New England Aquarium exterior panel corr.frame: Analogy for "bought it in the right condition then transformed it." Stainless steel exterior panels purchased in passivated condition, then mechanically abraded for texture, which removed the passivation.
New England Aquarium exterior panel corr.case_name: New England Aquarium exterior panel corrosion

New England Aquarium exterior panel corr.title: SMS_F2013_10
New England Aquarium exterior panel corr.frame: Passivation defeated by post-passivation mechanical abrasion. Mill-passivated 304 panels were ground to create fish-scale texture, which removed the protective chrome oxide. In marine environment (Boston Harbor chlorides), the oxide could not reform. Rust appeared along grinding marks and along bumper scrapes at the loading dock. Tom tested citric acid and Diet Coke (phosphoric acid) as environmentally acceptable cleaning agents.
New England Aquarium exterior panel corr.case_name: New England Aquarium exterior panel corrosion

New England Aquarium exterior panel corr.title: WM_Su2014_07
New England Aquarium exterior panel corr.frame: Fish-scale facade specified as passivated stainless but ground for texture, leaving active surface; rust in grinding marks within a year. Tested citric/phosphoric acid/Coke/naval jelly for in-place re-passivation.
New England Aquarium exterior panel corr.case_name: New England Aquarium exterior panel corrosion
