Aircraft landing gear and turbine engine.title: CAS_Su2011_06
Aircraft landing gear and turbine engine.frame: Commercial aircraft landing gear and engine rotors/shafts are double vacuum arc remelted to bring inclusions below 10 microns, since at 250 ksi yield, 100-micron flaws threaten fatigue life.

Aircraft landing gear and turbine engine.frame: Triple vacuum arc remelting as the standard for aircraft crankshafts, landing gear, transmission shafts, and turbine engine shafts. Used to illustrate why inclusion control matters for fatigue-critical components.
Aircraft landing gear and turbine engine.case_name: Vacuum arc remelting of aerospace steel

Boomer Submarine Trident Tube Retrofits.frame: Navy built full-size 30-foot HY100 sections for boomers in the 90s for welding experience before committing to an all-HY100 hull.

Boomer Submarine Trident Tube Retrofits.frame: Brief mention. The Electric Boat–trained welder whose shop took the Millstone contract was simultaneously doing SSGN conversion work — inserting clusters of ~19 non-nuclear warhead tubes inside former Trident tubes as part of SALT-era nuclear arsenal reductions. Used to establish the welder's credentials.

SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem.title: WM_Su2015_16
SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem.frame: Even with prototype experience, Sea Wolf hull welding had major problems. In §7 the case is developed: they thought they had HY100 filler but got HY80-equivalent due to property scatter, hydrogen control inadequate, 18% of the ship welded with undermatched filler.
SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem.case_name: SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem

SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem.title: CS_Su2012_04
SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem.frame: A grinder smoothing welds on the first Seawolf-class submarine noticed grinding swarf lining up in lines under a sixteenth of an inch — a flaw size below anything the specification had ever required inspectors to find. Destructive sampling revealed clusters of micro-cracks throughout the welds; 18% of the hull had been completed. Tom contributed to the investigation report and identifies the weld-wire chemistry being on the high side as a contributing factor. Repair costs Tom heard ranged from half a billion to ~$2 billion — comparable to building a new boat. Two Seawolves were built before the program was canceled with the end of the Cold War. Tom uses the case to dramatize how improvements in measurement capability create disputes about flaws the original specification never contemplated.

SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem.title: WM_Su2015_11
SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem.frame: Brief reference. Source of lessons on welding high-strength steels. Used as a parallel to the Thresher in Petroski's framing of "we learn from failure."

Magnesium anode nickel contamination fai.title: WM_Su2015_16
Magnesium anode nickel contamination fai.frame: Hot-water-tank sacrificial anode. Nickel solubility in magnesium is ~7 ppm; excess nickel forms precipitates that cause local galvanic self-consumption — anode disappears in hours without protecting the steel vessel.

Magnesium anode nickel contamination fai.title: SMS_F2014_06
Magnesium anode nickel contamination fai.frame: Spine of the corrosion thread. The anode's high-purity magnesium spec (<7 ppm nickel) used to teach concentration-cell corrosion; the Juarez fabrication line used to teach how design accommodates real-world coating defects.
Magnesium anode nickel contamination fai.case_name: Magnesium anode in steel hot water tanks (Juarez maquiladora glass-line repair)

Massachusetts Supreme Court ICC bumper j.title: WM_Su2015_16
Massachusetts Supreme Court ICC bumper j.frame: Case law on expert testimony scope. Man jacking truck by ICC bumper, bumper welds broke without frame deformation. Tom's testimony (defective welds based on Lincoln Electric reference) was challenged at the Massachusetts Supreme Court; ruling established what a welding expert may say in MA courts.
Massachusetts Supreme Court ICC bumper j.case_name: Massachusetts Supreme Court ICC bumper jack failure case

Egon Orowan dislocation discovery (rug a.frame: Origin of the dislocation concept in 1930s Hungary; Orowan watching a maid kick a dislocation across an oriental rug. Used to introduce the concept of dislocations as one-atom-row-at-a-time deformation.

Egon Orowan dislocation discovery (rug a.title: SSW_S2013_02
Egon Orowan dislocation discovery (rug a.frame: Hungarian cleaning lady, working in Orowan's office, moves a Persian rug across the floor by introducing a small fold and kicking it across the room. Egon Orowan dislocation discovery (rug a.case_name: Egon Orowan's cleaning-lady rug analogy for dislocations

Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.title: DP_S2012_10
Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.frame: 1940s iron whiskers with axial screw dislocations measured at 2 million PSI when pulled along the screw axis. Used to establish that theoretical strengths are achievable only in idealized geometries.

Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.title: SMS_S2016_03
Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.frame: Counter-example to the "defects destroy strength" rule — iron whiskers grown as single crystals with one axial screw dislocation achieved 2.2 million psi because the dislocation was not loaded.

Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.title: DP_S2012_01
Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.frame: 1950s growth of single-crystal iron whiskers containing only a screw dislocation along the axis. Pulled to 2 million PSI experimental strength — the theoretical strength of perfect crystal steel. Used to argue that physicists' claims about carbon nanotube strength (the "rope to the moon") are decades behind what materials scientists already demonstrated and refuted.

Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.title: CS_Su2012_02
Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.case_name: Iron whiskers at 2 million PSI (vs. modern graphene/carbon nanotube hype)

Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.title: SSW_S2013_02
Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.frame: Single-crystal iron whiskers grown in the 1950s with only a screw dislocation (no edge dislocations), measured at ~1.2 million PSI — close to the theoretical Lennard-Jones prediction of ~2 million PSI. Used to validate the dislocation theory of weakening.
Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation s.case_name: Iron whiskers — 1950s near-theoretical strength single crystals

High-temperature superconductor critical.title: DP_S2012_10
High-temperature superconductor critical.frame: The scaling argument: pinning-site size scales inversely with critical temperature, so 40-70 K superconductors need pinning sites smaller than an electron — impossible.
High-temperature superconductor critical.case_name: High-temperature superconductor critical current density problem

High-temperature superconductor critical.title: DP_S2012_10
High-temperature superconductor critical.frame: Papers in *Science* magazine around 1990 measuring critical current with field parallel to current (zero J-cross-B force), reporting fantastic values that would never apply to a wound magnet where J and B are perpendicular. Seven orders of magnitude difference.
High-temperature superconductor critical.case_name: High-temperature superconductor critical current measurement error

High-temperature superconductor critical.title: MSE_F2016_06
High-temperature superconductor critical.frame: *Science* magazine papers reporting critical currents two orders of magnitude above Tom's thesis values — measured with conductor parallel to the magnetic field, which is physically meaningless (J×B = 0). The peer reviewers didn't catch it. "One of the problems when there's lots of money, you bring out all the people who don't know what they're doing."
High-temperature superconductor critical.case_name: High-temperature superconductor critical current measurement error

Niobium-titanium superconductor developm.title: DP_S2012_10
Niobium-titanium superconductor developm.frame: John Wulff's work; critical temperature ~9 K, fields ~6 Tesla. The 1970s workhorse superconductor.
Niobium-titanium superconductor developm.case_name: Niobium-titanium superconductor development for high-energy physics

Niobium-titanium superconductor developm.title: SMS_F2013_08
Niobium-titanium superconductor developm.frame: GE niobium-tin and other manufacturers' niobium-titanium magnets, ~1960, for physics. Establishes the pre-1986 commercial baseline against which high-Tc was hyped.
Niobium-titanium superconductor developm.case_name: Niobium-titanium superconductor development for high-energy physics

Niobium-3.5tin superconductor with zirco.title: DP_S2012_10
Niobium-3.5tin superconductor with zirco.frame: Mark Benz at GE Research; 1% zirconium internally oxidized to form 20-30 nm zirconium oxide precipitates spaced ~100 nm apart, providing the pinning sites that gave good critical field. The case Tom was originally going to lecture on.
Niobium-3.5tin superconductor with zirco.case_name: Niobium-3.5tin superconductor with zirconium oxide pinning precipitates

Wire drawing thesis project on supercond.title: DP_S2012_10

Wire drawing thesis project on supercond.frame: Tom's undergraduate thesis: $1,000 worth of diamond dies bought in 5% increments, which Tom now identifies as the wrong approach — should have used 30–50% draws to avoid high-delta operations and centerline cracking.

American Superconductor commercial viabi.title: DP_S2012_10
American Superconductor commercial viabi.frame: MIT spin-off founded by Greg Yurek (with Vander Sande and Yet-Ming Chiang) using silver internal-oxidation route to HTSC ceramics. American Superconductor commercial viabi.title: SMS_F2013_08
American Superconductor commercial viabi.frame: Greg Yurek's 1989 departure from MIT to found American Superconductor; company has never made money but draws hundreds of millions in research grants on the promise.

DC transmission line in Manhattan.title: DP_S2012_10
DC transmission line in Manhattan.frame: Brief mention as one of American Superconductor's deployments. Not developed.

US Navy SQUID magnetic anomaly detection.title: DP_S2012_10

US Navy SQUID magnetic anomaly detection.case_name: US Navy SQUID magnetic anomaly detection program

Ship dismantling in Bangladesh.title: FW_Su2013_02
Ship dismantling in Bangladesh.frame: Decommissioned commercial ships beached and cut up for scrap by workers earning ~50 cents/day with acetylene torches; average occupational lifespan ~5 years.

Ship dismantling in Bangladesh.title: CS_F2012_12
Ship dismantling in Bangladesh.frame: Used as illustration of disposal end-of-life problem analogous to aircraft parked in Arizona desert. Workers cut up beached ships with acetylene torches, exposed to asbestos and residual chemicals; reported life expectancy of three years for workers. Navy nuclear reactor disposal practices.title: FW_Su2013_02
Navy nuclear reactor disposal practices.frame: Brief Q&A with student. Tom believed reactors were buried in the Atlantic off Norfolk; student corrects to Washington State (Hanford).

Liquid copper jet cutting research.frame: Anonymized company developing superheated molten copper laminar jet cutting at 10× plasma cutting speed. Worked at 10-foot lab scale; ceramic nozzle lifetime was the limiting factor.

Alabama aluminum foundry freeze-up.frame: Phone call to Tom as junior faculty (~1978). Foundry's 2-foot deep aluminum melting pot froze after a day-long power outage; Tom couldn't help.

Alabama aluminum foundry freeze-up.title: CAS_Su2011_06
Alabama aluminum foundry freeze-up.frame: Alabama foundry loses power for a day; holding pot solidifies 2 feet of aluminum; can't be flame-cut due to protective oxide. Years later Tom learns from Alcoa's Peter O'Brien that the standard remedy is to call a specialist in Pittsburgh who blows it out with explosive charges.

Alcoa aluminum potline freeze-up explosi.title: FW_Su2013_02
Alcoa aluminum potline freeze-up explosi.frame: Dinner conversation ~15 years after the Alabama call with Alcoa senior VP "Peter." Steel mills cut breakouts with oxyacetylene; aluminum can't be flame-cut, so Alcoa called a Pittsburgh specialist who drilled holes, set explosive charges, and blew the frozen aluminum apart — sometimes destroying the potline in the process.

## Figures referenced (not cases)

America's Cup 4340 welding procedure dev.title: SMS_F2013_10
America's Cup 4340 welding procedure dev.frame: Used to introduce the hardenability concept. A four-inch-thick keel beam couldn't be made from HY-130 (too soft, plastically deforming in trials) so they wanted 4340, but didn't know how to weld it in that section thickness. Tom showed them how.

Sub-Zero refrigerator hinge failure.title: SMS_F2013_10
Sub-Zero refrigerator hinge failure.frame: Illustrates the consequence of 303 vs. 304 mix-up. Manufacturer used 303 (sulfur-bearing, non-weldable) instead of 304 for a pin-to-plate weld. Cracked at the weld, plated over, doors fell off in service. ~$7M in repairs.

Sub-Zero refrigerator hinge failure.title: WM_Su2014_23
Sub-Zero refrigerator hinge failure.frame: Tom's consulting case. Sub-Zero (twelve-thousand-dollar refrigerators) had a TIG-welded hinge pin made by a subcontractor from free-machining sulfur-bearing steel; sulfur formed iron sulfide and the welds cracked. ~3000 units repaired in the field at ~$7 million. Used as the headline example of the design/fab/field 1:10:100:1000 cost-of-failure escalation, and the example that wealthy customers are litigious.

Sub-Zero refrigerator hinge failure.title: SMS_F2014_03
Sub-Zero refrigerator hinge failure.frame: Physical sample (the hinge from his son's $11,000 refrigerator). Used to illustrate the low-value-per-pound end of the materials market — plain carbon steel.

316 stainless steel heat exchanger tube.title: SMS_F2013_10
316 stainless steel heat exchanger tube.frame: Dramatic 304-vs-316 substitution case. Original 316 cooker ran 10-20 years with no problems. Replacement parts mis-specified as 304 cracked and rusted within weeks in the high-salt steam environment.
316 stainless steel heat exchanger tube.case_name: 316 stainless steel heat exchanger tube pitting failure (Fenway Frank application)

Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.title: SMS_F2013_10
Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.frame: Closing case of the lecture. MIT doctoral student Krivsky, working under John Chipman in the Building 8 basement, doing basic carbon-monoxide-reaction research. Discovered low oxygen potential of argon would pull carbon and oxygen out of molten steel. Not patented at MIT; Krivsky commercialized it at a company. Now used for virtually all stainless steel and most nickel superalloys worldwide. Tom estimates ~$1B/year value to the world steel industry. The case Tom uses to illustrate "MIT lost the patent" lessons elsewhere in the corpus.

Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.title: MSE_F2016_09
Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.frame: Discovered in MIT Building 8 basement; Chipman's [Chapman's] student William Krivsky takes it to a small NY State steel company; AOD enables low-ppm carbon in stainless steel, drops stainless price by ~3X. Now used for essentially all stainless steel and aerospace alloys (with VOD for the latter).
Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.case_name: Argon Oxygen Decarburization at MIT (Chipman / Krivsky)

Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.title: WM_Su2015_03
Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.frame: "Christy" (Chipman doctoral student, 1950s) studied the carbon-monoxide reaction in steel melts using argon-diluted oxygen. The technique went from MIT thesis to Crucible Steel + Union Carbide commercial process. All 5M tons of stainless steel today made by AOD; price reduced to one-third of 1950s value.

Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.title: MSE_F2017_06
Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.frame: Born in basement of Building 8 from a John Chipman graduate student (Krivsky [?]) doing basic carbon-burnout chemistry; commercialized at a small steel company because the majors wouldn't risk it. Dropped stainless steel price by 5–10×, enabled <0.03% C for weldability and corrosion resistance, recovered chromium from slag.

Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.title: SMS_S2016_11
Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.frame: AOD reduces carbon from 300 ppm to 30 ppm by argon blowing. Basic science done at MIT under John Chipman by Krivsky in the 1950s; process invented when Krivsky moved to a small steel company. 99% of stainless steel today made by AOD.

Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) proce.frame: Tom identifies AOD as an MIT-originated process (basic research in the basement of Building 8) that today accounts for ~98% of world stainless-steel production. By bubbling argon through the molten bath, the partial pressure of CO in the gas bubbles is suppressed by ~100×, allowing the equilibrium C·O activity product to drive carbon down below 300 ppm even at high chromium content. The economic consequence: cost of stainless steel roughly halved per ton since the 1960s.

Infinium magnesium extraction process de.title: SMS_F2013_10
Infinium magnesium extraction process de.frame: Forward-reference to Adam Powell's upcoming guest lecture. Spinoff from MIT via Boston University; ~$10-20M in funding for an environmentally clean metals extraction process.

Japanese steel soda cans.title: SMS_F2013_10
Japanese steel soda cans.frame: Policy-protected industrial choice — Japanese government protected domestic steel by keeping vending-machine soda in steel cans rather than aluminum, since Japan has no indigenous aluminum industry. Aluminum has now displaced steel as the protection eased. Used as the lecture-opening illustration of how non-technical factors drive materials selection.

Steel vs. aluminum auto markets US vs. E.title: SMS_F2013_10
Steel vs. aluminum auto markets US vs. E.frame: Fuel-price economics would favor aluminum cars in Europe, but European manufacturers must build for the US market where fuel prices favor steel. Illustrates how exporting drives materials selection.
Steel vs. aluminum auto markets US vs. E.case_name: Steel vs. aluminum automobiles (US vs. Europe market split)

Hadfield's manganese steel (prison bars.title: SMS_F2013_10
Hadfield's manganese steel (prison bars.frame:
12-13% Mn steel that work-hardens during machining, making it nearly impossible to saw or file. Used historically for prison bars. Distinct alloy class from the 200-series stainless steels Tom is discussing.

Private Mach 2.5 aircraft crash and wing.title: WIE_F2015_11
Private Mach 2.5 aircraft crash and wing.course: How to be a Successful Engineer

Private jet friction-welded titanium sta.frame: Failed venture used to illustrate friction-welding limits above aluminum (mandrel wear with reactive titanium).

1849-1850 Royal Commission bridge safety.course: How to be a Successful Engineer
1849-1850 Royal Commission bridge safety.frame: The Commission asked Charles Fox and other bridge designers what safety factor to use; answers ranged from 3 to 7; the Commission chose 6. Used to anchor the 150-year safety-factor trajectory (6 → 1.67) at the section's pivot to modern practice.

New Orleans Canal Levee Failure.frame: Reported post-Katrina safety factor of 1.3 — the lowest Tom knows of in a structural application. Personal connection: Tom's great-grandfather, a civil engineer, worked on the levees around 1880.

New Orleans Canal Levee Failure.title: CS_F2012_12
New Orleans Canal Levee Failure.frame: Safety factor 1.3. Tom emphasizes the levees did not fail by strength — they were overtopped. Personal note: Tom's grandfather built levees in New Orleans in the 1880s.

Cincinnati Red Stadium I-beam collapse.title: FW_Su2013_03
Cincinnati Red Stadium I-beam collapse.frame: Roy McCauley (head of welding at Ohio State, deceased) showed the contractor how to flame-straighten a 30°-bent giant I-beam after a crane cable broke during erection of the Cincinnati Reds Stadium roof in the Pete Rose era. Replacement lead time was 18 months from the mill; flame straightening saved the schedule. Tom uses it as the canonical demonstration that residual stress always pulls in the opposite direction of the applied heat expansion.

USS Iowa gun turret explosion.title: FW_Su2013_03
USS Iowa gun turret explosion.frame: Tom recalls the 1989 Iowa turret explosion (attributed at the time to a sailor in a failed relationship lighting off a powder charge inside a 16-inch gun). In 1985 Tom spent summers at David Taylor in Annapolis, where the Navy was trying to figure out how to repair the turret — but no one in 1985 knew how to make the welds being made in 1945. The repair was abandoned and all battleships decommissioned within five years.

USS Iowa gun turret explosion.title: WM_Su2014_12
USS Iowa gun turret explosion.frame: 1989 turret explosion. Navy could not repair because they had lost the heavy-section peening technology for 14-inch armor steel welds; the turret was abandoned rather than repaired. Used to teach the disappearance of mid-century heavy-section welding expertise.
USS Iowa gun turret explosion.case_name: USS Iowa turret explosion — Puerto Rico

Three-tank RPG penetration test (1985).title: FW_Su2013_03
Three-tank RPG penetration test (1985).frame: One of Tom's students worked for the Army in the mid-1980s. The Army developed improved sabots that could penetrate multiple armor layers; a field demonstration with three old tanks lined up showed the round going through all six armor layers. The general present reportedly vomited at the implication for tank crews.

1991 Gulf War M1 Abrams vs T-72 tank eng.title: FW_Su2013_03
1991 Gulf War M1 Abrams vs T-72 tank eng.frame: Tom recounts the episode from Tom Clancy's *Armored Cav* of a stuck-in-mud M1 Abrams that defeated three successive T-72s — the first two firing rounds that bounced off; the third trying to hide behind a sand berm and being killed through the berm via infrared sighting. Tom uses it as the bookend of meaningful tank warfare; he frames tank battles since the 1973 Suez War (2.5-minute average lifetime) as anachronistic in the helicopter-RPG era.
1991 Gulf War M1 Abrams vs T-72 tank eng.case_name: 1991 Gulf War M1 Abrams vs T-72 engagement

Western Massachusetts laser cutting mach.title: FW_Su2013_03
Western Massachusetts laser cutting mach.frame: A $2–3M oxygen-assist laser cutting machine running lights-out in a Western Massachusetts factory caught fire and was destroyed. The plaintiffs hypothesized that metal-powder accumulation under the machine ignited. Tom (called in after another fire investigator) noted that with oxygen-assist cutting, the powders are already iron oxide — "you can't burn wood twice." Plaintiffs withdrew the suit at mediation.
Western Massachusetts laser cutting mach.case_name: Western Massachusetts laser cutting machine factory fire

Tom Eagar LNG welding sunburn incident.title: FW_Su2013_03
Tom Eagar LNG welding sunburn incident.frame: En route to a New Orleans conference in the early 1980s, Tom stopped at Alcoa in Pittsburgh, where they were developing a 600-amp gas tungsten arc process for welding 4–8 inch aluminum on LNG ship spheres. Holding the torch ungloved for 15–20 seconds gave Tom a UV sunburn on the exposed lower half of his hand (the torch shielded the upper half) — a vivid demonstration of arc radiation losses and aluminum's reflectivity.
Tom Eagar LNG welding sunburn incident.case_name: Tom Eagar LNG welding sunburn incident

Civil War cannonball drop towers.title: FW_Su2013_03
Civil War cannonball drop towers.frame: Embedded within the Alpha submarine arc as a Watertown Arsenal origin story. During the Civil War the Arsenal pursued a research program to drop molten cast iron from towers to form spherical cannonballs. Without knowledge of heat transfer or dimensionless numbers (chemical engineering wasn't invented until the 1880s, at MIT), they needed a ~50-mile-tall tower; surface-tension/gravity ratio also required drops below 3 mm. The program produced only splats. Tom uses it as a contrast to Watertown's eventual post-WWII success developing Ti-6Al-4V.
Civil War cannonball drop towers.case_name: Watertown Arsenal Civil War cannonball drop towers

SSN-21 Sea Wolf submarine hull cracking.title: FW_Su2013_03
SSN-21 Sea Wolf submarine hull cracking.frame: Brief closing reference: Captain Millard Firebaugh (a graduate of MIT's program) was designing the SSN-21 in the mid-1980s when Congress zeroed the next year's budget, saying they wouldn't build another steel sub while the Soviets had titanium subs — and that the U.S. should leapfrog to composite submarines. Tom mentions attending a four-day workshop on composite subs which he calls "a laughing mess." Setup for a future lecture.
SSN-21 Sea Wolf submarine hull cracking.case_name: SSN-21 Sea Wolf submarine budget zeroing

Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair.title: WM_S2014_26
Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair.frame: Recent (Jan 24, 2014) consulting question from "Chuck," chief engineer at an FAA-approved aircraft piston engine crankcase repair shop. Customer's 3/8" stud stripped at 204 inch-pounds in a 4043-filler weld repair. Tom walks through SAE/AMS specifications, Aluminum Association filler metal recommendations (4043, 4145, 4009, 4010, 4011, 4047), and the reasoning for matching vs. over-matching vs. under-matching filler metal selection.
Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair.case_name: Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair consulting case

Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair.title: WM_S2014_23
Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair.frame: Foreshadow only — Tom announces the case will be developed in detail on Friday. The shop is one of the only FAA-authorized aluminum casting weld repair operations in the US; they had been using 4043 filler metal since 1976 and were criticized in a Canadian Aviation Authority report following a crash investigation. Used to set up a filler-metal-selection case study.
Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair.case_name: Canadian aluminum casting repair consulting case

Canadian Transportation Board filler met.title: WM_S2014_26
Canadian Transportation Board filler met.frame: Prior (fall 2013) accident investigation in Canada where the Canadian Transportation Safety Board concluded the under-matching 4043 filler metal caused a fatigue crack. Canadian Transportation Board filler met.case_name: Canadian Transportation Board filler metal composition criticism

Johnson & Johnson laser surgery instrume.frame: Early-1980s consulting case. J&J's surgical instruments division wanted laser-cutting hand tools (scissors, drills, reamers) that wouldn't reflect the laser onto unintended tissue. Tom recommended anodized aluminum (oxide layer for absorption + aluminum substrate for thermal diffusion), helped them design the experiment with 4/6/8/10-micron anodized discs, and confirmed the 6–10 micron optimum.
Johnson & Johnson laser surgery instrume.case_name: Johnson & Johnson laser surgery instrument coating

Johnson & Johnson laser surgery instrume.title: WM_Su2015_11
Johnson & Johnson laser surgery instrume.frame: Patent and held-harmless arrangement. Tom developed an anti-reflective surface coating for J&J laser surgical instruments to prevent burn injury from reflected laser energy. Took six months of J&J legal department to issue a hold-harmless letter.

Independent consultant patent liability.title: WM_S2014_26

Boeing 747 C-5A competition.frame: Tom's anecdote about the 747 being Boeing's losing C-5A military transport design, repurposed as a commercial jetliner — used to illustrate the bet-your-company scale of aerospace capital investment. Tokyo Narita anecdote of forty-seven 747s on the ground.
Boeing 747 C-5A competition.case_name: Boeing 747 origin from C-5A military transport competition

Boeing 747 C-5A competition.title: MSE_F2016_12
Boeing 747 C-5A competition.frame: Origin story of the 747. Boeing lost the four-or-five-billion-dollar C-5A military airlift contract to Lockheed (Marietta, Georgia); used their sunk investment to pitch the 747 as a commercial transport. Used to teach the magnitude of bet-your-company aerospace programs.

Copper-bearing carbon steel railroad app.title: WM_Su2015_07

HSLA 65 carrier weight-reduction study.title: WM_Su2015_07
HSLA 65 carrier weight-reduction study.frame: NAVSEA-funded million-dollar Newport News study finding 2,000-ton weight savings possible by substituting HSLA-65 for 50 ksi steel on Nimitz-class carriers. Tom's punchline: his "10× material cost" rule of thumb predicts the same answer. Also frames the broader Nimitz weight-creep problem (250 tons/year) and the $50M cost of designing a new hull.
HSLA 65 carrier weight-reduction study.case_name: Nimitz-class carrier weight creep / HSLA-65 study (1996)

HSLA 65 carrier weight-reduction study.title: SMS_S2016_05

Stainless steel dinnerware bleach pittin.title: WM_Su2014_06
Stainless steel dinnerware bleach pittin.frame: Domestic illustration of the chloride + oxygen pitting mechanism on stainless. Mother-in-law sterilized dinnerware in Clorox overnight.
Stainless steel dinnerware bleach pittin.case_name: Stainless steel dinnerware bleach pitting (personal anecdote)

Stainless steel dinnerware bleach pittin.title: WM_Su2015_08
Stainless steel dinnerware bleach pittin.frame: Tom's mother soaked dinnerware in dilute bleach overnight; oxygenated chloride pitted the stainless in 24 hours. Used as a domestic-scale demonstration of the Manwich mechanism.
Stainless steel dinnerware bleach pittin.case_name: Stainless steel dinnerware bleach pitting (personal anecdote)

Arizona warehouse roof corrosion failure.title: WM_Su2014_06
Arizona warehouse roof corrosion failure.frame: The worst carbon-steel corrosion rate Tom has ever seen (40–80 mil/year). Diurnal wet-dry cycling between vapor barrier and roof decking created a sauna in the ceiling cavity that destroyed galvanized steel hangers within a year.

Arizona aircraft boneyard (Davis-Monthan.title: WM_Su2014_06
Arizona aircraft boneyard (Davis-Monthan.frame: Brief reference, not a forensic case. Used to make the moisture-pathway point by counterexample (low-humidity desert preserves metals) and to contrast with Navy practice of storing assets in seawater.
Arizona aircraft boneyard (Davis-Monthan.case_name: Mothballed B-52s at the Arizona aircraft boneyard

Navy reactor shutdown hydrazine oxygen s.title: WM_Su2014_06
Navy reactor shutdown hydrazine oxygen s.frame: Pedagogical contrast with commercial pre-boiler sparging. Navy uses hydrazine; commercial plants can't afford it and use steam sparge instead.
Navy reactor shutdown hydrazine oxygen s.case_name: Nuclear submarine / carrier reactor shutdown with hydrazine

HIP vessel explosion (16-ton fragment ej.title: CAS_Su2011_07
HIP vessel explosion (16-ton fragment ej.frame: Tail of a case from a prior session. The world's only HIP vessel capable of all aircraft-engine disc work; a sixteen-ton piece landed a quarter mile away in random direction. Saved from being a multi-billion-dollar problem because a second vessel was coming on stream in three months.

Navy internally cooled recuperator (ICR).title: CAS_Su2011_07
Navy internally cooled recuperator (ICR).frame: Heat exchanger to preheat incoming air using stack gases on oil-fired surface ships, intended to raise cruise efficiency from ~10% to 30%, eliminating off-station refueling time. First built version lasted two minutes before tearing itself apart from transient thermal stresses. Eagar served on a Blue Ribbon panel investigating it.

Bell Labs zone melting semiconductor pur.title: CAS_Su2011_07
Bell Labs zone melting semiconductor pur.frame: Bell Labs technician Pfann invents zone melting in the 1950s to purify silicon and germanium to 6-9s (one part per million) for early semiconductors. Still the basis of high-purity silicon production.

Sea Wolf welding wire high-side chemistr.title: CAS_Su2011_07
Sea Wolf welding wire high-side chemistr.frame: Two-billion-dollar Navy problem traced to welding wire drawn from an enriched (high-side-chemistry) region of a twenty-ton ingot. Yield strength came in at 140 ksi instead of 100 ksi; hydrogen sensitivity scaled accordingly. All within spec but at the wrong end of the range. Used to land the teaching point that microsegregation in the original casting propagates through downstream processing.
Sea Wolf welding wire high-side chemistr.case_name: Sea Wolf welding wire high-side chemistry / hydrogen cracking

Single-crystal turbine blade growth in g.title: CAS_Su2011_07
Single-crystal turbine blade growth in g.frame: GE and Pratt cast 16–24 blades per investment sprue; Rolls-Royce uses 4. Ten-hour pull through a 1000° gradient, $3M furnace per ~16–32 blades/day. Cost per blade ~$6,000 but justified by life-of-engine fuel savings. Used to teach that the steep gradient suppresses constitutional supercooling and gives planar-front solidification.
Single-crystal turbine blade growth in g.case_name: Single-crystal turbine blade growth in gradient furnaces

US Steel / Bethlehem Steel generator rot.title: CAS_Su2011_07
US Steel / Bethlehem Steel generator rot.frame: Six-story-tall forging facility, originally used for WWI battleship gun barrels. 450-ton ingot → 200-ton forging after oxide loss and machining. Only one such facility remaining in the US; Bethlehem's steel plant is now an amusement park.
US Steel / Bethlehem Steel generator rot.case_name: Generator rotor forging (US Steel or Bethlehem Steel)

Cold-heading insert for particle-board f.title: CAS_Su2011_07
Cold-heading insert for particle-board f.frame: Stage-direction demonstration. Eleven-step cold-heading sequence: wire chop → size → extrude hole partway → extrude further → head → punch out waste → finishing size → knurl grip → thread inside → plate. Phosphate-stearate lubrication after WWII reduced die count and made it economical. 180 dB shops; seven heading strokes per second.

Isothermal forging \u2014 Pratt & Whitne.title: CAS_Su2011_07
Isothermal forging \u2014 Pratt & Whitne.frame: Process developed by Pratt & Whitney based on 1938 German superplasticity work (lost in WWII). Dies heated to ~1000°C, slow squeeze (10–15 min), single set of dies. 250 lb → 15 lb conventional becomes 126 lb → 15 lb isothermal.

Backofen's rediscovery of superplasticit.title: CAS_Su2011_07
Backofen's rediscovery of superplasticit.frame: Al Backofen and grad student Don Avery, early '60s, working titanium and zircaloy through phase transformations to ultrafine grain (1–2 μm). Found m (strain-rate sensitivity) goes up dramatically with fine grain; 1000% elongation possible. Backofen took an aluminum-zinc alloy to Taunton silversmiths, used a candy-dish die, and pulled in a single draw what would normally require four or five operations. Tom keeps the resulting sample as the Smithsonian-grade demonstration.
Backofen's rediscovery of superplasticit.case_name: Backofen's rediscovery of superplasticity / Taunton candy-dish die

Post-office summer job and Naval Air rew.title: CAS_Su2011_07
Post-office summer job and Naval Air rew.frame: Tom's path to working in Backofen's lab. Includes the Norfolk Naval Air rework facility rebuilding Vietnam-era jet engines as a $1.92/hr job. Function in the lecture: setup for "I decided to take a real research job and ended up with Backofen."
Post-office summer job and Naval Air rew.case_name: Post-office summer job and Naval Air rework facility (Norfolk)

Reynolds Aluminum foil manufacturing.title: CAS_Su2011_07
Reynolds Aluminum foil manufacturing.frame: Reynolds founded an aluminum company to produce foil for packaging cigarettes — wanted moisture control for the tobacco product. Used as the why-foil-matters framing for pack rolling.

Reynolds Aluminum foil manufacturing.title: SMS_F2013_09
Reynolds Aluminum foil manufacturing.frame: R.J. Reynolds Tobacco needed something to wrap tobacco in, so started making aluminum foil around 1900; the aluminum business eventually grew separate from tobacco. Used to teach the historical breadth of the aluminum industry beyond Alcoa.

Davenport Iowa Alcoa plate gauge variati.title: CAS_Su2011_07
Davenport Iowa Alcoa plate gauge variati.frame: World's largest rolling mill, 8-ft × 15-ft rolls, rolling 747 wing plate. ~20% off-gauge plate. LFM student thesis ~1990 mapped the variation along plate length. Root cause: water from roll-cooling pooling on the curled end of hot plate, locally cooling and stiffening the aluminum, producing thicker ends. Solution: a $10,000 compressed-air knife. Alcoa's NIH culture refused to implement. Tom bet Owen Richmond $10,000 it wouldn't happen; a year later he was right.
Davenport Iowa Alcoa plate gauge variati.case_name: Davenport Iowa Alcoa plate gauge variation / air knife

LIGO gravitational wave detector corrosi.title: SSW_S2013_01
LIGO gravitational wave detector corrosi.frame: Tom's consulting trip to Livingston, Louisiana the previous day. Used as opening anecdote (§1) and developed in §6 as the prototype "billion-dollar facility jeopardized by a tiny failure at a joint" — mice nested on stainless steel insulation, urine and feces caused chloride corrosion, leak in 4-km ultra-high-vacuum beam tube.
LIGO gravitational wave detector corrosi.case_name: LIGO gravitational wave detector — mouse-induced corrosion of vacuum vessel

Liberty ships and SS Schenectady / SS Ma.title: SSW_S2013_01
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady / SS Ma.frame: The canonical case for "welds create continuous crack paths whereas rivets stop cracks at plate boundaries." 4,694 ships built; 1,442 reported casualties; more than one fracture per ship on average. Schenectady cracked in harbor; SS Manhattan cracked at sea. Used to launch the post-WWII brittle-fracture research history (Weck/British Welding Institute, Pellini/NRL, Cohen-Averbach/MIT).
Liberty ships and SS Schenectady / SS Ma.case_name: Liberty ships and SS Schenectady / SS Manhattan brittle fracture

Pellini explosion bulge test / Naval Res.title: SSW_S2013_01
Pellini explosion bulge test / Naval Res.frame: Second of the three post-WWII brittle-fracture research centers. Pellini at NRL, later came to MIT in retirement.
Pellini explosion bulge test / Naval Res.case_name: Pellini explosion bulge test / Naval Research Lab brittle fracture work

MIT brittle fracture research (Cohen, Av.title: SSW_S2013_01
MIT brittle fracture research (Cohen, Av.frame: Third of the three post-WWII brittle-fracture research centers. Cited as the origin point for most of what is known about brittle fracture of steels.
MIT brittle fracture research (Cohen, Av.case_name: MIT brittle fracture research — Morris Cohen and Ben Averbach

Big Inch Pipeline.title: SSW_S2013_01
Big Inch Pipeline.frame: First critical structure made by arc welding — 30-inch pipeline, Louisiana to New Jersey, 1930. Cited as the historical pivot from riveted to welded long-distance transmission infrastructure.

Big Inch Pipeline.title: CAS_Su2011_02
Big Inch Pipeline.frame: Cited as the first major all-welded structural project — 30-inch Louisiana-to-New-Jersey pipeline, welded rather than riveted to avoid material penalty and joint leaks.

Big Inch Pipeline.title: WM_Su2015_03
Big Inch Pipeline.frame: First critical welded structure, early 1930s. Predecessor and proof-of-concept for welded ship construction in WWII.
Big Inch Pipeline.case_name: Big Inch pipeline (Louisiana to New Jersey, 30-inch)

Friction stir welded jet aircraft propos.title: SSW_S2013_01
Friction stir welded jet aircraft propos.frame: Cautionary footnote to the Liberty ship lesson. Late-70s British Welding Institute invention; startup proposed friction-stir welding aluminum/titanium small business jet. Tom skeptical: an SS Manhattan crack in mid-Atlantic gives passengers lifeboats; a fuselage crack at altitude does not. Company went bankrupt before product release.
Friction stir welded jet aircraft propos.case_name: Friction stir welded jet aircraft proposal

Bethlehem Steel generator rotor forging.title: SSW_S2013_01
Bethlehem Steel generator rotor forging.frame: Tom's 1970s consulting at Bethlehem Steel — could a 700-ton generator rotor forging be replaced by welding two smaller forgings, to avoid $2 billion capital investment in new heat-treatment facilities? Tom did not solve it; other technology obviated the need. Used as the case for "largest single product without a joint" and as the historical hinge to battleship-gun-barrel facilities being repurposed for generator rotors.
Bethlehem Steel generator rotor forging.case_name: Bethlehem Steel generator rotor forging — welding feasibility study

Battleship gun barrel manufacturing faci.title: SSW_S2013_01
Battleship gun barrel manufacturing faci.frame: Government-built early-20th-century heat-treatment facilities for long tubular forgings. Repurposed for generator rotors after WWII. Cited as the example of government-funded capability creating downstream commercial industry.

Intel Pentium chip wire bonding.title: SSW_S2013_01
Intel Pentium chip wire bonding.frame: Physical-object demonstration of "ubiquity from chips to ships" — 400 leads per chip, 20-year-old bonding technology still in use.

MIT Lincoln Lab 300 GHz radar dish struc.title: SSW_S2013_01
MIT Lincoln Lab 300 GHz radar dish struc.frame: Football-field-sized aluminum structure, tolerance of ~3 mm over 100 yards. Project budget grew from $20M to $100M. No welding shop would bid because tolerances were beyond imagination. Eventually fabricated by a firm doing Electric Boat submarine work. Belmonte's prior firm helped design it. Used to illustrate joint efficiency, gusset-plate design, and welding-shop capacity limits.
MIT Lincoln Lab 300 GHz radar dish struc.case_name: MIT Lincoln Lab 300 GHz radar dish structure (Millstone)

Space Shuttle Challenger O-ring.title: SSW_S2013_01
Space Shuttle Challenger O-ring.frame: 1986 Challenger explosion. Tom's reflexive prediction: "I bet it failed at a weld." Correction: O-ring seal — not a weld but still a joint. Used to anchor the "failures happen at joints" thesis.

Pelloux quote \u2014 \"something won't f.title: SSW_S2013_01
Pelloux quote \u2014 \"something won't f.frame: Tom's first year on faculty; MIT mechanical engineering professor Reggie Pelloux's classroom remark, later delivered by Tom in the 1992 Houdremont Lecture to 500 welding engineers at the International Institute of Welding in Montreal. Used as both job-security joke and frame for §7 (why welds actually do fail).
Pelloux quote \u2014 \"something won't f.case_name: Pelloux quote — "something won't fail unless it's been welded"

Nuclear submarine hull steel (HY-80).title: SMS_F2013_04
Nuclear submarine hull steel (HY-80).case_name: HY80 submarine hull steel sample (General Dynamics)

X-33 space plane.title: SMS_F2014_03
X-33 space plane.frame: Physical sample shown to illustrate the $12,000/lb fabrication cost in aerospace.
X-33 space plane.case_name: X-33 space plane liquid hydrogen tank

X-33 space plane.title: DP_S2012_01
X-33 space plane.frame: Brief mention as the would-be reusable-shuttle successor that "had problems." Foreshadowed for later lectures.

X-33 space plane.title: SMS_F2013_08
X-33 space plane.frame: $12,000-per-pound composite hydrogen tanks, 8,000 lb total mass, $100 million total market — the limiting case for boutique-composite economics.

Eagar torn cartilage and Vietnam draft e.title: SMS_F2013_04
Eagar torn cartilage and Vietnam draft e.case_name: Tom's knee injury and Vietnam draft

Pellini explosion bulge test development.title: SMS_F2014_08
Pellini explosion bulge test development.frame: Pellini at NRL develops fracture methods for Navy nuclear submarine steels; retires to MIT Ocean Engineering; his "ratio analysis diagram" referenced as the diagnostic plot to be discussed.
Pellini explosion bulge test development.case_name: Naval Research Lab fracture program (Bill Pellini)

Pellini explosion bulge test development.title: WM_Su2014_09
Pellini explosion bulge test development.frame: William S. Pellini at the Naval Research Laboratory developed the explosion bulge test to characterize ship-steel ductile-brittle behavior. Tom describes the 14-inch test specimen, the explosive-charge protocol, the ductile-brittle transition discovery (around room temperature), and the $50K–$100K per test cost today. Tests now run at remote sites (formerly White Oak).

Pellini explosion bulge test development.title: SMS_F2014_09
Pellini explosion bulge test development.frame: Pellini, at NRL, developed the ratio analysis diagram from his work on WWII Liberty ship brittle fracture. Tom built on Pellini's diagram thirty years ago.
Pellini explosion bulge test development.case_name: Pellini ratio analysis diagram (NRL Liberty ship fracture work)

Boeing 777 advanced composites program.title: MSE_F2016_12
Boeing 777 advanced composites program.frame: Cited as the "$20 billion bet-your-company" precedent. Drawing-board ambition was 100% composite; final delivery was 12% composite (in the nacelle).

Boeing 777 advanced composites program.title: SMS_F2013_08
Boeing 777 advanced composites program.frame: Originally planned for 80–90% composite; reduced because the V-22-style economics didn't scale to commercial aviation. The $188-per-pound-saved Boeing internal figure (vs. the industry guess of $200) is the cost-analysis anchor.

Boeing 777 advanced composites program.title: SMS_S2016_06
Boeing 777 advanced composites program.frame: Originally intended as all-composite; cost-engineered down to 30% composite, 70% aluminum.

Boeing 777 advanced composites program.title: MSE_F2016_06
Boeing 777 advanced composites program.frame: The 777 was supposed to be 80% composites; got canned after a couple of years and made mostly aluminum. Professor Gutowski's LFM-program students worked on it. Used to set up Jim Williams's corollary: "we need *cheaper* composites, not better composites."

Electron beam deposition on naval propel.title: FW_Su2013_06
Electron beam deposition on naval propel.frame: Post-cold-war research contract using nickel-manganese-aluminum bronze samples to demonstrate ridge buildup on propeller-grade castings. Surface tension defects and residual stress limit buildup to about half an inch.
Electron beam deposition on naval propel.case_name: Electron beam deposition on naval propellers

Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive.title: FW_Su2013_06
Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive.frame: Office of Naval Research contract at Pratt & Whitney around 1976-77 to build up turbine discs with high-power laser. 15 lb/day deposition rate. Tom frames this as the predecessor of today's additive manufacturing hype: "a whole new generation of people who refuse to believe that the people before them were not completely stupid."
Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive.case_name: Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive manufacturing experiment

Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive.title: AM_F2019_05
Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive.frame: The historical precedent for laser-based additive manufacturing — Pratt & Whitney demonstrated in 1975 that going slowly enough you can achieve 100% density. Tom uses this to anchor the claim that the physics has been known for over 40 years; what's new is the commercial packaging.
Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive.case_name: Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive manufacturing experiment

Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive.title: AM_F2019_03
Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive.frame: brief historical anchor — first attempt to additively manufacture a turbine disk, 1975, Pratt Whitney's 75 kW research laser, six-inch disk contract. Tom truncates and ends the lecture.
Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive.case_name: Pratt & Whitney 1975 laser disk additive manufacturing experiment

Wyoming gas plant heat exchanger explosi.title: FW_Su2013_06
Wyoming gas plant heat exchanger explosi.frame: Active consulting case at time of lecture. 70-week lead time for $20M aluminum cryogenic heat exchanger replacement; quarter-billion-dollar project down. Tom uses this to motivate the case for rapid-fabrication EB/laser deposition.
Wyoming gas plant heat exchanger explosi.case_name: Wyoming gas plant heat exchanger explosion and failure

Yoel Fink perfect mirror / Bragg fiber d.title: FW_Su2013_06
Yoel Fink perfect mirror / Bragg fiber d.frame: MIT doctoral thesis ~1998 developing dielectric mirror via index-of-refraction layering, with quantum-confined reflection. First application: laser surgery fiber optics. Now used for higher-power laser welding.
Yoel Fink perfect mirror / Bragg fiber d.case_name: MIT perfect mirror (Yoel Fink doctoral work)

Naval Research Lab Laser Welding of HY-8.title: FW_Su2013_06
Naval Research Lab Laser Welding of HY-8.frame: 30-year-old NRL result: 25 kW laser welding HY-80 produced *better* weld-metal properties than the base material, because the laser preferentially vaporized oxide and sulfide inclusions. Tom's preferred illustration of the "laser couples better to inclusions" principle.
Naval Research Lab Laser Welding of HY-8.case_name: Naval Research Lab Laser Welding of HY-80

Naval Research Lab Laser Welding of HY-8.title: CAS_Su2011_06
Naval Research Lab Laser Welding of HY-8.frame: Ed Metzbower found laser-welded HY-80 weld metal cleaner than the base plate — superheat vaporized inclusions, yielding better fatigue properties in weld than parent metal.
Naval Research Lab Laser Welding of HY-8.case_name: Naval Research Laboratory laser welding of HY-80 (Metzbower)

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries spherical st.title: FW_Su2013_06
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries spherical st.frame: The one heavy-section EB welding application Tom considers a real success. Two-inch-thick stainless steel spherical vessels, welded in a chamber the size of a two-story building, ~10 minutes per pass. Justified by hundreds-of-vessels production volume for a nuclear program. Stainless steels are also more weldable than carbon steels in heavy section.
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries spherical st.case_name: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries spherical stainless steel reactor vessel welding

Japanese heavy-section electron beam wel.title: FW_Su2013_06
Japanese heavy-section electron beam wel.frame: Mid-80s Japanese national project, ~$200M, to weld 6-8 inch thick steel pressure vessels for coal gasification. Tom spent a year there. The problem-list catalog of §7 derives from this experience. Includes thermocouple/Seebeck effect on beam path (§1.p3) and oxide-induced porosity (§7.p3).
Japanese heavy-section electron beam wel.case_name: Japanese heavy-section electron beam welding project

Japanese heavy-section electron beam wel.title: FW_Su2013_05
Japanese heavy-section electron beam wel.frame: Built a 600 kV / 60 kW machine for EB welds in 4–8 inch thick steel. Tom flags that "it didn't work all that well" but does not develop the case in this lecture.
Japanese heavy-section electron beam wel.case_name: Japanese 600 kV electron beam welder for heavy-section steel

Laser-welded aluminum window frames (cir.title: FW_Su2013_06
Laser-welded aluminum window frames (cir.frame: Illinois plant, 10 lasers, 300 million feet/year, double-pane window aluminum frames. Tom's favorite "the exception that proves the rule" example: laser-welding aluminum is unreliable, but the *inherent* unreliability produced the slightly-porous breathing weld the application needed. Eventually supplanted by mechanical stitching.

Kodak film plant exclusion from Japan (l.title: FW_Su2013_06
Kodak film plant exclusion from Japan (l.frame: Tom's classic case for how Japanese non-tariff barriers protected Fuji's rise. Kodak's request to build a Japanese film plant was never answered.
Kodak film plant exclusion from Japan (l.case_name: Kodak film plant exclusion from Japan (late 1970s–1980s)

Kodak manufacturing inefficiency in mono.title: FW_Su2013_06
Kodak manufacturing inefficiency in mono.frame: Kodak Park tour: stainless-steel custom conveyors and elevators built rather than purchased, because Kodak was "printing money" and needed to spend it before showing too much profit attracted antitrust scrutiny. Building Six = Eastman Building. (Sidenote: Eastman bailed MIT out of bankruptcy in 1917.)
Kodak manufacturing inefficiency in mono.case_name: Kodak manufacturing inefficiency in monopoly era (mid-1990s)

U.S. Steel Industry Crisis and Japanese.title: FW_Su2013_06
U.S. Steel Industry Crisis and Japanese.frame: Bethlehem Steel 1973 most-profitable-year-ever as the high-water mark before two decades of decline. US steel's 75% world capacity in 1945 → 25% by mid-1970s. The "fully depreciated 1911 coke ovens" anecdote from the 1975 Bethlehem new-hire training serves as Tom's archetype of monopoly-era managerial complacency.
U.S. Steel Industry Crisis and Japanese.case_name: U.S. Steel Industry Crisis and Japanese Competition

America's Cup HY-80 keel failure.title: WM_S2014_21
America's Cup HY-80 keel failure.frame: Used to illustrate that 130 ksi welded keel beam, four feet wide and eight inches thick, bent under sail loads — concentrating force in a single bending moment was beyond what HY130 could carry at that geometry. Tom names it as HY130 (the Navy submarine steel), not HY-80; the canonical cluster name may need reconciliation against other lectures.

General Motors and Ford minivan spot-wel.title: WM_S2014_21
General Motors and Ford minivan spot-wel.frame: Mid-1980s lightweighting initiative. GM and Ford substituted high-strength steel and assumed fatigue life would scale with ultimate strength. The spot welds — stress concentrations — did not benefit, and minivan owners experienced rattles within a couple of years.
General Motors and Ford minivan spot-wel.case_name: General Motors and Ford minivan spot-weld fatigue failures

Egyptian-Israeli Tank War.title: WIE_F2015_04
Egyptian-Israeli Tank War.frame: Used as a metaphor for the West Point pedagogical style — "they tell you how it's done" — contrasted with the Harvard Business School case-study method and the MIT Sloan quantitative method. Not a forensic teaching case here; cited rhetorically.
Egyptian-Israeli Tank War.case_name: Egyptian-Israeli tank war (1973) as a West Point teaching exemplar

US Steel industry decline.title: WIE_F2015_04
US Steel industry decline.frame: Tom's setup for the Sputnik-as-wake-up-call narrative. The 75%-to-25% collapse over twenty-five years is a framing statistic Tom uses across multiple lectures to motivate discussions of the US steel industry decline and Japanese competition.
US Steel industry decline.case_name: US share of world steel production (1945: 75%, ~1970: 25%)

US Steel industry decline.title: CAS_Su2011_03
US Steel industry decline.frame: US mills operating at 50–60% of capacity while Korea, Japan, China, Romania build new plants for political-economic reasons; Kennedy's 1962 price rollback; US Steel built world's largest Open Hearth (450 tons, Pittsburgh) around 1970 when process was already dead.

Materials engineering share of practicin.title: WIE_F2015_04
Materials engineering share of practicin.frame: Tom cites a study finding ~25% of practicing engineers are directly doing materials work and another ~35% indirectly — for ~60% total. Used to motivate the Course Three / materials subgroup point in §4.p3.
Materials engineering share of practicin.case_name: Materials engineering share of practicing engineers (~60%)

Alexander Kielland disaster.title: WM_Su2014_21
Alexander Kielland disaster.frame: North Sea five-legged pentagon rig built at French Dunkirk shipyard in the 1970s. Crack started at a fillet weld attaching a sonar flange plate (a vestigial appendage from when the rig was a drilling ship; never used in its hotel-conversion role). Maintenance crew (loose procedures) versus fabrication crew (strict procedures) — the maintenance weld killed the rig. Heat-affected zone hardness 350 (Rockwell C35); flange plate ductility one to seven percent.

Alexander Kielland disaster.title: WM_Su2014_14
Alexander Kielland disaster.frame: Extended case study (sustained across §2). Maintenance welders welding without proper procedure controls created a hydrogen crack at a hydrophone-mount weld; the crack grew by fatigue to 50 feet over ~18 months until one of five legs separated and the platform capsized in a North Sea storm. Source attribution: Easterling textbook.

Alexander Kielland disaster.title: SSW_S2013_04
Alexander Kielland disaster.frame: Catch-up follow-up to prior session. Tom returns to the dimensions of the platform, the 1060-steel hydrophone bracket weld that initiated failure, and the Norwegian commission's focus on inadequate life rafts after conversion from drilling platform to hotel. 220 fatalities.

Alexander Kielland disaster.title: SSW_S2013_02
Alexander Kielland disaster.frame: Extended case on why non-critical welds matter. A 16-inch sonar-bracket pipe welded to a 24-foot-diameter leg, with a thumbnail-sized crack in high-carbon steel, grew by fatigue to 20+ feet before a storm snapped the structure. Over 200 dead.

High-speed helicopter drive shaft hydrog.title: WM_Su2014_21
High-speed helicopter drive shaft hydrog.frame: Post-break Q&A continuation. Warehouse inventory center in North Carolina etched a unique identifier code into high-speed steel drive shafts; the etching introduced hydrogen into the high-strength steel and 100% of the etched parts failed in fatigue simulation. Subsequent move to laser scribing produced the same problem by a different route (rapid surface melt → high hardness → brittle initiation). Pulled together with the PMI (positive materials identification) serialization-of-parts program of the 1970s–80s.
High-speed helicopter drive shaft hydrog.case_name: Coast Guard / military helicopter drive shaft etching hydrogen cracking

IMT North Andover hot isostatic press ex.title: WM_Su2014_21
IMT North Andover hot isostatic press ex.frame: World's largest HIP at the time. 60-inch ID, 300-ton forged vessel, 200-ton cylinder with 50-ton plugs top and bottom, holding 20,000 psi argon at 1500°F for jet engine disc and rotor consolidation. Japanese-forged vessel (no U.S. capability in 1980s). Brittle fracture initiated outside at a threaded stress concentration; top piece flew a quarter mile; one 5-ton fragment crushed the operator's chair (vacant by ~3 feet, 2 AM shift change). Three-factor teaching case: material deficient (renormalization without prolongation, substitute test piece cooled wrong), stress higher than predicted (transient thermal stress on outside, not the steady-state inside max from the supercomputer model), environment corrosive (phosphate water-treatment chemistry pitting the outside like a Dalmatian). Critical flaw size went from a predicted 15 inches to a measured half-inch initiating fatigue crack. Pratt Whitney, GE, Rolls-Royce all dependent on this furnace for aircraft engine disc HIP; fortunately a sister vessel was under construction.
IMT North Andover hot isostatic press ex.case_name: IMT North Andover hot isostatic press explosion

Gas pipeline brittle fracture propagatio.title: WM_Su2014_21
Gas pipeline brittle fracture propagatio.case_name: Gas vs. liquid pipeline fracture mechanics

Boeing aluminum wing manufacturing waste.title: DP_S2012_06
Boeing aluminum wing manufacturing waste.frame: Reference to Boeing wings machined from plate, ~20:1 buy-to-fly ratio. Brief — back-reference to earlier lecture treatment.

Boeing aluminum wing manufacturing waste.title: WM_S2014_23
Boeing aluminum wing manufacturing waste.frame: 80–90% of the heat-treated Alcoa plate is machined away as chips to produce the final wing structure with bosses and thinner sections. Used to motivate why welding is avoided (residual stresses) and machining is preferred despite the waste.

German plastic injection molding machine.title: DP_S2012_06
German plastic injection molding machine.frame: 20-foot forged shaft, fatigue crack after ~18 months in service originating from a 1-inch × 1/4-inch forging lap. Used to illustrate that forging laps are diagnostic: oxidized surface from 2,000°F formation in air gives them away. German manufacturer initially denied.
German plastic injection molding machine.case_name: German plastic injection molding machine shaft forging lap

Gulf of Mexico oil pipeline defect.title: DP_S2012_06
Gulf of Mexico oil pipeline defect.frame: Seamless pipe with a 3/4-inch × 3/8-inch surface flaw 80% through-wall, made in Ohio, passed two factory hydro tests, failed third hydro test after installation in Gulf. Cause: piece of fatigued piercing mandrel embedded in pipe surface. Defect was on pipe end, where eddy current couldn't reach; magnetic particle inspection (manual) missed it.
Gulf of Mexico oil pipeline defect.case_name: Gulf of Mexico oil pipeline defect

Gulf of Mexico oil pipeline defect.title: CS_F2012_12

SS Libra LNG vessel tail shaft failure.title: CAS_Su2011_04
SS Libra LNG vessel tail shaft failure.frame: In October 1980, the SS LNG Libra — a 125,000-ton liquefied-natural-gas tanker built at Quincy Shipyard — lost power fully loaded in the Philippine Sea when her thirty-three-inch solid steel tail shaft sheared in two. ABS surveyors transferred the LNG cargo to a sister ship at Davao City and dry-docked the vessel in Singapore, where Tom Eagar examined the fracture. The shaft contained a football-sized shrinkage pipe (the ingot had not been topped enough because the Seattle steel mill was at its maximum ingot-casting capacity and was already losing money on prior scrapped attempts) and a brittle "clink" crack — an internal flaw caused by thermal stresses when the cold, brittle interior of a large ingot is heated too rapidly in a forging furnace. A lab technician had detected the void by ultrasonics and documented it in writing; his supervisor refused to act. The shaft was shipped to Quincy without incoming inspection, ran for three to four years until the fatigue crack reached critical size, and broke. Litigation settled with the shipyard paying $6–8 million of a roughly $15 million loss, despite the steel mill being the primary culprit, because of pre-existing bad blood between the shipowner and General Dynamics.

Middletown Connecticut gas pipeline expl.title: CS_F2012_05
Middletown Connecticut gas pipeline expl.frame: Developed forensic case. Super Bowl Sunday ~2010, gas-fired utility under construction. A106 pipe standards conflict.title: CS_F2012_05
A106 pipe standards conflict.frame: Developed forensic case. ~$5B refinery built by financial-investor consortium during a period of pipe shortage. Pipe purchased to ASTM A106 with installation under ASME B31.1. One in-service leak; refinery rejected remaining 600 lengths and hired a long-distance consultant who applied non-destructive electromagnetic testing (12.5% wall-thickness flaw threshold) rather than the hydrostatic test the pipe was sold under. Tom, retained by the other side, inspected all 600 lengths over a week and found zero failures even by the stricter NDE threshold. Dispute value: $60M, ongoing at lecture date.

A106 pipe standards conflict.title: CS_Su2012_04
A106 pipe standards conflict.frame: A petrochemical refinery purchased ~600 lengths of Romanian-mill ASTM A106 seamless carbon steel pipe (6–20 inch diameter) during a global steel-pipe shortage. The purchase order specified hydrostatic testing (the default in A106 §13, roughly 40% of yield, ~1500 PSI for the smaller diameters). After one leak was found in service, the owner had non-destructive electric testing (ultrasonic/eddy current/magnetic particle) performed, which uses a much more stringent 12.5%-of-wall flaw criterion not called out in the purchase order. Tom and colleagues spent August on site inspecting all 600 lengths and found no defects exceeding the 12.5% threshold. The owner nonetheless sought ~$60 million on an originally couple-million-dollar order, having already torn out installed pipe. Tom frames this as the canonical "you only get what you paid for" dispute and as a case of engineers unable to read their own purchase specifications or the English of the standard itself.

Hot isostatic pressing vessel explosion.title: WM_Su2015_13
Hot isostatic pressing vessel explosion.frame: Tom's longest sustained case in the lecture. 250-ton HIP vessel containing Harley-Davidson cylinder heads and other castings. Broke into 70 pieces averaging 5 tons each at 2 AM. Operator nearly killed by a five-ton fragment that landed on his desk. Tom and John McNichol of Chromalloy were the first two into the pit. Three-circle analysis: (1) transient thermal stresses (vessel designed for steady-state only, no 3D model); (2) bad microstructure (Charpy testing done on a too-small surrogate piece that cooled faster than the 200-ton forging, masking the real properties); (3) hydrogen embrittlement / SCC from Nalco molybdenum oxide water-treatment inhibitors pitting the outer wall ("101 Dalmatians"). Designed as leak-before-break; should have leaked at an 11-inch critical flaw, but actual critical flaw size was 1 inch because each circle compromised the toughness.

Subsea pipeline tool fragment defect.frame: A US-made seamless 4-inch, ~half-inch-wall pipe for an underwater Gulf of Mexico oil line passed mill hydrostatic, magnetic particle, and eddy current inspections. A 3–4 inch fragment of the piercing tool used in seamless-pipe manufacture had broken off and wedged into 80% of the wall thickness, plugging the defect so that hydrostatic tests passed. After welding, yellow corrosion coating, and ocean-bottom installation, a final hydrostatic test at lower pressure leaked — the wedge having loosened under prior tests. Recovery cost ~$4 million plus project delay. Tom uses it to illustrate that defects can survive multiple non-destructive and hydrostatic inspections by passing through critical-but-poorly-inspected zones.
Subsea pipeline tool fragment defect.case_name: Gulf of Mexico subsea pipeline tool fragment defect

Shipyard fillet weld measurement dispute.title: CS_Su2012_04
Shipyard fillet weld measurement dispute.frame: Tom evaluated a Maritime Administration program for an automatic laser-based fillet-weld size inspector accurate to ±0.010 inch. Field testing against shipyard inspectors using hand gauges showed inspectors could not do better than ~±0.020 inch. The new instrument exceeded inspector accuracy by 2x, but Tom recounts an Electric Boat engineer telling him years earlier: "the last thing I want is another thing I can measure, because I'm going to be held to that standard." Used to make the broader point that improving measurement capability creates disputes the original specification never anticipated.

Georgia missile-handling building Farada.title: CS_Su2012_04
Georgia missile-handling building Farada.frame: Student in the class describes a Faraday cage installed at a missile-handling building in Georgia — four towers approximately 300 yards apart with cables strung between them in an X pattern — for communications security (preventing eavesdropping rather than for radiation containment). Tom uses it to illustrate Faraday-cage principles in the context of lightning protection code history.

NASA X-33 space plane program.title: CS_Su2012_04
NASA X-33 space plane program.frame: Tom cites the $1.3 billion X-33 space plane program — given to Lockheed Martin Skunk Works on a 30-month design-through-test-flight schedule as a flagship of post-Gulf-War rapid-prototyping ambition — as a definitive failure of the rapid-prototyping doctrine. "We didn't have the ability to do it in thirty months."

First Gulf War helicopter engine failure.title: CS_Su2012_04
First Gulf War helicopter engine failure.frame: Tom notes that during the 1990–1991 Gulf War buildup, Saudi sand sandblasted helicopter engines so severely that engines lasted hours rather than hundreds of hours. The six-month deployment window forced rapid identify-and-solve cycles and helped seed the early-1990s ARPA emphasis on rapid prototyping.

MIT undergraduate germanium thermometer.title: CS_Su2012_04
MIT undergraduate germanium thermometer.frame: As an MIT undergraduate working in a superconductivity lab attempting to break the (then ~20.3 K) world record, Tom's group owned a single $500 germanium thermometer. Buying a second one to hedge against failure produced six months of confusion because the two thermometers disagreed by a couple of tenths of a degree near liquid helium — and they could not determine which was correct. Used as a personal illustration that adding a second measurement can destroy confidence rather than build it.

Pratt & Whitney TLP bonding patent (1972.frame: Origin case for transient liquid phase diffusion bonding as practiced in the superalloy industry. Varian cross-field amplifier brazing fai.title: SSW_S2013_08
Varian cross-field amplifier brazing fai.frame: Beverly MA company called Tom in to consult on phased-array radar component (Aegis missile system context). Crossed-field amplifier had molybdenum tips brazed to a copper body with Au-18Ni eutectic braze; the 18% nickel was forming Ni₃Mo intermetallic at the moly tip, occasionally breaking off and destroying the electron beam. Tom suggested TLP joint approach. Varian had also independently tried 37Au-3Ni-60Cu and found 180-degree bend ductility; Navy refused the substitution as "cost savings" until Tom relabeled it "transient liquid phase diffusion bonding" in a letter. The Navy accepted the new label.

Varian cross-field amplifier brazing fai.title: DP_S2012_08
Varian cross-field amplifier brazing fai.frame: Tom's mid-1980s consulting case at Varian (North Shore, MA). Gold-nickel braze on copper-to-molybdenum joints in radar crossfield amplifiers failed 5T bend tests because Mo–Ni intermetallics are brittle. Varian had stumbled empirically onto a transient liquid phase diffusion bond using 65Cu-35Au-3Ni; Tom diagnosed it after metallography. He had to write a letter to convince the Navy the cheaper alloy was actually better.
Varian cross-field amplifier brazing fai.case_name: Varian crossfield amplifier brazing (gold-nickel → copper-gold-nickel TLP bond)

Navy submarine transformer solder joint.title: SSW_S2013_08
Navy submarine transformer solder joint.frame: Raytheon's Waltham defense facility was making transformers for nuclear submarine control rod actuators ($1M apiece). Specified solder was 95Pb-5Sn (melts ~300°C). A technician used 63Sn-37Pb eutectic solder (183°C) instead; during the 200°C post-pot thermal soak, liquid metal seeped out through a feed-through. Four transformers ($4M) sitting in the furnace. Pencil tests showed the joint actually didn't fail until 300°C — TLP soldering had occurred (tin diffused into copper, leaving lead-rich solid). Tom wrote a one-page letter explaining this as TLP diffusion soldering; Navy accepted the parts. Tom: "I think I made $700 on the deal."

Pratt & Whitney turbine blade grinder an.title: SSW_S2013_08
Pratt & Whitney turbine blade grinder an.frame: Pratt & Whitney's manufacturing plant 20 years ago held turbine blades to one-ten-thousandth (~2.5 micron) tolerances using a $10M grinder room-sized machine. Blades cast in Wood's metal (50% Bi alloy that expands on freezing) so there's zero looseness during grinding. Plant restructuring moved from a football-field-sized layout with separated machine types to cellular manufacturing — travel distance cut from miles to ~100 yards.
Pratt & Whitney turbine blade grinder an.case_name: Pratt & Whitney Christmas-tree blade attachment / Wood's metal fixturing

Chrysler sports car fuel injector failur.frame: Chrysler sports car with Italian-made fuel injectors had O-ring damage on installation causing fuel leaks; injectors were being air-freighted by Learjet from Italy to Detroit. Tantalum-vanadium diffusion bonding brit.title: SSW_S2013_08
Tantalum-vanadium diffusion bonding brit.frame: Diffusion-bonded tantalum-to-vanadium joints shatter on tapping because Ta-V forms brittle intermetallic. Inserting a niobium foil between them — niobium being chemically close to tantalum (the "twin" ores, hence the names; Don Satterthwaite's doctoral thesis was Ta/Nb separation) but not forming Nb-V intermetallics — produces a good bond. No commercial application; pure teaching illustration of the brittle-intermetallic constraint on dissimilar diffusion bonding.

WWII armor plate stress-relief welding.frame: Brief reference — 17-inch-thick WWII armor steel required slow welding partly because stick electrodes were slow anyway, but also because hydrogen had to be allowed to diffuse out. Used as the historical precedent for the Fore River advice.

Electric Boat administration building fl.frame: Brief aside — 25 years ago Tom was brought in by Electric Boat, taken to lunch in their new cafeteria building, which was welded with flux-core. Boston Navy Yard chrome-moly to stainles.title: WM_Su2015_08
Boston Navy Yard chrome-moly to stainles.frame: Tom's earliest major consulting success. Destroyer steam-system weld between chrome-moly tube and stainless steel; six weeks of failed attempts using the Inconel filler the Navy spec required. Tom's intervention was a joint-geometry change (machine a different groove profile to put the root pass in a lower-restraint position), which reduced residual stress and let the weld pass dye penetrant inspection. Used as the structural worked example of the microstructure/stress/hydrogen Venn diagram — diagnosis was welding metallurgy, solution was residual stress.
