Initial cement truck tank explosion and.frame: First in-plant failure of the cement truck tank line. Worker lost a leg during pressurization testing with 100 PSI air instead of water. Company paid insurance and continued production without investigation. The setup case for the fatal Pennsylvania failure.
Initial cement truck tank explosion and.case_name: Initial cement truck tank explosion and worker leg amputation

Robert Merton Sloan-to-Harvard departure.title: SMS_S2016_01
Robert Merton Sloan-to-Harvard departure.frame: Lester Thurow's "extinct volcanoes" line, used as the punchline of Tom's "it's not what you say, it's how you say it" lesson. Not a materials case; a teaching-craft anecdote that touches on the 2008-era derivatives world tangentially.

Eagar three-thousand-spot-welds rhetoric.title: SMS_S2016_01
Eagar three-thousand-spot-welds rhetoric.frame: Tom's own 1989 Gatlinburg keynote where he coined "they put three thousand spot welds in the average automobile because you need two thousand good ones." Recurring rhetorical anchor in his teaching.
Eagar three-thousand-spot-welds rhetoric.case_name: Spot welds in automobiles (3000/2000 rhetorical figure)

Hydrothermal quartz reactor explosion ne.title: SMS_F2014_09
Hydrothermal quartz reactor explosion ne.frame: Bob Laudise's hydrothermal quartz process at Bell Labs; the reactor walls run ~10 inches thick at ~10,000 psi, and one ruptured at a McDonald's near Chicago airport, killing a customer. Used to ground the "quartz watches became cheap because someone figured out how to grow quartz fast" story.
Hydrothermal quartz reactor explosion ne.case_name: Hydrothermal quartz reactor explosion near Chicago

Swiss watch industry survival via quartz.title: SMS_F2014_09
Swiss watch industry survival via quartz.frame: Used as Tom's framing case for "what makes something expensive" — at the low end, Swatches sold as fashion; at the high end, titanium-cased, ceramic-bezeled fifty-thousand-dollar luxury watches. The titanium watch becomes the segue to the broader discussion of why titanium is even available as a metal.
Swiss watch industry survival via quartz.case_name: Swiss watch industry transition (Swatch / Rolex bifurcation)

Hot isostatic press / hydrothermal vesse.title: SMS_F2014_09
Hot isostatic press / hydrothermal vesse.case_name: Hot isostatic press / hydrothermal vessel explosion lineage

H.C. Starck Newton facility \u2014 MIT v.title: SMS_F2014_09
H.C. Starck Newton facility \u2014 MIT v.frame: Cited as an example of how WWII-era vacuum metallurgy at MIT spun off into commercial reactive-metals firms. Now a Bayer Chemical subsidiary.

Tesla Nevada gigafactory water siting.title: SMS_F2014_09
Tesla Nevada gigafactory water siting.frame: Tom argues the Nevada siting is a mistake because manufacturing requires enormous water input; recalls a similar GM Sloan-program team that proposed Nogales, Arizona for the same maquiladora-labor reason and was challenged on water access.
Tesla Nevada gigafactory water siting.case_name: Tesla Nevada gigafactory water siting decision

Aircraft landing gear high-strength stee.title: SMS_F2014_09
Aircraft landing gear high-strength stee.frame: Landing gear are designed first because they take the highest stresses, and they are steel at 250–280 ksi because no composite can match the critical-flaw-size / strength combination. Triple vacuum arc melted, magnetic particle inspected.

Ritchie 2014 cryogenic high-entropy allo.title: SMS_F2014_09
Ritchie 2014 cryogenic high-entropy allo.frame: Rob Ritchie (formerly MIT, now Berkeley) and collaborators published an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy with excellent cryogenic fracture toughness in *Science*. Tom: "all they did was add iron to MP35N" and the strengthening mechanism (twinning) is the same. The Ashby plot reproduced in the paper is, in Tom's reading, a rediscovery.

MP35N cobalt-nickel-chrome-molybdenum al.title: SMS_F2014_09
MP35N cobalt-nickel-chrome-molybdenum al.frame: Tom's "favorite alloy." 35Co-35Ni-20Cr-10Mo, developed by Gaylord Smith at International Nickel in the 1960s. Non-magnetic, strengthens by twinning under cold work, reaches 280 ksi yield as bolt stock. Four MP35N bolts hold the 747 wing onto the fuselage. ASTM-specced for surgical implants since 1978.

Boeing 747 wing-to-fuselage MP35N bolt s.title: SMS_F2014_09
Boeing 747 wing-to-fuselage MP35N bolt s.frame: Four MP35N bolts, ~300 ksi, hold each 747 wing on. Sourced from Standard Pressed Steel (Philadelphia).

Brain aneurysm clip ferromagnetism contr.title: SMS_F2014_09
Brain aneurysm clip ferromagnetism contr.frame: Dr. McFadden (Johnson & Johnson consultant) and a rival neurosurgeon fought over what alloys could safely be implanted near the brain given 5-tesla MRI fields. The 304 stainless martensitic-transformation argument made some MDs argue any iron-containing alloy was unsafe; Tom recommended MP35N (zero iron) and resolved the ASTM-spec dispute in McFadden's favor.
Brain aneurysm clip ferromagnetism contr.case_name: Neurosurgical brain aneurysm clips and MRI ferromagnetism dispute

Army microcrystalline titanium kinetic-e.title: SMS_F2014_09
Army microcrystalline titanium kinetic-e.frame: Christopher Schuh (MIT DMSE) is funded by the Army to develop microcrystalline titanium as a non-radioactive high-density alternative to depleted uranium.

Hadlock platinum eyelid weights for faci.title: SMS_F2014_09
Hadlock platinum eyelid weights for faci.frame: Dr. Tessa Hadlock (Mass Eye and Ear, HST graduate, Tom's ENT) embedded platinum weights in the eyelid of a young woman whose facial muscles had been severed, so she could close her eye. Platinum chosen for density (small weight, no bulge), corrosion resistance, and bio-inertness.
Hadlock platinum eyelid weights for faci.case_name: Tessa Hadlock platinum eyelid weights (Mass Eye and Ear)

Tom Eagar's copper roof (personal).title: SMS_F2014_09
Tom Eagar's copper roof (personal).frame: $9,000 for ~50 sq ft of copper roofing on Tom's house, justified as a 100–300 year lifetime. Lateral example of when copper's price is worth paying.

Concorde maintenance and operational fai.title: WM_S2014_23
Concorde maintenance and operational fai.frame: Tom's claim that the 2000 Paris crash (runway debris from a preceding aircraft) was used as cover for retiring a fleet that was already past its useful life. Personal note: Tom mentions consulting for the company that dropped the debris.
Concorde maintenance and operational fai.case_name: Concorde retirement and Air France Flight 4590

Qatar LNG tank explosion and Shell litig.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Qatar LNG tank explosion and Shell litig.frame: Tom recalls (via Professor Pelloux) that roughly thirty years before this lecture, a Shell-designed LNG storage tank in the Persian Gulf at Qatar suffered brittle fracture and destroyed the harbor. The tank had been built to a 1940s API/British specification in the 1970s–'80s despite mature knowledge of brittle fracture, with poor steel and significant welding defects. Qatar took Shell to the World Court; Shell prevailed by arguing the failure was an RPG strike by the Emir's enemies rather than material/weld failure. Shell was barred from doing business in Qatar for several decades.
Qatar LNG tank explosion and Shell litig.case_name: Qatar LNG tank explosion and Shell litigation

Cleveland LNG explosion.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Cleveland LNG explosion.frame: Cited as the prototypical historical LNG disaster — a tank failure in the late 1940s destroyed a substantial portion of Cleveland, Ohio, and remains findable in public sources (in contrast to the Qatar event).

Big steel companies decline through mark.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Big steel companies decline through mark.frame: An early-1990s study found that essentially zero of the major steel-industry process innovations over the prior 75 years originated within steel companies. AOD came from gas-supply companies, continuous casting from machinery vendors, BOP from oxygen suppliers. Tom attributes this to complacent post-WWII US steel management — including the Bethlehem Steel executives whose Learjets at Allentown airport existed to ferry them to Florida golf weekends.
Big steel companies decline through mark.case_name: Steel industry innovation study (no innovations from steel companies)

Generator rotor shaft welding feasibilit.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Generator rotor shaft welding feasibilit.frame: As a young engineer at Bethlehem Steel (~1975), Tom was asked whether two ~40-inch-diameter forgings could be welded together to make the 750,000-pound (375-ton) generator rotor shafts required for 1,000 MW power plants. Only Bethlehem Steel, US Steel, Creusot-Loire in France, and one Japanese forging house (Tom guesses "Tokyo Steel" but is uncertain — historically Japan Steel Works) had the ingot/forging/heat-treatment capacity, originally installed ~1910–1915 for battleship gun barrels. Forging takes more than a year per shaft. Electroslag or narrow-gap welding could in principle have done it; no one funded the trial.
Generator rotor shaft welding feasibilit.case_name: Generator rotor shaft welding feasibility study (Bethlehem Steel)

MIT Plasma Fusion Center welding project.title: CAS_Su2011_04
MIT Plasma Fusion Center welding project.frame: Roughly 1990, MIT plasma-fusion researchers approached Tom about welding 20-inch-thick by ~4-foot stainless steel sections for the top dome of the ITER reactor (now being built in France) because no available forging shop could produce the part in one piece.
MIT Plasma Fusion Center welding project.case_name: MIT Plasma Fusion Center heavy-section stainless welding

Bethlehem Steel BOF retiree suicide.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Bethlehem Steel BOF retiree suicide.frame: During Tom's tenure at Bethlehem Steel, a recently retired employee returned to the plant and dove into the BOF molten steel bath; operators saw the body spread-eagled on the surface via TV monitor. The standard practice was to "bury" one ingot from that heat.

Steel mill worker injuries (1930s-1940s.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Steel mill worker injuries (1930s-1940s.frame: In 1930s–40s bar mills, mile-long red-hot bars traveled at ~40 mph and were caught with tongs by workers between rolling stands. A "cobble" — the bar curving as it exited — could amputate an arm while simultaneously cauterizing the wound. Tom's second child was born in Bethlehem, PA, in a hospital located steps from the steel mill, sized accordingly.

Bethlehem Steel forge-shop slag-shovelin.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Bethlehem Steel forge-shop slag-shovelin.frame: Two bare-chested workers shoveling ~1000°F slag in perfect alternating rhythm across a hot July forge-shop floor — thirty years of practice synchronized them so neither caught the other's throw in the face.

Henry Rowan Inductotherm acquisition and.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Henry Rowan Inductotherm acquisition and.frame: MIT alumnus Henry Rowan acquired Inductotherm and Lepel — the two or three dominant induction-melting furnace builders — and consolidated near-monopoly. Wanting a university named for him, he was rebuffed by MIT and NJIT (the latter declining at $100–200M) before endowing what became Rowan University in New Jersey.

Wind turbine shaft clink failure (Dallas.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Wind turbine shaft clink failure (Dallas.frame: Tom's second-ever encounter with a clink defect: roughly 2000, a ~24-inch wind-turbine generator shaft in a Dallas metallurgical shop showed a brittle fracture surrounded by fatigue, which the shop had been unable to diagnose. Tom identified it immediately from the Libra precedent.

Bethlehem Steel Learjet corruption (Alle.title: CAS_Su2011_04
Bethlehem Steel Learjet corruption (Alle.frame: Three or four Learjets parked at the Allentown airport whose primary winter function was ferrying Bethlehem Steel executives to Florida golf outings. Tom's parallel example: US Air Force Reserve C-5As flying cases of Coca-Cola to Tokyo so reservist pilots could log flight hours while shopping for cheap stereos.

Rolls-Royce M250 BLISK (bladed disk) for.title: SMS_S2016_06
Rolls-Royce M250 BLISK (bladed disk) for.frame: Cited as the only high-volume cast blisk engine in production (~50,000 units, 30+ years). Used to introduce the collateral-weight-savings argument.
Rolls-Royce M250 BLISK (bladed disk) for.case_name: Rolls-Royce M250 BLISK (bladed disk) for helicopters

Sprague's first law (framing principle,.title: SMS_S2016_06
Sprague's first law (framing principle,.frame: Bob Sprague (head of materials, GE aircraft engines, Cincinnati): first reported properties of a new material are the best it will ever have. Corollary (Jim Williams): first price is the lowest it will ever have.
Sprague's first law (framing principle,.case_name: Sprague's first law (framing principle, not a case)

Bringing New Materials to Market\" (1995.title: SMS_S2016_06
Bringing New Materials to Market\" (1995.frame: Tom's own publication. Twenty-year payback for new materials companies; at 8% IRR, $1 invested today must return $20 in twenty years. Used to explain why venture capital avoids materials.
Bringing New Materials to Market\" (1995.case_name: "Bringing New Materials to Market" (1995 Technology Review article)

Twenty-year oil reserves industry invest.title: SMS_S2016_06
Twenty-year oil reserves industry invest.frame: Industry maintains twenty years of proven reserves because longer-horizon returns are uneconomic at typical IRRs. Used as parallel example to the materials-investment problem.
Twenty-year oil reserves industry invest.case_name: Oil reserves and twenty-year proven-reserve floor

National Academy of Sciences Air Force p.title: SMS_S2016_06
National Academy of Sciences Air Force p.frame: Tom's NRC service ~12 years before this lecture (c. 2004). Forty-member committee advising Air Force on $300M/year for improved jet engines.
National Academy of Sciences Air Force p.case_name: National Academy of Sciences Air Force propulsion research committee

Baltimore Gas and Electric under-deposit.title: COR_Su2016_02
Baltimore Gas and Electric under-deposit.frame: Brief reference — Admiralty brass condenser tubes failed by under-deposit attack thirty or forty years ago at BG&E.
Baltimore Gas and Electric under-deposit.case_name: Baltimore Gas and Electric under-deposit corrosion

New England Aquarium sea water piping co.title: COR_Su2016_02
New England Aquarium sea water piping co.frame: Stainless steel failed (pitting from dirt), Monel was intermediate, titanium would have been best but cost-prohibitive. Used to illustrate the trade-off ladder for seawater service.
New England Aquarium sea water piping co.case_name: New England Aquarium sea water piping corrosion

Under-deposit corrosion in cast iron (Hu.title: COR_Su2016_02
Under-deposit corrosion in cast iron (Hu.frame: Student-presented case (Brian). Graphitic corrosion of cast iron component exposed to seawater after Hurricane Sandy; the silicon-derived glassy passive film was breached by chlorides under deposits. Tom appends the "cleanliness is next to godliness" corrosion rule.
Under-deposit corrosion in cast iron (Hu.case_name: Under-deposit corrosion in cast iron (Hurricane Sandy context)

Mormon Temple heat exchanger erosion-cor.title: COR_Su2016_02
Mormon Temple heat exchanger erosion-cor.frame: Belmont, MA. Copper heat exchanger failed by erosion-corrosion at tube-sheet inlet after one year. Tom recommended 70/30 cupro-nickel; only 90/10 was available within the two-week shutdown window; 90/10 has worked for fifteen years. Sub-plot on contractor markup (16k quoted vs 6k from manufacturer).
Mormon Temple heat exchanger erosion-cor.case_name: Mormon Temple heat exchanger erosion-corrosion failure

Phoenix warehouse accelerated corrosion.title: COR_Su2016_02
Phoenix warehouse accelerated corrosion.frame: Million-square-foot warehouse roof. Insulation got wet during construction rainstorm; deck closure trapped moisture in an 8-inch greenhouse cavity under Arizona sun. Corrosion rate of 20 mils/year (5× typical) perforated 1/16" sheet metal within three years.
Phoenix warehouse accelerated corrosion.case_name: Phoenix warehouse accelerated corrosion during construction

Helms Project penstock.title: WM_Su2014_20
Helms Project penstock.frame: Tom's most-developed case in the session. Eight-and-a-half-month delayed hydrogen crack on a 22-foot-diameter PG&E penstock at 6,000 ft elevation. Used to illustrate (a) that hydrogen crack delay can extend far beyond the standard "first couple of weeks" rule if the weld is frozen, (b) that boiler-and-pressure-vessel-code exceptions for inch-and-a-quarter material with fillet welds can be load-bearing in failure analysis, and (c) the litigation politics of expert witnesses ("the guy whose wife drove around in a Rolls-Royce").

Helms Project penstock.title: WM_S2014_14
Helms Project penstock.frame: Full forensic case study. PG&E pumped-storage project in the Sierra Nevada; American Bridge (division of U.S. Steel) field-fabricated a 22-foot diameter, inch-and-a-quarter wall penstock across a granite canyon. Welders skipped preheat in winter (welding inch-and-a-quarter steel with three feet of snow inside the pipe), skipped post weld heat treatment, and after frozen storage and spring pressurization the vessel failed by delayed hydrogen cracking 20 hours after reaching 188 psi service pressure. Released the upper lake, scoured 100 feet of granite, $100M loss on $800M project. Six-week trial in Fresno (early 1990s); jury found for American Bridge on a foundational-failure theory; Tom testified as the last witness.

Boston Navy Yard destroyer boiler pipe w.title: WM_Su2014_20
Boston Navy Yard destroyer boiler pipe w.frame: Tom's first big consulting case as a young MIT faculty member, ~1978. Stainless-to-2.25Cr-1Mo transition weld with persistent root cracking; NAVSEA procedure specified Inconel filler, contractor wanted to substitute stainless steel. Tom's solution: change the joint geometry (J-prep with a long land) to reduce restraint, leaving filler-metal specification intact. Used to illustrate (a) the Venn-diagram methodology applied under constraint and (b) that solutions sometimes come from the only variable left when the obvious ones are fixed.
Boston Navy Yard destroyer boiler pipe w.case_name: Boston Navy Yard destroyer boiler weld

Seawolf submarine hull cracking.title: WM_Su2014_20
Seawolf submarine hull cracking.frame: Recap from an earlier session. Over-matching by 30–40% combined with insufficient preheat for the resulting higher hardenability. Used here as the lead-in to the Helms Project — "this still occurs on a fairly regular basis."

Nautilus submarine austenitic filler met.title: WM_Su2014_20
Nautilus submarine austenitic filler met.frame: Brief reference. Early Nautilus foundations welded with austenitic filler (half the strength of HY80) as a deliberate under-matching strategy to absorb hydrogen and limit residual stress, until higher-strength procedures were qualified.
Nautilus submarine austenitic filler met.case_name: Nautilus submarine austenitic filler metal foundations

Navy under-matching filler metal studies.title: WM_Su2014_20
Navy under-matching filler metal studies.frame: Tom's "about every twenty-five years" lament. The Navy spent millions in the 1960s on near-full-scale under-matched test panels with explosive loading; spent millions again about 25 years later; reached the same conclusion both times. Used to make the fracture-mechanics point: severe undermatching concentrates strain in the weld metal.
Navy under-matching filler metal studies.case_name: Navy under-matching filler metal studies (multiple rounds)

Newport News engineering oversight failu.title: WM_Su2014_20
Newport News engineering oversight failu.frame: Tom refers back to a student presentation from the previous day. Used to land the "real engineering expertise" point closing §5. Not developed here.

Lead-acid battery terminal corrosion fro.title: SSW_S2013_10
Lead-acid battery terminal corrosion fro.frame: Used as a real-world illustration of how trace chloride catalyzes a self-regenerating corrosion cycle on lead — Tom's mechanism for why halogen-activated flux residue destroys printed circuit boards.

Tom's aluminum soldering demonstration f.title: SSW_S2013_10
Tom's aluminum soldering demonstration f.frame: Personal anecdote — Tom's assistant-professor-era aluminum soldering demo using tin/zinc chloride flux fell apart in his hands a year later because retained flux on blind joints was hygroscopic. Illustrates why reaction fluxes for aluminum are limited in practice.

Amtrak derailment near Philadelphia.title: WM_Su2015_05
Amtrak derailment near Philadelphia.frame: Used as the worked example of the Five Whys root-cause technique. Tom walks through alternative causation hypotheses — texting, drugs, rock-dropping from overpasses — that were being explored in the press at the time.

Teenage rock-dropping from overpasses.title: WM_Su2015_05
Teenage rock-dropping from overpasses.frame: Hypothesized as an alternative cause for the Amtrak derailment. Tom uses it to motivate the protective-fencing practice on busy highways.

Lehigh University welding metallurgy pro.title: WM_Su2015_05
Lehigh University welding metallurgy pro.frame: Origin story for the metallurgical bias in American welding education — "if the only tool you have is a hammer." Tom names Bob Stout, *Stout & Doty Weldability of Steels* (1940s), and the migration of Lehigh graduates to US Steel for HY steel development. Returns at §6.p4 to discuss Karl Meyer's reheat-cracking thesis.
Lehigh University welding metallurgy pro.case_name: Lehigh University welding metallurgy tradition (Stout, Doty, Pense, Meyer)

Rensselaer welding metallurgy program (W.title: WM_Su2015_05
Rensselaer welding metallurgy program (W.frame: Parallel to the Lehigh tradition. Doc Savage as the second great American welding metallurgy mentor, with John Lippold as one of his last students.
Rensselaer welding metallurgy program (W.case_name: Rensselaer welding metallurgy program (Warren Savage / Doc Savage)

Bay Bridge California corrosion-induced.title: WM_Su2015_05
Bay Bridge California corrosion-induced.frame: Don Sadoway forwarded Tom a link to this case. Tom uses it to illustrate that hydrogen embrittlement of steel doesn't require a welding arc — corrosion in seawater plus stress is enough.
Bay Bridge California corrosion-induced.case_name: Oakland Bay Bridge steel tie rod hydrogen cracking

Bay Bridge California corrosion-induced.title: WM_Su2015_06
Bay Bridge California corrosion-induced.frame: The 46-inch-diameter steel tie rods cracked within weeks after corrosion-generated hydrogen diffused into the steel. Used to extend the hydrogen-cracking framework from welds to corrosion.
Bay Bridge California corrosion-induced.case_name: Bay Bridge tie-rod corrosion-driven hydrogen cracking

Pipeline Safety Administration buried pi.title: WM_Su2015_05
Pipeline Safety Administration buried pi.frame: 45,000 miles of buried oil and gas distribution pipe, much of it installed in the 1940s–50s. DOT requirement that pipeline companies prove the in-ground properties. Motivates Belmar's instrumented scratch-test commercialization.
Pipeline Safety Administration buried pi.case_name: Pipeline Safety Administration / DOT buried-pipe property verification

Belmar instrumented scratch test (MIT sp.title: WM_Su2015_05
Belmar instrumented scratch test (MIT sp.frame: Brendan Belmar's MIT doctoral thesis on metal-on-metal scratching scaled to a startup deriving the full stress-strain curve from groove geometry. Coupled with the DOT buried-pipe case as the customer.

Nazi ball bearing factory management fai.title: WM_Su2015_05
Nazi ball bearing factory management fai.frame: Told as the United Technologies VP of manufacturing's parable about how management overhead inflates to fill available space. Origin story attributed to a colonel running an underground Hitler-era ball-bearing plant.
Nazi ball bearing factory management fai.case_name: Critical mass of management (Nazi ball bearing factory)

MIT metallurgy department founding (1888.title: WM_Su2015_05
MIT metallurgy department founding (1888.frame: Brief institutional history — MIT founded 1865 as geology and mining; metallurgy arrives 1888 in concert with Sorby and the petrography-to-steel turn.

Bethlehem Steel offshore platform lamell.title: WM_Su2015_05
Bethlehem Steel offshore platform lamell.frame: Tom's first-hand context for the lamellar tearing era. Big oil-platform plates 3–4 inches thick, 400 ppm sulfur in the steel, dirty 1911-era blast furnaces. Tom's office mate at Bethlehem worked on it.
Bethlehem Steel offshore platform lamell.case_name: Bethlehem Steel mid-1970s offshore platform lamellar tearing

Karl Meyer reheat cracking thesis (Lehig.title: WM_Su2015_05
Karl Meyer reheat cracking thesis (Lehig.frame: Meyer was Tom's supervisor at Bethlehem Steel. His thesis identified residual sulfur, arsenic, phosphorus, and antimony as the agents of reheat cracking during stress relief.
Karl Meyer reheat cracking thesis (Lehig.case_name: Karl Meyer reheat cracking doctoral thesis (Lehigh)

Bethlehem Steel Charpy bar machining wor.title: WM_Su2015_05
Bethlehem Steel Charpy bar machining wor.frame: Lesson about supplier relationships: time your machining requests to the foreman's slack capacity to get cheaper bars. Tom presents this as a transferable management insight.
Bethlehem Steel Charpy bar machining wor.case_name: Bethlehem Steel Charpy machining workaround (machine shop foreman)

LNG vessel heat treatment coupon substit.title: WM_Su2015_05
LNG vessel heat treatment coupon substit.frame: Same case as above, framed from the testing-circumvention angle. Tom presents this as a generalizable pattern of how shipyards game qualification testing.
LNG vessel heat treatment coupon substit.case_name: LNG vessel heat treatment coupon substitution and testing failure

Watertown Arsenal Charpy bar standards.title: WM_Su2015_05
Watertown Arsenal Charpy bar standards.frame: The historical source of calibrated standard Charpy bars, now superseded by NIST. Tom notes Watertown Arsenal is "a mall now."

Watertown Arsenal Charpy bar standards.title: CS_F2012_08
Watertown Arsenal Charpy bar standards.frame: Origin story of Charpy bar calibration — Army arsenal at Watertown (now Watertown Mall) calibrated impact bars from ~1900 because Army was interested in steel impact properties. NIST took over after Mansfield Amendment (~1972).

Pre-stressed concrete core test report f.title: WM_Su2015_05
Pre-stressed concrete core test report f.frame: Aside in response to a student's incredulity. Tom names (in general terms) a Boston-south test lab that issues qualification reports without receiving the cores. Used to extend the LNG test-plate point.
Pre-stressed concrete core test report f.case_name: Pre-stressed concrete core test-report fraud (Boston-area lab)

Bethlehem-vs-US-Steel weathering steel b.title: WM_Su2015_05
Bethlehem-vs-US-Steel weathering steel b.frame: Tom's first job at Bethlehem Steel. A highway bridge plate with terrible toughness was blamed on Bethlehem; Tom showed by chromium content that it was actually US Steel weathering-steel chemistry. Companion case to the Gulf of Mexico pipeline at §9.p3–§9.p9.
Bethlehem-vs-US-Steel weathering steel b.case_name: Bethlehem weathering steel highway bridge (US Steel chromium fingerprint)

Untempered 100 ksi bridge plate (mill pr.title: WM_Su2015_05
Untempered 100 ksi bridge plate (mill pr.frame: Bob Summers's scuttlebutt explanation for a plate with 160 ksi strength and 5 foot-pound Charpy toughness — it slipped through the mill without tempering.

Submarine and rocket fastener heat-treat.title: WM_Su2015_05
Submarine and rocket fastener heat-treat.frame:
Recounted by a student (likely a Navy officer in the class) as a paperwork-fraud case: fastener manufacturer's certs claimed compliance "if heat-treated," but the parts were never heat-treated. Tom uses this as the lecture's climactic illustration that paperwork ≠ properties.

## Cases / figures referenced as background
Submarine and rocket fastener heat-treat.case_name: Submarine and rocket fastener heat-treatment recall

General Electric vacuum tube laser repai.title: SSW_S2013_02
General Electric vacuum tube laser repai.frame: Earliest commercial laser welding application. GE used a soft electron-laser pulse to make contact between failed tungsten/molybdenum wires inside a sealed glass vacuum tube, then a power pulse to weld, saving the tube without breaking the vacuum.

Avco Everett laser welder demonstrations.title: SSW_S2013_02
Avco Everett laser welder demonstrations.frame: AVCO Everett Research Labs developed 25-kilowatt lasers under government contract for heavy-steel laser welding. Tom's student worked there; his main job was making sure the laser worked for customer demos, because 90% of the time it didn't.
Avco Everett laser welder demonstrations.case_name: AVCO Everett 25 kW laser welder demonstrations

US Navy particle beam weapons welding re.title: SSW_S2013_02
US Navy particle beam weapons welding re.frame: Navy spent a quarter billion dollars on proton-beam anti-missile weapons through the mid-80s to early 90s. After the Cold War ended, the program looked for applications. Tom was invited to a workshop to assess welding nuclear submarines with the 5-megawatt beams; he pointed out you only need tens of kilowatts. He got a mid-90s research project to evaluate the technology for welding and heat treatment.

Soviet underwater welding program at Pat.title: SSW_S2013_02
Soviet underwater welding program at Pat.frame: B. E. Paton Sr. weld-repaired Soviet tanks during WWII; his son took over the institute named after him. As one of seven members of the Soviet Academy of Sciences and head of the Ukrainian branch, Paton directed disproportionate national research funding to his 10,000-person institute. Tom: "Corruption at its best." Used as background for Soviet titanium submarine welding capability.

Soviet Alpha-class titanium submarine cr.title: SSW_S2013_02
Soviet Alpha-class titanium submarine cr.frame: Soviets built titanium submarines using Paton Institute technology. Within 2–3 years, they parked them in harbor due to leaks. Tom in 1980 was asked at Navy workshops how the Soviets solved the creep-fatigue interaction problem in titanium under continuous compressive stress; answer: they didn't.
Soviet Alpha-class titanium submarine cr.case_name: Soviet Alpha-class titanium submarine creep-fatigue failure

Bullet-resistant glass installation fail.title: SSW_S2013_02
Bullet-resistant glass installation fail.frame: Show-and-tell artifact: 3 layers of glass + polycarbonate, adhesively bonded, voids forbidden. Military vehicles use ~5-inch laminate; presidential limousine also ~5 inches; rated against shaped-charge anti-tank rounds.

Residential gas pipeline explosions from.title: SSW_S2013_02
Residential gas pipeline explosions from.frame: Steel gas mains corrode after 30–40 years, leak into soil, blow up homes. Plastic replaces steel; corrosion-resistant but can fail at welded joints.
Residential gas pipeline explosions from.case_name: Buried plastic gas distribution pipe replacing steel

Fighter jet canopy ejection system.title: SSW_S2013_02
Fighter jet canopy ejection system.frame: Laser-welded aluminum tube filled with explosive; provides non-electrical percussive ejection of canopy when pilot loses electrical power. Made at a California factory; shown as physical sample.
Fighter jet canopy ejection system.case_name: Fighter jet canopy explosive ejection (laser-welded aluminum)

Asbestos fibers strength measurement.title: SSW_S2013_02
Asbestos fibers strength measurement.frame: Asbestos fibers measured at ~700,000 PSI. Used to compare claimed (untested) carbon-nanotube strengths against historically validated single-crystal fiber strengths.

ALVIN deep research submarine hull trans.title: SSW_S2013_02
ALVIN deep research submarine hull trans.frame: Only US titanium submarine ever built; built as Navy prototype program "to learn to weld titanium for bigger ships."
ALVIN deep research submarine hull trans.case_name: Deep-sea research vessel ALVIN as US titanium submarine prototype

Comfort Adams and the founding of the Am.title: SSW_S2013_02

NASA X-33 liquid hydrogen tank failure.title: MSE_F2016_06
NASA X-33 liquid hydrogen tank failure.frame: Extended teaching unit with physical artifact. $1.3 billion program, cancelled. Rapid prototyping forced substitution of 3M adhesive + Nomex honeycomb + graphite tape for the originally specified 3D-woven composites. Adhesive shelf life trap: data sheet said 10 days out of refrigeration; actual strength after 10 days was 10% of new. Delaminations dropped safety factor from 2 to 1.05. Liquid hydrogen got into the pores and exploded during the Huntsville test.
NASA X-33 liquid hydrogen tank failure.case_name: NASA X-33 liquid hydrogen tank failure

Military ultra-long-range aircraft requi.title: MSE_F2016_06
Military ultra-long-range aircraft requi.frame: Air Force wanted a 25,000-mile-unrefueled aircraft because they anticipated losing all overseas air bases (Philippines, Okinawa, Diego Garcia). Tom's response: the earth's circumference is 25,000 miles, so 12,000 miles is the maximum useful range; he had just flown Dallas-Sydney on an A380 (17 hours, ~12,000 miles) to make the point.

V-22 Osprey prototype Ship 2 crash.title: MSE_F2016_06
V-22 Osprey prototype Ship 2 crash.frame: Boeing Vertol Philadelphia. Ship 2 was hovering 10–12 feet up; oscillated and flipped on its back because two control wires had been miswired (right and left reversed). Test pilot walked away. "Sort of an embarrassment."

Naval ship recuperator heat exchanger fa.title: SSW_S2013_12
Naval ship recuperator heat exchanger fa.frame: $100 million Navy program (early 1990s), Rolls-Royce-built room-sized brazed stainless steel heat exchanger for preheating destroyer/frigate combustion air. Designed for 100,000 hours; failed in two minutes. Cause: 2D finite element model assumed symmetric gas flow; asymmetric heating snapped six-inch hardened-steel tie bars. Tom served on the post-mortem team. Teaching point: "wishful thinking is not good engineering."
Naval ship recuperator heat exchanger fa.case_name: Naval ship recuperator heat exchanger failure

Aerospace company gold-nickel braze powd.title: SSW_S2013_12
Aerospace company gold-nickel braze powd.frame: Mid-1970s New England aerospace company. Turbine shroud honeycomb seals brazed with 82Au-18Ni alloy applied from a literal salt shaker (50-oz jars, ~$16,000/jar at $400/oz gold). Brazing supervisor doubled his requisition during a production scale-up, kept the rate after scale-down, and stole one jar/week for 16 months — $1.6M to $2.5M total. Caught by tip, not by controls. Tom hired by the insurance bonding company (not the aerospace contractor, which was on cost-plus) to audit losses. Connecticut thief got one-year sentence; New York middleman six months suspended; NYC fence walked.
Aerospace company gold-nickel braze powd.case_name: Aerospace company gold-nickel braze powder inventory control failure

Molybdenum-copper cross-field amplifier.title: SSW_S2013_12
Molybdenum-copper cross-field amplifier.frame: Brief reference back to a prior lecture's case. 82Au-18Ni braze of Mo to Cu formed Ni3Mo intermetallic, snapping at five degrees of bend. Reformulated to a low-Ni transient-liquid-phase braze (3% Ni, mostly Cu) — eliminated intermetallics, allowed 180° hairpin bend.
Molybdenum-copper cross-field amplifier.case_name: Molybdenum-copper cross-field amplifier radar waveguide braze joint

San Diego vacuum brazing furnace zinc co.title: SSW_S2013_12
San Diego vacuum brazing furnace zinc co.frame: $2M brazing furnace contaminated when wrong (Zn-bearing) braze alloy was run. Attempted recovery by raising furnace temperature to vaporize Zn out; instead redistributed Zn from hot zones to cooler water-cooled walls. Recovery attempt destroyed the furnace.
San Diego vacuum brazing furnace zinc co.case_name: San Diego vacuum brazing furnace zinc contamination disaster

Aluminum radiator field brazing developm.title: SSW_S2013_12
Aluminum radiator field brazing developm.frame: Pre-1980, automotive radiators were Cu, field-repairable by mechanics with propane torches. All-Al radiators (e.g., Corvette) required factory brazing only. Around 1980, Alcan Aluminum developed a fluoride-based field-brazable flux for Al. Result: industry-wide transition Cu → Al for radiators.

Air Force One friction welding blade-to-.case_name: Air Force One friction welding blade-to-disc program

Louisiana polymer laboratory production.title: SMS_F2013_03
Louisiana polymer laboratory production.frame: Standalone parable. GE 1950s vacuum tube laser repair.title: FW_Su2013_01
GE 1950s vacuum tube laser repair.frame: Earliest commercial laser welding application. Used to illustrate that any new heat source gets tried for welding.

Naval Surface Warfare Center particle be.title: FW_Su2013_01
Naval Surface Warfare Center particle be.frame: Post-Cold-War repurposing question — could relativistic electron beams weld submarines? Tom's answer: too much power, too much shielding, not practical. Used to illustrate the upper end of the heat-intensity scale and the limits of "just throw more energy at it."

World Trade Center collapse article.title: FW_Su2013_01
World Trade Center collapse article.frame: Tom's 2001 article (written three weeks after 9/11) used as a handout to teach flame chemistry. The teaching point: steel did not melt — it can barely be melted with oxy-acetylene in air. Bessemer's 1856 process exists *because* melting steel is hard.

MAPP gas discontinuation.title: FW_Su2013_01
MAPP gas discontinuation.frame: Live torch demonstration comparing C₃H₈ (propane) vs C₃H₄ (MAPP) — MAPP heats faster, steel reaches red heat first. Used to illustrate enthalpy-of-reaction effect on flame temperature. Side teaching: MAPP no longer manufactured (EPA closure of Chicago plant ~2011); plumbers now use propylene C₃H₆ in yellow cylinders.

Elihu Thomson invention of resistance sp.title: FW_Su2013_01
Elihu Thomson invention of resistance sp.frame: Historical origin of automotive spot welding. Thomson — MIT EE professor, one-year MIT president, GE co-founder with Edison in Lynn, MA. ~380 patents (#2 after Edison's ~400).
Elihu Thomson invention of resistance sp.case_name: Elihu Thomson and the invention of resistance spot welding

Automotive spot welding (GM and Ford vol.title: FW_Su2013_01
Automotive spot welding (GM and Ford vol.frame: 3,000 spot welds per automobile to get 2,000 good ones; nickel per weld → ~$150/car. GM ~50 billion spot welds per year. Aerospace combustor cans: ~$3/weld due to QC overhead.
Automotive spot welding (GM and Ford vol.case_name: Automotive spot welding (GM and Ford volumes)

Lawrence Livermore plutonium weld observ.title: FW_Su2013_01
Lawrence Livermore plutonium weld observ.frame: Tom shown a weld cross-section with no visible heat affected zone. Material concealed; Tom pinned them down after asking four or five times. Answer: plutonium, very low thermal conductivity. Used to illustrate that HAZ size scales with thermal conductivity.

Avco Everett 25 kW laser welder developm.title: FW_Su2013_01
Avco Everett 25 kW laser welder developm.frame: Tom's student hired in early '80s to keep the laser working when customers came for demos — 90% of the time it wasn't running. Used to illustrate that high-power laser welding was a research curiosity, not a production tool, despite the capital investment. Avco facility location: Everett, across from BNY Mellon building.
Avco Everett 25 kW laser welder developm.case_name: Avco Everett 25 kW laser welder development

Naval Research Laboratory 25 kW laser we.title: FW_Su2013_01
Naval Research Laboratory 25 kW laser we.frame: First non-classified 25 kW laser welder in the country, mid-1970s. Cited as a Navy investment that didn't pan out economically because shipyard work lacks both aerospace value-add and automotive volume.
Naval Research Laboratory 25 kW laser we.case_name: Naval Research Laboratory 25 kW laser welder

Ford catalytic converter electron beam w.title: FW_Su2013_01
Ford catalytic converter electron beam w.frame: Six out-of-vacuum EB welders at Ford sealing stainless-steel clamshell converters around ceramic filters. Speed ~60 cm/s. Used as the canonical automotive high-volume EB case. Maintenance nightmare on out-of-vacuum head (deferred to later lecture).
Ford catalytic converter electron beam w.case_name: Ford catalytic converter electron beam welding

Ford catalytic converter electron beam w.title: FW_Su2013_05
Ford catalytic converter electron beam w.frame: Ford used six Westinghouse out-of-vacuum EB machines to weld stainless steel clamshells on catalytic converters — would have needed ~200 gas tungsten arc stations for equivalent throughput. Maintenance was a nightmare (the German-trained engineer who pitched it; the Ford plant manager who would "pull out a knife" at the mention of the technology). Ford eventually abandoned.
Ford catalytic converter electron beam w.case_name: Ford out-of-vacuum electron beam catalytic converter welding

GE titanium compressor case EB porosity.title: FW_Su2013_01
GE titanium compressor case EB porosity.frame: Extended teaching case (~9 minutes, the longest narrative unit of the lecture). Two $30K titanium rings welded circumferentially in a chamber half the size of the room. Persistent porosity. Tom diagnoses: industrial-grade acetone (oil-contaminated, demonstrated via Newton's rings on a glass slide) + dust falling on the joint surface in the welding room. Fix: reagent-grade acetone. Savings: $500K/year. Tom: no credit, no payment, no letter of commendation; engineer Lyle got a letter.
GE titanium compressor case EB porosity.case_name: GE titanium compressor case EB porosity (the acetone case)

GE SWAC (Spot Welding Adaptive Control).title: FW_Su2013_01
GE SWAC (Spot Welding Adaptive Control).frame: GE Research Schenectady spent $7M over 5-6 years developing adaptive feedback control for spot welding combustor cans. Tom (with postdoc and grad student, while Tom was in Japan as ONR liaison) demonstrated the algorithm didn't start measuring until 0.2 sec into a process that completes in 0.1 sec — controlling after the fact. Tom was funded as a "whipping boy" to discipline GE Research; he received ~$40-50K against their >$1M/year.
GE SWAC (Spot Welding Adaptive Control).case_name: GE SWAC (Spot Welding Adaptive Control) failure

Bimetallic bandsaw/hacksaw blade electro.title: FW_Su2013_01
Bimetallic bandsaw/hacksaw blade electro.frame: Springfield (western Mass) firm with vacuum air feed-through EB system welding strip of high-speed steel (Mo/W tooth alloy) to spring-steel backing strip. Goes back to late '40s/'50s, among the earliest EB applications. Teaching point: niche EB application where the production-volume and value-added economics work.
Bimetallic bandsaw/hacksaw blade electro.case_name: Bimetallic bandsaw/hacksaw blade electron beam welding

Alcoa Davenport quench-and-temper failur.title: WM_Su2015_06
Alcoa Davenport quench-and-temper failur.frame: A plugged water jet on the world's largest aluminum rolling mill at Davenport produced under-quenched streaks in plate that had already been machined onto flying Boeing aircraft. Government-Alcoa-airlines partnership developed an electrical-resistivity NDT probe to find affected wings in service.
Alcoa Davenport quench-and-temper failur.case_name: Davenport Iowa Alcoa quench-line plugged-jet failure

Citicorp Tower.title: WM_Su2015_06
Citicorp Tower.frame: Used to illustrate Tom's thesis that very large failures get resolved cooperatively when senior leadership (John Reed) sets attorneys aside and authorizes at-cost repair work. Tom partially corroborated the story with Reed himself.

Bell Helicopter supplier liability case.title: WM_Su2015_06
Bell Helicopter supplier liability case.frame: Brief invocation of the Bell chief counsel's rule that you can't sue your suppliers because they'll stop supplying you. Used as a general principle, not developed.

Johnson & Johnson Tylenol recall.title: WM_Su2015_06
Johnson & Johnson Tylenol recall.frame: The credo-driven recall as a case where doing the right thing improved the business by more than the cost.

Amtrak catenary wire procurement fraud c.title: WM_Su2015_06
Amtrak catenary wire procurement fraud c.frame: A British contractor on the Amtrak Northeast Corridor electrification project tried to install a sub-spec copper wire (Rome, NY) to capture margin on a fixed-cost contract, told the federal government no other supplier existed, and was caught when the FBI walked passports off the executive team after a mediation Tom helped resolve. The Providence test track shows the inferior wire arcing on the train pass.
Amtrak catenary wire procurement fraud c.case_name: Amtrak / British Rail / Phelps Dodge copper-wire fraud

Destroyer rudder steel preheating logist.title: WM_Su2015_06
Destroyer rudder steel preheating logist.frame: Student in the class describes welding thick destroyer rudder steel where preheat made the work environment an oven.

USS Cole.title: WM_Su2015_06
USS Cole.frame: Cited as another case where the repair cost exceeded new-build cost, for strategic-signaling reasons — the US didn't want to concede the loss of a capital ship.

Naval Research Lab HY80 laser welding st.title: WM_Su2015_06
Naval Research Lab HY80 laser welding st.frame: Early-1980s NRL finding that laser welding HY-80 vaporized inclusions and gave better toughness — used to argue that ultra-clean steel resists hydrogen cracking, but isn't producible at tonnage scale.
Naval Research Lab HY80 laser welding st.case_name: Naval Research Lab HY-80 laser welding (clean-steel finding)

America's Cup yacht keel beam \u2014 434.title: WM_Su2014_12
America's Cup yacht keel beam \u2014 434.frame: Tom's consulting case with Prof. Jerry Ingram (MIT Course 13) on a David Koch–funded America's Cup yacht. Four-inch HY-80 centerboard was bending in sea trials; Tom developed a 4340 welding procedure with 600°F preheat. Used to teach the cost/weldability tradeoff in high-strength alloy steels.
America's Cup yacht keel beam \u2014 434.case_name: America's Cup yacht keel beam — 4340 steel welding procedure

USS Sea Wolf submarine high-side weld ch.title: WM_Su2014_12
USS Sea Wolf submarine high-side weld ch.frame: Sea Wolf welding wire chemistry was on the high side of every alloying-element range, producing weld metal that behaved like HY-130 rather than HY-100. Cracking resulted. Repair required 400°F preheat with welders in cooled "blue jelly suits"; $500K hull required $2B repair.
USS Sea Wolf submarine high-side weld ch.case_name: USS Sea Wolf submarine high-side weld chemistry and HY-100 cracking

Inland Steel HSLA development and Navy /.title: WM_Su2014_12
Inland Steel HSLA development and Navy /.frame: Inland Steel pioneered water-spray cooling for HSLA sheet in the early 1960s but couldn't sell it to automakers. Japanese steel mills applied the technique to shipbuilding plate (sweetheart deal with shipyards). Tom's 1980s Navy-sponsored ONR trip to Japan led to $100M of Title III funding for Lukens Steel's HSLA plate line in the 1990s.
Inland Steel HSLA development and Navy /.case_name: Inland Steel HSLA development and Navy / Japan technology transfer

Quonset Point submarine sections and Sov.title: WM_Su2014_12
Quonset Point submarine sections and Sov.frame: Submarine hull sections fabricated indoors or under tarps at Quonset Point because Soviet satellites could measure wall thickness from space, revealing classified diving depth. Used as an aside about how hull thickness encodes operational capability.
Quonset Point submarine sections and Sov.case_name: Quonset Point submarine sections and Soviet satellite reconnaissance

1920s steel bridge repair consulting (MT.title: WM_Su2014_12
1920s steel bridge repair consulting (MT.frame: Consulting work for a Boston civil engineering company on a 1920s-vintage steel structure with no ASTM spec. Tom's procedure: get drillings analyzed for composition + thickness, match against Stout & Doty's table of 200 steels, retrieve welding procedure. Used to teach that being-an-expert is sometimes just knowing where to look.
1920s steel bridge repair consulting (MT.case_name: MGH MTA station rebuild — Stout & Doty lookup case

Fire sprinkler system plastic pipe failu.title: MSE_F2017_05

Fire sprinkler system plastic pipe failu.case_name: Fire sprinkler system plastic pipe failures

Turbine blade cooling and thermal barrie.title: MSE_F2017_05
Turbine blade cooling and thermal barrie.frame: Internal air cooling above the melting point of the alloy; zirconium oxide TBCs as the only ceramic matching the CTE of nickel; $5,000-per-blade cost driven by EB vapor deposition.
Turbine blade cooling and thermal barrie.case_name: Turbine blade cooling and thermal barrier coatings

Air Force engine research committee and.title: MSE_F2017_05
Air Force engine research committee and.frame: Tom's service on an Air Force engine-research advisory committee (~2005) where the Mach 17 air-breathing strike requirement was justified by the bin Laden ordnance-reach problem. Used to teach the divergence of military and civilian engine technology, and the implausibility of the National Aerospace Plane copper-skin / liquid-hydrogen design.
Air Force engine research committee and.case_name: Air Force engine research committee and Mach 17 / National Aerospace Plane

Niobium silicide intermetallics (Air For.title: MSE_F2017_05
Niobium silicide intermetallics (Air For.frame: Higher melting point (~2000°C) but unsolved brittleness problem; Tom's dismissive close ("I'm not invested in that one right now").

Polyurethane insulation fires in homes.title: MSE_F2017_05
Polyurethane insulation fires in homes.frame: Exothermic polymerization of polyurethane sprayed too thickly (more than 2 inches) self-ignites. Demonstrated experimentally by Tom's group with cast blocks. Codes now restrict layer thickness.

Roman concrete longevity and volcanic as.title: MSE_F2017_05
Roman concrete longevity and volcanic as.frame: 2,000-year durability of Roman concrete vs. 100–200-year modern concrete, attributed to volcanic ash chemistry. Source for student papers.

Adobe construction with manure binder (M.title: MSE_F2017_05
Adobe construction with manure binder (M.frame: Past student project on traditional adobe in Mexico — straw plus manure (the manure repels flies, but the house smells for a few years).

Bessemer converter invention (1856).title: MSE_F2017_05
Bessemer converter invention (1856).frame: Henry Bessemer in 1856 develops air-blown cast-iron conversion to steel, enabling the Carnegie steel era.

Andrew Carnegie steel empire and philant.title: MSE_F2017_05
Andrew Carnegie steel empire and philant.frame: Carnegie's rise via Bessemer steel, his quote ("Take away my people, leave my factories..."), his philanthropy (Carnegie libraries, Carnegie Mellon), juxtaposed with Rockefeller [misspoken as "Roosevelt"] handing out dimes. Tom's grandfather's role at the University of Chattanooga briefly invoked.

Linz BOF development (Austria).title: MSE_F2017_05
Linz BOF development (Austria).frame: 1950s Linz, Austria — replaced air-blown Bessemer with pure-oxygen blow using Linde liquefaction. 300 tons of steel in 20 minutes vs. 24–48 hours in open hearth. By the 1970s had taken over the global industry. U.S. Steel built the last open hearth in the early 70s — "they were stupid to build that one."

U.S. Steel's last open hearth.title: MSE_F2017_05
U.S. Steel's last open hearth.frame: Built in the early 1970s when the BOF had already won; Tom's verdict: "they were stupid to build that one."

LNG tanker tail shaft fatigue failure, P.title: DP_S2012_02
LNG tanker tail shaft fatigue failure, P.frame: Illustration of an internal forging defect originating in the as-cast structure of a great-big forging blank: solidification weakness at the centerline gets carried through forging, then propagates as a fatigue crack. Ship stopped dead with a full cargo of LNG in the Philippine Sea.
LNG tanker tail shaft fatigue failure, P.case_name: LNG tanker tail shaft fatigue failure, Philippine Sea (1985)

Lou Gerstner IBM building access inciden.title: REC_F2018_02
Lou Gerstner IBM building access inciden.frame: First day as CEO, Gerstner can't get into the building (no ID); when finally inside, turns off the PowerPoint projector mid-meeting and asks executives to "just talk about your business." Tom uses this as the centerpiece of his anti-PowerPoint argument, sourced from Tufte.

IBM Customer Driven Quality MIT faculty.title: REC_F2018_02

Forging press repair weld failure.title: FW_Su2013_05
Forging press repair weld failure.frame: Centerpiece worked example for the Fourier-number argument. Welders preheated a 12-inch-thick press for 10–12 minutes instead of the ~2.5 hours required by the Fourier number; got residual stress, hydrogen embrittlement, cracking. Repeated, cracked again. Third attempt with full-penetration weld held until loaded, then cracked. Press scrapped — $5M loss, ~$50M to replace.

1985 automotive galvanized steel spot-we.title: FW_Su2013_05
1985 automotive galvanized steel spot-we.frame: Post-1972 oil embargo, automakers shifted to galvanized steel for rust warranties. Zinc alloyed with copper electrode tips, creating high-resistance interface. Ford spec demanded 2,000 welds; plants getting 100–200. Used as worked example for Fourier number (third-of-a-second weld vs. 2–3 second cycle) and then for Laplace-equation current concentration at electrode tip angle (15° vs. 45°).
1985 automotive galvanized steel spot-we.case_name: 1985 automotive galvanized steel spot-weld electrode failure

Chrysler refrigerated spot-weld electrod.title: FW_Su2013_05
Chrysler refrigerated spot-weld electrod.frame: A vendor offered Chrysler a $50M chilled-water refrigeration system to extend electrode life. Won a $55K research contract to formally demonstrate this (used a 55-gallon trash can full of ice water).

Siaki camshaft laser heat-treatment crac.title: FW_Su2013_05
Siaki camshaft laser heat-treatment crac.frame: Sciaky (Chicago, originally French, brought to U.S. ~1940 for gas tungsten arc) built a high-power laser system for automotive camshaft lobe surface hardening. Because laser energy deposits entirely on the surface, the hottest zone was the surface — leading to tensile residual stresses on cooling, surface cracks, spalling. $10M machine was garbage. Switched to electron beam (which deposits ~4 thousandths of an inch subsurface), got compressive surface stresses — the wear-favorable state — and a successful process.
Siaki camshaft laser heat-treatment crac.case_name: Sciaky camshaft laser heat-treatment cracking failure

Amorphous metals development.title: AM_F2019_03
Amorphous metals development.frame: Dave's extended case study of a 1980s materials cause célèbre. The physics (no grain boundaries → low hysteresis loss for transformers), the splat-cooling origin in Nick Grant's MIT lab in the early 1970s, the engineering breakthrough (sessile-drop ribbon casting on a cold wheel), ten years and $100 million to commercialize, and the disappointing market outcome (~$250M business, mostly Japanese, mostly high-energy-cost markets) as silicon iron incumbents improved their product.

Turbine blade cooling technology develop.title: AM_F2019_03
Turbine blade cooling technology develop.frame: Tom's $2B (1990s, now ~$6B) fuel savings for a 50°F operating temperature increase. Gas at 3,000°F running over a 2,400°F-melting-point alloy, kept solid by compressor-bled cooling air. Includes the historical attribution to Professor Schenck at MIT and Nick Grant, who developed the underlying alloy technology at Pratt Whitney in the 1960s–70s.
